conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is an invasive fungal infection (IFI)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A deep, systemic infection by fungi that invades blood and organs (unlike superficial thrush or tinea). IFIs carry high mortality and are largely diseases of the immunocompromised host.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the unifying clinical rule for suspecting an invasive fungal infection?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Suspect an IFI in any immunocompromised or critically ill patient with a fever that fails to respond to broad-spectrum antibiotics — classically persistent neutropenic fever despite 4–5 days of antibacterials, which triggers empirical antifungal therapy.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which fungal infections are classically associated with neutropenia (chemotherapy, leukaemia, BMT)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Invasive aspergillosis and invasive candidiasis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which fungal infections are associated with a low CD4 count in advanced HIV?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) at CD4 <200, and Cryptococcus at CD4 <100.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which fungal infection is classically associated with diabetic ketoacidosis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Mucormycosis (Rhizopus/Mucor) — particularly the rhino-orbito-cerebral form. Also seen in haematological malignancy and iron overload/deferoxamine use.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which patients are most at risk of candidaemia / invasive candidiasis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• ICU patients with central venous catheters
  • TPN
  • recent abdominal surgery
  • broad-spectrum antibiotics
  • and neutropenia.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does Aspergillus appear on microscopy?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Septate hyphae branching at acute (~45°) angles.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does Mucor/Rhizopus appear on microscopy, and how does this differ from Aspergillus?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Broad, ribbon-like, aseptate (non-septate) hyphae branching at wide (~90°) angles — in contrast to the thinner septate hyphae of Aspergillus that branch at acute (~45°) angles.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does Cryptococcus appear on India ink microscopy?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: An encapsulated yeast with a clear halo (the wide polysaccharide capsule) around it.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why can Pneumocystis jirovecii not be diagnosed by routine culture?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It cannot be cultured — it is detected by silver stain, immunofluorescence or PCR on induced sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the commonest invasive fungal infection acquired in hospital, and where does it originate?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Invasive candidiasis. Candida is normal gut/skin commensal flora that becomes invasive via central lines, TPN, abdominal surgery, broad-spectrum antibiotics and neutropenia.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What complications can candidaemia cause by seeding other organs?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Endophthalmitis (eyes)
  • infective endocarditis (heart valves)
  • osteomyelitis (bone) and other deep organ abscesses
— so arrange fundoscopy and an echocardiogram.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the first-line treatment for candidaemia, and what source-control step is essential?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: An echinocandin (caspofungin/anidulafungin/micafungin) is first-line (step down to fluconazole if sensitive). Remove or replace the central venous catheter and repeat blood cultures to confirm clearance.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why is Candida auris significant?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It is a multidrug-resistant Candida species and a major infection-control hazard, requiring patient isolation and strict measures to prevent hospital spread.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which patients get invasive aspergillosis, and how does it present?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Profoundly neutropenic patients (e.g. AML, allogeneic BMT). Inhaled Aspergillus fumigatus spores invade lung and blood vessels, presenting with fever, cough, pleuritic chest pain and haemoptysis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What CT chest signs suggest invasive pulmonary aspergillosis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The 'halo sign' (a nodule with surrounding ground-glass) early, then the 'air-crescent sign' as the lesion cavitates during recovery.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which serum/BAL biomarker supports a diagnosis of invasive aspergillosis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Galactomannan (an Aspergillus cell-wall antigen); β-D-glucan is also positive but is non-specific.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the first-line antifungal for invasive aspergillosis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Voriconazole (or isavuconazole); liposomal amphotericin B is an alternative.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Distinguish invasive aspergillosis, aspergilloma and ABPA.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Invasive aspergillosis = tissue-invasive disease in the immunocompromised
  • Aspergilloma = a 'fungal ball' colonising a pre-existing cavity (e.g. old TB)
  • ABPA (allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis) = a hypersensitivity reaction in asthma or cystic fibrosis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does cryptococcal meningitis present, and in whom?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: In advanced HIV (CD4 typically <100): a subacute meningitis — headache, fever and malaise over days to weeks — with raised intracranial pressure as a hallmark and often few classic meningism signs.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is cryptococcal meningitis diagnosed?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: LP showing a high opening pressure, CSF cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) and India ink showing encapsulated yeasts. Serum CrAg is a useful screening test.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the treatment of cryptococcal meningitis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Induction with liposomal amphotericin B + flucytosine, then fluconazole (consolidation/maintenance). Repeated therapeutic LPs are critical to manage raised intracranial pressure; optimise antiretroviral therapy (watching for IRIS).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the classic clinical triad of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Dry cough, exertional dyspnoea and fever — with marked desaturation on exertion and a chest that often sounds clear. CXR shows bilateral perihilar interstitial infiltrates and LDH is often raised.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the first-line treatment for PCP, and when are steroids added?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: High-dose co-trimoxazole (trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole). Add corticosteroids if the patient is hypoxic (PaO₂ <9.3 kPa or SpO₂ <92% on air).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: When is PCP prophylaxis indicated and with what?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis when CD4 <200 (or on relevant immunosuppression such as prolonged steroids/transplant).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does rhino-orbito-cerebral mucormycosis present?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Facial pain and swelling
  • nasal discharge
  • a black necrotic eschar on the palate or nasal turbinates
  • proptosis
  • ophthalmoplegia and spread to the brain
— typically in a diabetic in ketoacidosis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the management of mucormycosis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
A true emergency:
  • urgent surgical debridement
  • liposomal amphotericin B
  • reversal of the underlying state (correct DKA/hyperglycaemia).
It has a high mortality.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why is it critical to recognise mucormycosis specifically among the moulds?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Mucor does NOT respond to voriconazole or echinocandins. It requires liposomal amphotericin B (posaconazole/isavuconazole are alternatives) plus aggressive surgery — antifungals alone are insufficient.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What does a β-D-glucan test detect, and what does it miss?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It is a broad fungal marker (positive in Candida, Aspergillus and PCP) but is negative in Mucor and Cryptococcus.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the mechanism of azole antifungals and a key adverse-effect/interaction issue?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Azoles inhibit ergosterol synthesis (14-α-demethylase). They have many CYP450 drug interactions; voriconazole classically causes visual disturbances.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the mechanism of echinocandins and their main gap in coverage?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Echinocandins inhibit β-1,3-glucan (fungal cell-wall) synthesis and are first-line for candidaemia. They have no useful activity against Cryptococcus or Mucor.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the mechanism and main toxicity of amphotericin B?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It binds ergosterol in the fungal membrane, forming pores. It has the broadest spectrum (including Mucor) but is nephrotoxic with electrolyte wasting (potassium and magnesium); the liposomal formulation is less toxic.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the general management principles for invasive fungal infections?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• High index of suspicion with empirical therapy in persistent neutropenic fever
  • source control (remove infected lines, debride mucor)
  • reverse the immune defect (treat DKA, reduce steroids, optimise antiretrovirals, support neutrophil recovery)
  • target the specific organism
  • and give prophylaxis to high-risk groups.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which organism causes tetanus, and what type of organism is it?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Clostridium tetani — a Gram-positive, spore-forming anaerobe found in soil and faeces.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What toxin is responsible for tetanus?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Tetanospasmin.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the mechanism of tetanospasmin?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It travels retrograde up motor neurons to the spinal cord and blocks the release of the inhibitory neurotransmitters GABA and glycine, causing unopposed muscle contraction (rigidity and spasms).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What type of wound classically predisposes to tetanus?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A deep, dirty or puncture wound that creates anaerobic conditions for the spores to germinate.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is often the first clinical sign of tetanus?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Trismus (lockjaw).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is risus sardonicus?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A fixed, sardonic grin caused by spasm of the facial muscles in tetanus.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is opisthotonus?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A rigid, arched back due to generalised muscle spasm in tetanus.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What autonomic features occur in tetanus?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Labile blood pressure and heart rate, sweating and arrhythmias (autonomic instability).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is neonatal tetanus and how does it arise?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Tetanus in a newborn from unsterile umbilical cord care — a major cause of neonatal death in low-income settings.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is tetanus diagnosed, and what bedside test can help?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Clinically (there is no reliable lab test); the spatula test — touching the posterior pharynx provokes a reflex masseter spasm (the patient bites down) instead of a gag.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Outline the management of established tetanus.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Wound debridement
  • tetanus immunoglobulin (TIG) to neutralise unbound toxin
  • metronidazole (or benzylpenicillin)
  • benzodiazepines to control spasms (± ICU/ventilation/magnesium)
  • and the tetanus vaccine
The patient stays fully conscious throughout, so sedation and analgesia are basic care.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which antibiotic is used to treat tetanus?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Metronidazole (or penicillin) to kill Clostridium tetani.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which drug class is used to control the spasms of tetanus?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Benzodiazepines (e.g. diazepam).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why is the tetanus vaccine given even to someone who has had tetanus?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Because the disease does not confer immunity — the toxin dose that causes disease is too small to immunise.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: For a tetanus-prone wound, what does the patient's immunisation status change?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Up to date (adequately primed, last dose within 10 years) — nothing is needed, whatever the wound
  • Primed but last dose over 10 years ago — a reinforcing dose of vaccine, plus tetanus immunoglobulin if the wound is high-risk
  • Incomplete or unknown — vaccine plus tetanus immunoglobulin for any tetanus-prone wound

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What features make a wound 'tetanus-prone'?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Puncture injuries from a contaminated environment (e.g. gardening)
  • wounds containing a foreign body
  • compound fractures
  • wounds or burns with systemic sepsis
  • and certain animal bites or scratches
It becomes high-risk if there is heavy contamination with soil or manure, extensive devitalised tissue, or surgery delayed beyond 6 hours — there is no longer a ‘wound over 6 hours old’ criterion.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What type of organism causes rabies?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A Lyssavirus (a rhabdovirus).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is rabies transmitted, and what is the commonest source worldwide?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: In the saliva of an infected animal; dog bites are the commonest source worldwide. The UK has been free of rabies in land animals for over a century, but UK bats carry a closely related lyssavirus, so any bat contact here needs prompt assessment.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the prognosis of symptomatic rabies?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Almost always fatal once symptoms begin. Post-exposure treatment prevents disease in almost every case if it is started promptly and given correctly — failures are rare and usually follow delay, a severe bite close to the head, or omitted or incorrectly infiltrated immunoglobulin.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe the pathophysiology of rabies.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The virus enters via a bite, replicates locally, travels retrograde along peripheral nerves to the CNS (encephalitis), then spreads centrifugally to the salivary glands to enable onward transmission.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the histological hallmark of rabies?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Negri bodies — eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions in neurons.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the incubation period of rabies, and what shortens it?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Weeks to months; it is shorter the nearer the bite is to the head/CNS.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is a classic prodromal clue to rabies?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Paraesthesia, pain or itch at the bite site (with fever and malaise).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the features of furious (encephalitic) rabies?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Hydrophobia
  • aerophobia
  • agitation and hyperexcitability
  • hypersalivation
  • autonomic instability and fluctuating consciousness

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is hydrophobia?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Painful pharyngeal spasms provoked by attempting to drink (or by the sight of water), characteristic of furious rabies.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the features of paralytic ('dumb') rabies?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: An ascending flaccid paralysis that can mimic Guillain–Barré syndrome.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is established, symptomatic rabies treated?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: There is no treatment of proven benefit once symptoms begin. Care is supportive and palliative, with the focus on symptom control and family support; experimental intensive-care regimens have not been shown to work.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the three components of rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Immediate wound washing (soap and water for about 15 minutes ± a virucidal)
  • the rabies vaccine — four doses on days 0, 3, 7 and 21 if never immunised, or only two booster doses if previously immunised
  • and human rabies immunoglobulin, for the previously unimmunised with a highest-risk exposure
There is no time limit on starting treatment.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the first and most important step of rabies post-exposure prophylaxis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Immediate, thorough washing of the wound with soap and water for about 15 minutes.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: When is rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) given, and how is it administered?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: For previously unimmunised people with a highest-risk exposure — saliva in direct contact with broken skin or a mucous membrane — and for the severely immunosuppressed. It is infiltrated into and around the cleansed wound, not into a distant muscle, and never in the same site or syringe as the vaccine. It is not given to someone already immunised, nor once more than 7 days have passed since the first vaccine dose.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which rabies exposures are highest-risk, and how are they managed?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Saliva in direct contact with broken skin or a mucous membrane — a bite, a scratch that breaks the skin, a lick on broken skin, or direct contact with a bat. Managed with immediate wound washing plus the vaccine, adding immunoglobulin if the person has not previously been immunised. UK practice assesses the country's rabies risk, the type of contact and the patient's immunisation status together, with the local health protection team advising.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Who should receive pre-exposure rabies prophylaxis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
High-risk groups —
  • travellers to endemic areas
  • vets
  • bat handlers
  • and laboratory workers

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is toxic shock syndrome (TSS)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A rare, life-threatening, toxin-mediated illness — abrupt fever, a sunburn-like rash, hypotension and multi-organ dysfunction — driven by bacterial superantigen toxins.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which two organisms cause TSS, and their toxins?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Staphylococcus aureus (toxin TSST-1) and Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A strep) via its exotoxins.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is a superantigen and how does it act?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A toxin that cross-links MHC class II on antigen-presenting cells directly to the T-cell receptor (bypassing normal antigen processing), activating up to ~20% of all T cells at once.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which cytokines drive the shock in TSS?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: TNF-α, IL-1, IL-2 and IFN-γ — causing capillary leak and vasodilation → distributive shock and multi-organ failure.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: In what settings does STAPHYLOCOCCAL TSS occur?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Any focus of S. aureus: burns, skin and soft-tissue infection, abscess, surgical or post-partum wounds, nasal packing — and the classic menstrual (high-absorbency or retained tampon) presentation. In UK practice non-menstrual cases outnumber menstrual ones and children are a substantial share, so no tampon history does not exclude TSS.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the classic setting for STREPTOCOCCAL TSS?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• A severe soft-tissue infection / necrotising fasciitis
  • post-partum sepsis
  • or following chickenpox (varicella) in children

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do blood cultures differ between staphylococcal and streptococcal TSS?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Often negative in staphylococcal TSS (it is toxin-mediated); often positive in streptococcal TSS (bacteraemia).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which type of TSS has the higher mortality?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Streptococcal TSS — substantially higher than staphylococcal, driven by the associated necrotising soft-tissue infection and bacteraemia.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the characteristic rash of TSS?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A diffuse macular erythematous rash resembling sunburn.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What happens to the skin 1–2 weeks after the onset of TSS?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Desquamation — peeling of the skin, especially the palms and soles.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the core clinical picture of TSS?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Abrupt high fever + diffuse sunburn-like rash + hypotension + multi-organ involvement, with later desquamation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: List the multi-organ features of TSS.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• GI (vomiting, diarrhoea)
  • muscular (myalgia, raised CK)
  • mucous membranes (hyperaemia of the conjunctivae, oropharynx or vagina)
  • renal (AKI)
  • hepatic (raised bilirubin/transaminases)
  • haematological (thrombocytopenia)
  • and CNS (confusion)

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What does the case definition for STAPHYLOCOCCAL TSS require?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Fever ≥38.9°C, diffuse macular erythroderma, hypotension (systolic BP ≤90 mmHg in adults; below the 5th centile for age in children), involvement of ≥3 organ systems, and desquamation at 1–2 weeks — with no alternative explanation on culture or serology. Four of the five counts as a probable case, because desquamation is a late feature.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does the case definition for STREPTOCOCCAL TSS differ?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It requires group A streptococcus to be isolated, plus hypotension, plus two or more of: renal impairment, coagulopathy (low platelets or DIC), liver involvement, ARDS, a generalised erythematous macular rash, or soft-tissue necrosis — necrotising fasciitis or myositis, signalled by pain out of proportion to the findings (UKHSA).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which key blood abnormalities occur in TSS?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Thrombocytopenia
  • raised CK
  • acute kidney injury (raised urea/creatinine)
  • deranged LFTs
  • raised lactate
  • and features of DIC

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the first step in managing TSS?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Treat as suspected sepsis: ABCDE, oxygen if hypoxic, NEWS2 to stratify risk, blood cultures and lactate, and broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour if high risk (NICE). Give crystalloid boluses and reassess after each; the shock is distributive, so vasopressors are often needed early. Escalate to critical care and microbiology immediately, and start source control.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why is source control essential in TSS, and what does it involve?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Removing the toxin source:
  • remove the tampon/nasal packing
  • drain an abscess
  • and urgently debride necrotising fasciitis

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What antibiotic regimen is used in TSS?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Start broad — you cannot distinguish staphylococcal from streptococcal TSS clinically, so empirical cover must include both, per local policy, PLUS clindamycin for its anti-toxin effect. Add MRSA cover (a glycopeptide such as vancomycin or teicoplanin, or linezolid) if MRSA is suspected or known. Narrow once cultures return: flucloxacillin for S. aureus, benzylpenicillin for S. pyogenes — clindamycin continues alongside.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why is clindamycin specifically added in TSS?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It inhibits bacterial protein synthesis and so switches off exotoxin production, and its effect does not depend on bacterial growth phase — unlike penicillin, which paradoxically loses potency at high bacterial density (the 'Eagle effect'). That penicillin weakness is why clindamycin is added.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the role of IV immunoglobulin (IVIG) in TSS?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It contains antibodies that neutralise the superantigen exotoxins. It is an adjunct considered early — on specialist advice — in severe invasive streptococcal infection and TSS (RCOG), alongside but never instead of source control and antibiotics.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What surgical intervention is life-saving in streptococcal TSS with necrotising fasciitis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Urgent surgical debridement/exploration of the affected tissue.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: List the major complications of TSS.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Refractory shock and multi-organ failure
  • DIC
  • ARDS
  • acute kidney injury
  • death
  • and recurrence (in menstrual staphylococcal TSS)

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why can menstrual staphylococcal TSS recur?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: If tampon use continues and S. aureus is not eradicated.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Is TSS a clinical or laboratory diagnosis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A clinical (criteria-based) diagnosis — treatment must not wait for confirmation, and staphylococcal blood cultures are often negative.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What public health action follows a diagnosis of streptococcal TSS?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Invasive group A streptococcal disease is notifiable — notify the proper officer / local UKHSA health protection team on clinical suspicion, phoned within 24 hours if urgent and in writing within 3 days. All household contacts are told what symptoms to watch for; antibiotic prophylaxis is offered only to selected higher-risk contacts, on health protection team advice. Staphylococcal TSS is not notifiable.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the mucous-membrane finding in TSS?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Hyperaemia — conjunctival, oropharyngeal or vaginal. A strawberry tongue may occur, but it is more characteristic of scarlet fever and Kawasaki disease, so it does not help separate them.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Approximately what proportion of T cells do superantigens activate compared with normal antigens?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Up to around 20% of T cells, versus well under 0.1% (roughly 1 in 10,000 or fewer) for a conventional antigen.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is microbiology, and what three clinical questions does it underpin?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
The study of microorganisms and their interaction with the host. It underpins
  • diagnosis (what's the bug?)
  • treatment (what kills it?)
  • and prevention (infection control + vaccines).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the five major groups of microbes?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Bacteria (prokaryote)
  • viruses (acellular)
  • fungi (eukaryote)
  • parasites (eukaryote — protozoa/helminths)
  • and prions (misfolded protein, no nucleic acid).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Contrast bacteria and viruses by cell type and genome.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Bacteria are prokaryotes (no nucleus, peptidoglycan wall, binary fission) with circular DNA
  • viruses are acellular obligate intracellular particles (protein capsid ± envelope) with either DNA or RNA.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What defines fungi and parasites structurally?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Both are eukaryotes. Fungi have a chitin cell wall and exist as yeasts (single-celled) or moulds (hyphae); parasites are protozoa (single-celled) or helminths (worms).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is a prion?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A misfolded protein — not a true organism, containing NO nucleic acid — that causes disease by templating misfolding of normal proteins.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why is the prokaryote vs eukaryote divide central to antimicrobial therapy?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Bacteria (prokaryotes) have 70S ribosomes and a peptidoglycan wall that human (eukaryotic, 80S-ribosome) cells lack; antibiotics target these to achieve selective toxicity.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Put the microbes in order of size.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Prions < viruses (nm) < bacteria (~1–10 µm) < fungi/protozoa < helminths (mm–cm, macroscopic). Viruses need electron microscopy and pass through filters that trap bacteria.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Define commensal, pathogen, colonisation and infection.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Commensal = lives on/in us without harm (normal flora)
  • pathogen = capable of causing disease
  • colonisation = present and multiplying but NOT causing disease
  • infection = tissue damage with a host response.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is an opportunistic pathogen?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A commensal or low-virulence organism that causes disease only when host defences are down (e.g. immunosuppression, breached barriers).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why does a positive culture not always mean infection?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It may represent colonisation or contamination rather than true infection — it must be interpreted in context (symptoms, host response, inflammatory markers).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Give an example of how the same organism can be commensal or pathogen depending on site.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• E. coli is a harmless gut commensal but causes disease in the urinary tract/bloodstream
  • Staph aureus is a nasal commensal but pathogenic in a wound or on a heart valve
— site matters as much as the organism.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is virulence, and what are the main categories of virulence factor?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Virulence is the degree of pathogenicity. Factors:
  • adhesins (pili/fimbriae — attachment)
  • capsule (resists phagocytosis)
  • toxins
  • enzymes (hyaluronidase and streptokinase spread through tissue; staphylococcal coagulase clots fibrin around the organism to shield it from phagocytes)
  • immune evasion (antigenic variation, intracellular survival) and biofilms.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Contrast exotoxins and endotoxin.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Exotoxins = secreted proteins (mainly Gram-positive), specific and potent, can be made into toxoid vaccines (tetanus/diphtheria).
  • Endotoxin = lipopolysaccharide (LPS) of the Gram-negative outer membrane, released on lysis, non-specific → fever, sepsis, DIC, shock; no toxoid.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is a biofilm and why does it matter clinically?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A protective community of organisms on surfaces such as prostheses and catheters; it causes chronic, antibiotic-resistant infection and often requires device removal.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the chain of infection, and how does infection control use it?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Pathogen → reservoir → portal of exit → mode of transmission → portal of entry → susceptible host. Breaking any link prevents infection (e.g. hand hygiene breaks contact spread; isolation breaks droplet/airborne).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: State Koch's postulates and their key caveat.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• The organism is found in all cases
  • isolated and grown in pure culture
  • reproduces the disease in a healthy host
  • and is re-isolated from that host.
Caveat: they fail for uncultureable organisms, asymptomatic carriers and viruses, but remain the conceptual basis of causation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are bacteria structurally?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Single-celled prokaryotes — no nucleus, a circular DNA chromosome, 70S ribosomes and (usually) a peptidoglycan cell wall — reproducing by binary fission.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the four axes used to classify bacteria?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• The Gram stain (cell-wall structure)
  • shape (cocci vs bacilli)
  • arrangement (clusters/chains/pairs) and oxygen requirement.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Contrast Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Gram-positive = purple, THICK peptidoglycan, no endotoxin.
  • Gram-negative = pink, THIN peptidoglycan plus an outer membrane containing LPS (endotoxin → sepsis).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: List the steps of the Gram stain in order.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Crystal violet → iodine (mordant) → alcohol (decolouriser) → safranin (counterstain). Gram-positives retain the crystal violet (purple); Gram-negatives are decolourised and take the pink safranin.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Give the shape/arrangement rule for the main bacteria.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Staphylococci = cocci in clusters
  • streptococci = cocci in chains
  • diplococci = pairs (Neisseria, pneumococcus)
  • bacilli = rods
  • spirochaetes = spiral.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Populate the four-quadrant Gram/shape grid.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Gram-positive cocci = Staph/Strep/Enterococcus
  • Gram-negative cocci = Neisseria/Moraxella
  • Gram-positive rods = Clostridium/Listeria/Corynebacterium/Bacillus
  • Gram-negative rods = Enterobacterales (E. coli, Klebsiella, Salmonella), Pseudomonas, Haemophilus, Campylobacter.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Classify bacteria by oxygen requirement with examples.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Obligate aerobe (Pseudomonas, M. tuberculosis)
  • obligate anaerobe (Clostridium, Bacteroides)
  • facultative anaerobe (most Enterobacterales, Staph, Strep)
  • microaerophilic (Campylobacter, Helicobacter).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Where do anaerobes dominate, and which drug is the classic anti-anaerobe?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Abscesses, deep/necrotic tissue, and the gut/oral cavity (low-oxygen sites); metronidazole is the classic anti-anaerobe.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What does the catalase test distinguish?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Staphylococci (catalase POSITIVE) from streptococci/enterococci (catalase NEGATIVE).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What does the coagulase test distinguish?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Staph aureus (coagulase POSITIVE) from other staphylococci such as S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus (coagulase negative).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe the haemolysis patterns of streptococci.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Alpha = partial/green (S. pneumoniae, viridans)
  • beta = complete/clear (Group A S. pyogenes, Group B S. agalactiae)
  • gamma = none (Enterococcus).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Outline the lab pathway for identifying Gram-positive cocci.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Catalase (Staph positive / Strep negative) → coagulase (S. aureus positive) → then haemolysis pattern and Lancefield grouping for streptococci.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which tests identify Gram-negative rods?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Oxidase (Pseudomonas and Neisseria positive; Enterobacterales negative)
  • and lactose fermentation on MacConkey (fermenters pink — E. coli, Klebsiella; non-fermenters — Salmonella, Shigella, Pseudomonas).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which organisms don't fit the Gram stain, and how are they detected?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Mycobacteria (waxy mycolic-acid wall — acid-fast/Ziehl-Neelsen)
  • atypicals (Mycoplasma no wall, Chlamydia, Legionella — serology/PCR)
  • spirochaetes (too thin — dark-field microscopy/serology).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why do β-lactams fail against atypical organisms?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Atypicals (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella) lack a standard peptidoglycan wall or are intracellular, so wall-targeting β-lactams don't work — treat with macrolides, tetracyclines or quinolones.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which bacteria form endospores, and why does it matter?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Some Gram-positive rods — Clostridium (tetani, botulinum, perfringens), Clostridioides difficile, and Bacillus (anthracis, cereus) — form dormant spores that resist heat, chemicals, desiccation and standard disinfection, needing autoclaving (C. difficile needs soap-and-water handwashing, not just alcohol gel).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which bacteria are encapsulated, and who is at particular risk?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, H. influenzae and Klebsiella; the anti-phagocytic capsule makes them dangerous in asplenic/hyposplenic patients, who should be vaccinated.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is a virus?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: An acellular, obligate intracellular parasite — a nucleic-acid genome (DNA or RNA) inside a protein capsid, sometimes wrapped in a lipid envelope — with no cell wall, ribosomes or metabolism of its own.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why don't antibiotics work against viruses?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Viruses lack the bacterial targets antibiotics exploit (no cell wall, no 70S ribosome, no metabolism); antivirals must instead target virus-specific steps (entry, genome replication, integration, processing, release).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the master axes of viral classification?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Genome (DNA vs RNA — the key divide)
  • envelope (enveloped vs non-enveloped) and replication strategy (e.g. retroviruses, hepadnaviruses).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Contrast enveloped and non-enveloped viruses.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Enveloped = fragile lipid envelope, spread by close contact/blood/respiratory/sexual routes, easily killed by alcohol/soap (HIV, HBV/HCV, influenza, herpesviruses, SARS-CoV-2, measles).
  • Non-enveloped ('naked') = tough protein capsid, faecal-oral/environmental spread, resistant (norovirus, rotavirus, hepatitis A, HPV, adenovirus).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why does alcohol gel work well against influenza but poorly against norovirus?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Influenza is enveloped (fragile → inactivated by alcohol); norovirus is non-enveloped (tough → resistant), so soap-and-water or chlorine is needed.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Contrast DNA and RNA viruses.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• DNA viruses are more stable, usually replicate in the nucleus and proofread (less drift).
  • RNA viruses replicate in the cytoplasm, mutate rapidly (no proofreading) → antigenic drift/shift.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why is a new influenza vaccine needed yearly, with no HIV/HCV vaccine yet?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Their RNA genomes mutate rapidly (antigenic drift/shift for flu; continual variation for HIV/HCV), so immunity and vaccines are quickly evaded.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Name the main DNA virus families.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Herpesviridae
  • Hepadnaviridae
  • Papillomaviridae
  • Adenoviridae
  • Poxviridae
  • Parvoviridae.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the defining behaviour of herpesviruses?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Lifelong latency after primary infection, with reactivation when immunity falls (e.g. VZV → shingles; CMV/EBV disease in transplant/HIV).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Where do the main herpesviruses establish latency?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• HSV-1/2 in sensory ganglia
  • VZV in dorsal root ganglia
  • EBV in B cells
  • CMV in many cell types.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Explain the retrovirus replication strategy (e.g. HIV).
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Retroviruses carry reverse transcriptase, converting their RNA genome into DNA that integrates into the host genome → lifelong infection; this provides drug targets (reverse-transcriptase, integrase and protease inhibitors).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Classify the hepatitis viruses by transmission and chronicity.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Vowels A and E = faecal-oral, usually acute (A is never chronic; E can persist only in the immunosuppressed)
  • consonants B, C, D = blood-borne, can be chronic (B and C → cirrhosis/HCC; D requires HBV co- or super-infection).
Hepatitis E is severe in pregnancy.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is unusual about the hepatitis B genome?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It is a DNA virus (hepadnavirus) that replicates via an RNA intermediate using reverse transcriptase.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why is aciclovir selective for herpesviruses?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It is only activated (phosphorylated) by the viral thymidine kinase, so it is concentrated in infected cells — an example of selective toxicity.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: List the key oncogenic viruses and their cancers.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• HPV (cervical/anogenital/oropharyngeal)
  • hepatitis B and C (hepatocellular carcinoma)
  • EBV (Burkitt/other lymphomas, nasopharyngeal carcinoma)
  • HHV-8 (Kaposi's sarcoma)
  • HTLV-1 (adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which viral replication step does oseltamivir target?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Release — it is a neuraminidase inhibitor used against influenza, preventing release of new virions from infected cells.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are fungi structurally?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Eukaryotes (nucleus, organelles, 80S ribosomes) with a cell wall of chitin and β-glucans and a membrane containing ergosterol (not cholesterol); they exist as yeasts, moulds or dimorphic forms.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why is selective toxicity harder with antifungals than antibiotics?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Fungi are eukaryotes and share much cell machinery with us, so antifungals must exploit the few fungus-specific structures (ergosterol, chitin/β-glucan) and tend to be more toxic and narrower than antibiotics.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Distinguish yeasts, moulds and dimorphic fungi.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Yeasts = single budding cells (Candida, Cryptococcus)
  • moulds = filamentous hyphae (Aspergillus, dermatophytes, Mucor)
  • dimorphic = 'mould in the cold (environment), yeast in the heat (host)' (Histoplasma, Blastomyces, Coccidioides).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Contrast superficial and systemic/invasive fungal disease.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Superficial = skin/hair/nails/mucosa, often immunocompetent, mild (tinea, thrush, pityriasis versicolor).
  • Systemic/invasive = deep organs/blood/lung/CNS, usually immunocompromised, life-threatening (invasive candidiasis/aspergillosis, cryptococcal meningitis, PCP, mucormycosis).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe Candida infections.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A commensal yeast (mouth, gut, vagina, skin) that turns opportunistic: oral thrush (infants, inhaled steroids, HIV, antibiotics), vaginal thrush, intertrigo, and invasive candidiasis/candidaemia (ICU, central lines, neutropenia).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe the spectrum of Aspergillus disease.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• ABPA (hypersensitivity in asthma/CF)
  • aspergilloma (fungus ball in an old cavity such as prior TB)
  • and invasive aspergillosis (in the neutropenic — high mortality).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe Cryptococcus neoformans infection.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: An encapsulated yeast (bird droppings) causing cryptococcal meningitis in HIV/AIDS with low CD4; diagnosed with India ink (capsule halo), cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) and CSF culture.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP).
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: P. jirovecii causes an AIDS-defining pneumonia when CD4 <200: dry cough, exertional dyspnoea, hypoxia and bilateral perihilar infiltrates; treated with co-trimoxazole, with prophylaxis when CD4 <200.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: State the HIV/CD4 fungal triad.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Oral/oesophageal Candida (early)
  • Pneumocystis (PCP) below ~200
  • Cryptococcus below ~100.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe dermatophyte infections.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Moulds of keratin causing 'tinea'/ringworm (pedis, corporis, capitis, cruris, unguium); diagnosed on skin scrapings with KOH; treated with terbinafine or azoles.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is mucormycosis and who gets it?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Aggressive angioinvasive infection by Mucor/Rhizopus (rhino-orbito-cerebral) in diabetic ketoacidosis or the immunocompromised — a medical/surgical emergency.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: List the predisposing factors for fungal disease.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• HIV/low CD4
  • neutropenia/chemotherapy/transplant
  • diabetes (especially ketoacidosis)
  • broad-spectrum antibiotics
  • indwelling lines/ICU/TPN
  • and corticosteroids/immunosuppressants
— always ask 'why?'.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How are fungal infections diagnosed?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Microscopy (KOH for skin/nails, India ink for Cryptococcus)
  • culture (Sabouraud agar, slower than bacteria)
  • histology (tissue invasion)
  • and antigen tests (cryptococcal antigen, galactomannan, β-D-glucan).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Name the antifungal classes and their targets.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Azoles (inhibit ergosterol synthesis — 14α-demethylase)
  • polyenes/amphotericin B (bind ergosterol → membrane pores, nephrotoxic)
  • echinocandins (inhibit β-glucan wall synthesis)
  • terbinafine (squalene epoxidase, for dermatophytes)
  • flucytosine (fungal DNA/RNA synthesis, with amphotericin for cryptococcal meningitis).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why are antifungals generally more toxic than antibiotics?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Because fungi are eukaryotes like human cells, there are fewer unique targets — so agents such as amphotericin (nephrotoxicity) and azoles (hepatotoxicity, drug interactions) have a narrower therapeutic window.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are parasites, and how are they grouped medically?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Eukaryotic organisms that live on/in a host at its expense: protozoa (single-celled) and helminths (worms), plus ectoparasites (arthropods — lice, scabies, ticks).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What two clinical reflexes dominate parasitology?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• 'Fever in a returning traveller → think malaria'
  • and 'eosinophilia → think helminths (worms)'.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Contrast protozoa and helminths.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Protozoa are single cells that multiply in the host → acute fever/diarrhoea/systemic illness (malaria, giardia, amoeba).
  • Helminths are worms that usually don't multiply in the host → chronic disease with eosinophilia.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Outline the malaria species.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Plasmodium falciparum (most dangerous — severe/cerebral malaria)
  • vivax and ovale (relapse via dormant liver hypnozoites → need primaquine)
  • malariae and knowlesi
transmitted by the female Anopheles mosquito.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is malaria diagnosed and treated?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Thick and thin blood films (thick to detect, thin for species/parasitaemia) plus rapid antigen — send three films before excluding; treat with artemisinin combination therapy (uncomplicated) or IV artesunate (severe).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe Giardia lamblia infection.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Faecal-oral/waterborne giardiasis causing chronic, fatty, non-bloody diarrhoea with bloating and malabsorption ('backpacker's diarrhoea'); treated with metronidazole.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe Entamoeba histolytica infection.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Amoebiasis causing bloody dysentery and a liver abscess ('anchovy sauce' pus); treated with metronidazole plus a luminal agent.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe Cryptosporidium infection.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Watery diarrhoea that is severe and chronic in HIV/AIDS; an opportunistic protozoan.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe Toxoplasma gondii infection.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Acquired from cat faeces or undercooked meat; causes congenital toxoplasmosis and cerebral toxoplasmosis in HIV (ring-enhancing brain lesions).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is leishmaniasis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A sandfly-borne protozoal infection causing either a cutaneous ulcer or visceral disease (kala-azar: fever, hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Name the three helminth groups with examples.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Nematodes (roundworms — Ascaris, hookworm, Strongyloides, Enterobius/threadworm, filaria)
  • cestodes (tapeworms — Taenia, Echinococcus/hydatid)
  • trematodes (flukes — Schistosoma, liver/lung flukes).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe Enterobius (threadworm) infection.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Common in UK children
  • causes perianal itch at night
  • diagnosed with the 'sellotape test'
  • treated with mebendazole.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What does hookworm classically cause, and how is it acquired?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Iron-deficiency anaemia; acquired by walking barefoot on contaminated soil (larvae penetrate skin).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why is Strongyloides important before immunosuppression?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It can persist for years by autoinfection and cause life-threatening hyperinfection when immunosuppressed (e.g. before steroids), so at-risk patients are screened/treated.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe schistosomiasis.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Freshwater snail-derived larvae penetrate skin; S. haematobium causes haematuria and predisposes to bladder cancer (others cause GI/liver disease); treated with praziquantel.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Summarise antiparasitic treatments.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Malaria → artemisinin combinations/IV artesunate
  • protozoal diarrhoea and trichomonas → metronidazole/tinidazole
  • roundworms → -bendazoles (albendazole/mebendazole)
  • flukes and tapeworms → praziquantel
  • Strongyloides/scabies → ivermectin
  • scabies/lice → topical permethrin.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe scabies.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Infestation with the mite Sarcoptes scabiei causing intense itch (worse at night) and burrows in the finger webs/wrists; treated with topical permethrin (treat close contacts).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is a prion?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: An infectious protein that uniquely contains NO nucleic acid — a misfolded form of a normal host protein (PrP) that propagates by converting normal protein into the abnormal form (a self-templating chain reaction).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe the molecular mechanism of prion propagation.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Normal PrP^C (α-helix-rich) is converted by contact with misfolded PrP^Sc (β-sheet-rich) into more PrP^Sc — an exponential chain reaction; aggregates accumulate in neurons causing spongiform (vacuolated) change.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do prions 'replicate' differently from all other pathogens?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: By conformational conversion — changing the shape of an existing protein — not by copying a genetic code; the 'information' is in the misfolded shape itself.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why do prions resist standard sterilisation?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Routine sterilisation works mainly by denaturing protein, and the aggregated misfolded prion protein is extraordinarily stable — it resists routine autoclaving, formaldehyde, alcohol and proteases. Having no nucleic acid, it is also unaffected by irradiation. So special decontamination (extended high-temperature autoclaving, sodium hydroxide/hypochlorite) or single-use instruments are needed for high-risk procedures.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why do prion diseases trigger no immune response?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The prion is a form of 'self' protein, so there is no fever, no raised inflammatory markers and typically normal routine CSF — distinguishing them from infective/inflammatory encephalopathies.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Classify the prion diseases (transmissible spongiform encephalopathies).
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Sporadic (sporadic CJD, ~85% — spontaneous misfolding, elderly)
  • inherited (familial CJD, GSS, fatal familial insomnia — PRNP gene mutations, autosomal dominant)
  • acquired (variant CJD from BSE beef, iatrogenic CJD, kuru).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Contrast sporadic and variant CJD.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Sporadic CJD = commonest, elderly (~60s), rapid dementia with myoclonus, death in months.
  • Variant CJD = younger (20s–30s), from BSE-contaminated beef, psychiatric/behavioural and sensory onset first, longer course (~1–2 years).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the clinical signature of prion disease?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A rapidly progressive dementia (weeks–months, far faster than Alzheimer's) with myoclonus (classic), ataxia, visual/cerebellar signs, behavioural/psychiatric change and late akinetic mutism — relentless and uniformly fatal.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the MRI findings in CJD?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Cortical ribboning and basal ganglia high signal on diffusion-weighted imaging; the pulvinar sign is characteristic of variant CJD.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the classic EEG finding in sporadic CJD?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Periodic sharp-wave complexes.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What CSF tests support a diagnosis of prion disease?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Routine analysis is normal, but 14-3-3 protein is elevated and RT-QuIC (a prion-seeding assay) is increasingly the key test.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the definitive diagnosis of prion disease?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Spongiform change with PrP^Sc on brain histology (biopsy/autopsy) — rarely done ante-mortem; PRNP gene analysis identifies inherited forms.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the management of prion disease?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: There is no cure — it is uniformly fatal; management is supportive/palliative (symptom control, MDT, end-of-life care).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the key public-health/infection-control measures for prions?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: For a patient with suspected or confirmed CJD, or at increased risk, instruments used on high-risk tissue (brain, spinal cord, cranial nerves and ganglia, posterior eye, pituitary; tonsil and lymphoid tissue for variant CJD) are single-use, destroyed, or quarantined for re-use on that patient alone; plus BSE controls (removing cattle from the food chain, feed bans) that reduced variant CJD, and blood/tissue donation restrictions for at-risk individuals.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How are the clinically important viral infections grouped in this topic?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: By family: the herpesviruses (sharing lifelong latency → reactivation) and the respiratory viruses (influenza, COVID-19).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the unifying herpesvirus principle?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Primary infection → lifelong latency → reactivation when immunity drops — which is why they dominate in immunosuppression.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the two antiviral mechanisms mentioned?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Aciclovir → inhibits viral DNA polymerase
  • neuraminidase inhibitors → block viral release.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How many human herpesviruses are there, and which form the alpha group?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
8 human herpesviruses, all establishing latency:
  • HSV-1
  • HSV-2
  • VZV (the alpha group — neurotropic, treated with aciclovir)
  • EBV
  • CMV
  • HHV-6/7
  • HHV-8 (Kaposi's sarcoma).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the shared treatment principle for herpesviruses, and how does resistance arise?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The '-ciclovirs' (aciclovir, valaciclovir, ganciclovir) inhibit viral DNA polymerase; resistance arises via mutation of viral thymidine kinase or DNA polymerase.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the side effects/toxicity of aciclovir?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Crystal nephropathy → AKI (dose by weight and renal function, infuse slowly, keep well hydrated, monitor U&E) and neurotoxicity (confusion, hallucinations, lethargy, myoclonus) — both more likely in renal impairment and the elderly. Contrast: ganciclovir/valganciclovir → bone-marrow suppression (monitor FBC).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What do HSV-1 and HSV-2 typically cause, and what are the reactivation triggers?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• HSV-1 → cold sores around the mouth
  • HSV-2 → genital herpes (overlap exists — either can cause either).
Reactivation triggers:
  • stress
  • infection
  • immunocompromise
  • UV light.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the serious presentations of HSV?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Herpes simplex encephalitis (HSV-1, temporal lobe — the can't-miss: start IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg 8-hourly empirically, confirm with CSF HSV PCR, and remember a negative PCR in the first 24–48 h does not exclude it; 14-day IV course)
  • neonatal herpes (peripartum)
  • eczema herpeticum (admit, IV aciclovir)
  • herpetic keratitis (dendritic ulcer — same-day ophthalmology, no topical steroids)
  • herpetic whitlow.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the treatment of HSV?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Aciclovir (topical for mild cold sores; oral/IV for significant or systemic disease).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: VZV: how does primary infection (chickenpox) present, and when is it most infectious?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Primary = chickenpox: fever + vesicular rash in crops (lesions at different stages). Infectious from 1–2 days before the rash appears until all lesions have crusted over (about 5 days from rash onset). Contact with shingles can give a non-immune person chickenpox, but not the reverse.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: VZV: how does reactivation (shingles) present?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Painful rash in a dermatomal distribution (doesn't cross the midline).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the complications of VZV?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Post-herpetic neuralgia
  • Ramsay Hunt syndrome (facial nerve → facial palsy + ear vesicles)
  • ophthalmic zoster (V1 — Hutchinson's sign, sight-threatening)
severe in pregnancy and immunocompromise.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the treatment for VZV, and when is the shingles vaccine offered?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Shingles: oral aciclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7 days (or valaciclovir/famciclovir), ideally started within 72 h of rash onset — and still treat later if new vesicles are forming, or if immunocompromised, ophthalmic or severe. Hutchinson's sign → same-day ophthalmology. Ramsay Hunt → antiviral plus prednisolone within 72 h. The shingles vaccine (recombinant, non-live, 2 doses) is offered routinely on turning 65, with a 70–79 catch-up cohort, and to severely immunosuppressed adults from 18.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does EBV infectious mononucleosis present?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
'Kissing disease' / glandular fever:
  • fever
  • malaise
  • sore throat
  • lymphadenopathy
  • hepatosplenomegaly
  • transient macular rash.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the amoxicillin trap in EBV?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Giving amoxicillin/ampicillin in EBV causes a florid maculopapular rash — a classic SBA clue. Crucially, it is NOT a true penicillin allergy, so do not label the patient penicillin-allergic; use phenoxymethylpenicillin if a sore throat needs treating and EBV is possible.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the investigations and management of EBV mononucleosis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Investigations:
  • lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes on the film
  • commonly deranged LFTs
  • and a heterophile antibody test (Monospot) positive from the 2nd week — often falsely negative in the first week and in children under about 12, so repeat it or send EBV-specific serology (VCA IgM = acute).
Management: conservative — rest, fluids, analgesia. Avoid contact and collision sports and heavy lifting for at least 4 weeks from symptom onset (commonly 4–6 weeks, and until symptom-free) because of splenic rupture, which can occur with trivial or no trauma and presents with left upper quadrant pain, left shoulder-tip pain and shock.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What malignancies are associated with EBV?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Burkitt's lymphoma (most strongly the endemic African form)
  • nasopharyngeal carcinoma
  • Hodgkin's lymphoma
  • and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does CMV present in the immunocompetent, and what discriminates it from EBV?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Typically a mononucleosis-like illness, but Monospot-negative — the discriminator from EBV; dormant in monocytes.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the importance of CMV in the immunocompromised?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
The real importance:
  • retinitis (HIV/AIDS)
  • colitis
  • oesophagitis
  • pneumonitis
  • hepatitis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is congenital CMV, and what are its features?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
The commonest congenital viral infection. Most babies are asymptomatic at birth; symptomatic disease →
  • growth restriction
  • microcephaly
  • jaundice
  • hepatosplenomegaly
  • petechial rash
  • thrombocytopenia
  • chorioretinitis and periventricular calcification (contrast toxoplasmosis: diffuse intracranial calcification).
Sensorineural deafness is the commonest sequela and may be late-onset, so hearing is followed up. Diagnose by urine or saliva PCR within the first 21 days of life; symptomatic cases are treated with valganciclovir (monitor FBC).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the treatment of CMV?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Ganciclovir (IV) or valganciclovir (its oral prodrug) — monitor FBC for bone-marrow suppression. CMV retinitis is the classic sight-threatening presentation in advanced HIV: painless visual loss or floaters, needing same-day ophthalmology alongside antiviral treatment.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Adenovirus: which three self-limiting syndromes does it typically cause, and what happens in immunocompromise?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Normally self-limiting:
  • keratoConjunctivitis
  • respiratory tract infection (respiratory)
  • and gastroEnteritis.
In immunocompromise:
  • encephalitis
  • pneumonitis
  • enterocolitis
  • hepatitis
  • haemorrhagic cystitis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does influenza present, and who are the at-risk groups?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Presentation:
  • abrupt fever
  • coryzal symptoms
  • lethargy
  • anorexia
  • arthralgia
  • headache
  • dry cough
  • sore throat
— more systemic and abrupt than a common cold. At-risk groups:
  • the elderly
  • pregnant women
  • chronic disease and the immunocompromised.
UK vaccination is offered annually to those aged 65 and over, 18–64s in clinical risk groups, all pregnant women, care-home residents, carers, close contacts of the immunocompromised, and frontline health and social care workers; children get the live attenuated nasal spray.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the complications and diagnosis of influenza?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Complications: pneumonia — primary viral or secondary bacterial (Staph aureus, pneumococcus). Diagnosis: viral nasal/throat swab PCR.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the management of influenza?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Most cases are supportive. At-risk patients within 48 h of symptom onset: oral oseltamivir (preferred in pregnancy, children and hospitalised patients) or inhaled zanamivir — neuraminidase inhibitors that block sialic acid cleavage and prevent viral release. Beyond 48 h, still treat if hospitalised, immunosuppressed, or the influenza is severe, complicated or progressive. Annual vaccination for prevention.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the causative virus, type, and incubation of COVID-19?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: SARS-CoV-2 — a single-strand positive-sense RNA virus; incubation typically 2–7 days (classically quoted as up to 14 days for the original strain).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does COVID-19 present, and how is it diagnosed?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Presentation:
  • anosmia
  • cough
  • fever
  • myalgia
  • headache
  • fatigue
  • respiratory failure if severe.
Diagnosis: RT-PCR of upper respiratory swab; CXR = bilateral lower-zone ground-glass infiltrates.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the management of COVID-19, and what is long COVID?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Most people: supportive care at home. Non-hospitalised patients at highest risk of progression are assessed for an oral antiviral (nirmatrelvir/ritonavir, or molnupiravir) started within a few days of symptom onset — beware ritonavir drug interactions. In hospital:
  • oxygen and respiratory support (CPAP → ventilation)
  • dexamethasone if needing supplemental oxygen
  • remdesivir in selected patients
  • tocilizumab in progressive inflammatory disease
  • plus VTE prophylaxis.
Long COVID: persistent fatigue, breathlessness and cognitive symptoms weeks to months after infection.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Exam pearl: how do you distinguish EBV from CMV mononucleosis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Both cause mononucleosis, but EBV is Monospot-positive and CMV is Monospot-negative.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: UK childhood immunisation schedule: what is given at 8 weeks (2 months)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• 6-in-1 (DTaP/IPV/Hib/HepB)
  • MenB (1st)
  • rotavirus (oral, live, 1st).
No PCV — under the 1+1 schedule PCV is a single primary dose, and that is now given at 16 weeks.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: UK childhood immunisation schedule: what is given at 12 weeks (3 months)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• 6-in-1 (2nd)
  • MenB (2nd)
  • rotavirus (2nd, oral).
The 2nd MenB dose moved forward to 12 weeks and PCV moved back to 16 weeks to make room for it, because most infant MenB disease occurs before 4 months (UKHSA).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: UK childhood immunisation schedule: what is given at 16 weeks (4 months)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• 6-in-1 (3rd)
  • pneumococcal (PCV, the single primary dose).
No MenB at this visit — the 2nd MenB dose is now at 12 weeks, and the MenB booster is at 1 year (UKHSA).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: UK childhood immunisation schedule: what is given at 12 months (1 year)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• MMRV 1st dose (MMRV has replaced MMR — it adds varicella)
  • pneumococcal (PCV) booster
  • MenB booster.
Hib/MenC has been withdrawn: there is no longer any MenC dose in infancy — MenC protection comes from the adolescent MenACWY programme — and the 4th Hib dose has moved to the new 18-month appointment (UKHSA).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: UK childhood immunisation schedule: what is given at 18 months, and what at 3 years 4 months?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• 18 months (a new appointment): 6-in-1 (DTaP/IPV/Hib/HepB) 4th dose — this now provides the 4th Hib dose that Hib/MenC used to give, and completes the hepatitis B course — plus MMRV 2nd dose, brought forward from 3 years 4 months
  • 3 years 4 months: the 4-in-1 preschool booster (dTaP/IPV) ONLY — there is no MMR-containing dose at this visit any more (UKHSA).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: UK childhood immunisation schedule: what is given at 12–13 years, and what does it protect against?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: HPV vaccine (girls + boys), given as a single dose. Protects against HPV 16/18 (cervical and anal cancer) and 6/11 (genital warts).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: UK childhood immunisation schedule: what is given at 14 years?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• 3-in-1 teenage booster (Td/IPV — tetanus, low-dose diphtheria, polio; no pertussis)
  • MenACWY.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which vaccines are given in pregnancy, and with what timing?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Pertussis-containing vaccine from 16 weeks, optimally 20–32 weeks, in EVERY pregnancy — to protect the newborn from whooping cough
  • inactivated influenza in any trimester
  • and RSV vaccine from 28 weeks.
COVID-19 only if she is in a currently eligible group — pregnancy alone is no longer an indication. Other inactivated vaccines can be given when clearly indicated. All live vaccines are contraindicated (UKHSA).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which vaccines are contraindicated in pregnancy?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Live vaccines are contraindicated in pregnancy —
  • MMR
  • varicella
  • yellow fever.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Vaccines for the elderly/specific adults: what is given at 65 years, 65+, and 70 years?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• 65 years: pneumococcal, single dose
  • 65 and over: influenza annually
  • Shingles — recombinant and NON-live, 2 doses — offered routinely on turning 65, with a 70–79 catch-up cohort; because it is non-live it is also offered to severely immunosuppressed adults from 18 years
  • RSV is offered to older adults from 75 (UKHSA).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which vaccines are recommended in asplenia/splenic dysfunction?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Pneumococcal
  • Hib
  • MenACWY
  • meningococcal B
  • and annual influenza.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Live attenuated vaccines: give examples.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• MMR/MMRV
  • varicella (chickenpox)
  • rotavirus (oral)
  • yellow fever
  • BCG
  • live attenuated nasal influenza
  • oral typhoid.
The UK shingles vaccine is recombinant and non-live — NOT a live vaccine — which is why it is offered to the severely immunosuppressed.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Live attenuated vaccines: dosing, antibody response, adjuvant need, and key contraindication.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• A single dose is often sufficient (produces strong cell-mediated immunity)
  • produces IgG + IgA antibodies
  • no adjuvant needed.
May cause mild disease — DON'T give to immunocompromised or pregnant patients.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Killed/inactivated/subunit vaccines: give examples.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• IPV
  • DTaP
  • hepatitis B
  • pneumococcal
  • HPV
  • injectable influenza
  • meningococcal.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Killed/inactivated/subunit vaccines: dosing, antibody response, adjuvant need, and safety.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Multiple doses needed plus a booster
  • produce mainly systemic IgG rather than mucosal IgA
  • safe in pregnancy and in immunosuppression, though the response may be blunted in significant immunosuppression
  • usually adjuvanted to boost immunogenicity — though not always (IPV and standard inactivated influenza are not).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Vaccine mechanism: how do the diphtheria + tetanus vaccines work?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Toxoid adsorbed onto aluminium adjuvant (inactivated toxin → antibodies against the toxin, not the bacteria).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Vaccine mechanism: how does the pertussis vaccine work, and why was it changed?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Purified pertussis proteins (acellular — it replaced the whole-cell vaccine because of side effects; the number of components varies by product).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Vaccine mechanism: how do the meningococcus + Hib vaccines work?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Capsular polysaccharide conjugated to a carrier protein (T-cell-dependent response → memory).
