conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Vaccine mechanism: how does the pneumococcus (PCV13) vaccine work?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A conjugate containing polysaccharide from 13 common capsular types.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Vaccine mechanism: how does the hepatitis B vaccine work?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Recombinant viral surface antigen (HBsAg).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Vaccine mechanism: how does the MMR vaccine work, and why is it given from 12 months?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Live attenuated strains — given from 12 months because maternal IgG would neutralise it earlier.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Vaccine mechanism: how does the rotavirus vaccine work, and why is it important?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Live attenuated, oral — rotavirus is a leading cause of severe diarrhoea and hospitalisation in infants. Strict timing: the 1st dose must be given before 15 weeks of age and the course completed by 24 weeks, because of the intussusception signal. Contraindicated in severe combined immunodeficiency and after previous intussusception (UKHSA).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Exam pearl: why is MMR given at 12 months and not earlier?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Maternal IgG (transplacentally acquired) would neutralise the live vaccine if given before this; maternal IgG wanes by ~6 months.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Exam pearl: what is the rule for live vaccines in immunocompromise?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Live vaccines + immunocompromise = absolute contraindication. Live vaccines in immunocompromised patients (HIV CD4 <200, on biologics, post-stem cell transplant) → risk of vaccine-strain disease.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Exam pearl: how do conjugated vs unconjugated polysaccharide vaccines differ?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Conjugated (PCV, Hib, MenACWY) elicit a T-cell-dependent response → memory formation
  • Unconjugated are only T-independent → no memory → not effective in <2 years.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Exam pearl: why is pertussis vaccination given in pregnancy, and when is it most important?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Maternal vaccination at 16–32 weeks → antibodies passively transferred to the neonate → protects the newborn for the first few weeks before their own vaccines. Particularly important as pertussis is most dangerous in <3 month infants.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Exam pearl: what proportion of cervical cancers and genital warts do the key HPV types cause, and what does the 9-valent HPV vaccine cover?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• HPV 16 + 18 cause 70% of cervical cancers
  • HPV 6 + 11 cause 90% of genital warts.
the 9-valent HPV vaccine now covers 90%+ of cervical cancer-causing strains.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the central problem in transplant immunology?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The recipient's immune system recognises donor tissue as non-self (via HLA mismatch) → mounts a rejection response → graft damage.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is HLA, and how does the degree of mismatch relate to rejection?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• HLA (human leukocyte antigen) = the human MHC — cell-surface molecules distinguishing self from non-self
  • the more mismatched, the stronger the rejection.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which T-cells recognise MHC Class I versus Class II?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• MHC Class I (HLA-A, -B, -C) — on all nucleated cells, recognised by CD8+ T-cells
  • MHC Class II (HLA-DR, -DQ, -DP) — on APCs/B-cells, recognised by CD4+ T-cells.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which HLA loci are most important to match, and which is most significant?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: HLA-A, -B, and -DR (the '6-antigen match'); DR is the most significant.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why must ABO blood group be compatible in transplantation?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: ABO incompatibility → hyperacute rejection.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the pre-transplant crossmatch, and what does a positive result mean?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Recipient serum is tested against donor lymphocytes to detect pre-formed anti-HLA antibodies — a positive crossmatch → hyperacute rejection → contraindication.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Allorecognition: describe the direct pathway and what it drives.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Recipient T-cells recognise intact donor HLA on donor APCs → drives acute rejection (early, vigorous).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Allorecognition: describe the indirect pathway and what it drives.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Recipient APCs process donor HLA and present it → drives chronic rejection (later).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Name the four graft types and which of them are rejected.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Autograft — from the patient to themselves (skin graft, vein graft): not rejected
  • Isograft — from a genetically identical individual (identical twin): not rejected, as HLA is identical
  • Allograft — from another, genetically different human: this is almost every clinical transplant, and it needs ABO/HLA matching plus lifelong immunosuppression
  • Xenograft — from another species (porcine heart valve): severe rejection, still experimental for whole organs

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Hyperacute rejection: timing, mechanism, hypersensitivity type, and outcome.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Timing: minutes–hours
  • Mechanism: pre-formed recipient antibodies vs donor ABO/HLA → complement → thrombosis + necrosis
  • Hypersensitivity Type II
  • Outcome: irreversible → remove graft; prevented by crossmatch

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Acute rejection: timing, mechanism, hypersensitivity type, and outcome.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Timing: days–6 months
  • Mechanism: T-cell-mediated (cellular) ± antibody; HLA mismatch
  • Hypersensitivity Type IV
  • Outcome: often reversible with ↑immunosuppression

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Chronic rejection: timing, mechanism, hypersensitivity type, and outcome.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Timing: months–years
  • Mechanism: antibody + cell-mediated → fibrosis, vascular damage (graft vasculopathy)
  • Hypersensitivity: mixed
  • Outcome: largely irreversible → graft failure

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the memory hook linking the three rejection types to their mechanisms and treatability?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Hyperacute = preformed antibodies (Type II, prevented by crossmatch)
  • acute = T-cells/HLA mismatch (Type IV, treatable)
  • chronic = fibrosis (untreatable).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), and in what setting does it occur?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The opposite of rejection: in bone marrow/stem cell transplants, the donor's immune cells attack the recipient's tissues (graft attacks host, not host attacks graft).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the classic triad of GVHD targets?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Skin (rash, classically palms and soles)
  • gut (diarrhoea and abdominal pain)
  • and liver (deranged LFTs/jaundice).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is GVHD classified, managed, and prevented?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Acute (classically within 100 days) vs chronic (later, more sclerodermatous — dry eyes and mouth, skin thickening, bronchiolitis obliterans). Prevented by
  • best-possible HLA matching
  • T-cell depletion of the graft
  • and drug prophylaxis (a calcineurin inhibitor — usually ciclosporin — with or without methotrexate)
Treated with corticosteroids first-line, escalating to further immunosuppression if refractory.The transfusion equivalent, transfusion-associated GVHD, is prevented by irradiating cellular blood components.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the key contrast between solid-organ transplant and marrow transplant?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Solid-organ transplant → host rejects graft
  • marrow transplant → graft rejects host (GVHD).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the overall immunosuppression strategy for preventing rejection?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Induction (intense, peri-transplant) then maintenance (lifelong, lower-dose); usually triple therapy.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Calcineurin inhibitors: examples, mechanism, and key cautions.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Examples: tacrolimus, ciclosporin. Mechanism: block calcineurin → ↓IL-2 → ↓T-cell activation (the backbone). Cautions:
  • nephrotoxic
  • hypertension
  • narrow therapeutic index → whole-blood pre-dose trough monitoring
They are CYP3A4 substrates —
  • inhibitors (clarithromycin, azoles, diltiazem, grapefruit) raise levels → toxicity
  • inducers (rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St John's wort) lower levels → rejection
Oral tacrolimus must be prescribed and dispensed by brand name (MHRA).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Antiproliferatives: examples and mechanism.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Examples: mycophenolate, azathioprine. Mechanism: inhibit purine synthesis → ↓lymphocyte proliferation. Both cause marrow suppression — monitor FBC.
  • Mycophenolate also causes GI upset and is a major teratogen: effective contraception before, during and for 6 weeks after in women of childbearing potential, and condoms for men during and for 90 days after (MHRA)
  • Azathioprine: check TPMT before starting, and never combine with allopurinol (life-threatening myelosuppression).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Corticosteroids and mTOR inhibitors in transplant: examples and mechanism.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Corticosteroids: prednisolone — broad anti-inflammatory/immunosuppressive; adverse effects include diabetes, weight gain, hypertension, osteoporosis, cataracts, skin thinning, proximal myopathy, mood change and adrenal suppression (never stop abruptly)
  • mTOR inhibitors: sirolimus (and everolimus) — block IL-2 signalling → ↓lymphocyte proliferation; adverse effects include impaired wound healing, mouth ulcers, proteinuria, hyperlipidaemia and cytopenias. They are used as a calcineurin-inhibitor-sparing option.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Induction immunosuppression: what is it, and what is the usual UK agent?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A short, intense course of immunosuppression given around the time of transplant, when the risk of acute rejection is highest, before settling onto lower-dose lifelong maintenance. The usual UK agent is basiliximab, a monoclonal antibody that blocks the IL-2 receptor on activated T-cells (NICE).It is not continued as maintenance.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is standard maintenance immunosuppression, and how is acute rejection treated?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Standard maintenance: tacrolimus + mycophenolate + prednisolone
  • Treating acute rejection: high-dose steroids first-line ± antibody therapy.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Complications of immunosuppression — infection: which opportunistic infections occur and what prophylaxis is used?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
The timing predicts the organism.
  • Under 1 month: surgical and healthcare-associated (wound, line, hospital-acquired pneumonia, UTI, C. difficile), rarely donor-derived
  • 1–6 months: the opportunistic window — CMV, PCP, BK virus, EBV/PTLD, invasive fungal infection, reactivated TB or hepatitis B
  • Over 6 months: community-acquired infection, with late opportunistic infection if immunosuppression is heavy
Prophylaxis: co-trimoxazole for PCP for the first months; for CMV either valganciclovir prophylaxis (highest risk is a CMV-positive donor into a CMV-negative recipient) or pre-emptive therapy guided by CMV viral load (PCR).These patients have an iatrogenic T-cell deficiency.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Complications of immunosuppression — malignancy: which cancers are increased?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Skin cancer is the commonest — mainly SCC, with the usual BCC-predominant ratio reversed and tumours more numerous and aggressive: sun protection plus regular skin surveillance
  • PTLD (post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease) is EBV-driven, highest risk when an EBV-negative recipient receives an EBV-positive graft; the first management step is to reduce immunosuppression, adding rituximab and/or chemotherapy if needed
  • HPV-related anogenital and cervical cancer and HHV-8-related Kaposi's sarcoma are also increased

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the drug-specific complications of the transplant immunosuppressants?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Calcineurin inhibitors: nephrotoxicity and hypertension in both — tacrolimus additionally causes new-onset diabetes after transplantation, tremor and hyperkalaemia, while ciclosporin causes gum (gingival) hypertrophy and hirsutism
  • Azathioprine and mycophenolate: marrow suppression (check TPMT before azathioprine; mycophenolate is also a major teratogen)
  • Corticosteroids: diabetes, osteoporosis, cataracts
  • Sirolimus: impaired wound healing, mouth ulcers, proteinuria

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which general complications arise from long-term corticosteroids in transplant patients?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Diabetes and weight gain
  • hypertension and cardiovascular risk
  • osteoporosis
  • cataracts
  • skin thinning and bruising
  • proximal myopathy
  • mood change
  • and adrenal suppression — so steroids must never be stopped abruptly, and the patient needs sick-day rules.
Bone protection is considered for long-term use.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why must TPMT be checked before starting azathioprine?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Azathioprine is a prodrug converted to 6-mercaptopurine, which TPMT (thiopurine methyltransferase) inactivates. Low or absent TPMT activity means the active metabolites accumulate → profound, potentially fatal marrow suppression, so TPMT activity is measured before starting and the dose adjusted or the drug avoided.For the same reason azathioprine must not be combined with allopurinol.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is inflammation, and what does it achieve?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Inflammation is the body's protective response to injury or infection — bringing immune cells and mediators to the site to
  • destroy the cause
  • clear debris
  • and begin repair.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is a granuloma, and what are the three types?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
A focal collection of epithelioid macrophages with a cuff of lymphocytes, often with multinucleate giant cells (Langhans giant cells have peripheral horseshoe-arranged nuclei) — formed when the immune system cannot clear a stimulus and walls it off instead; a Type IV (delayed, T-cell) hypersensitivity process.
  • Caseating (central cheesy necrosis) → TB and other mycobacteria
  • Non-caseating → sarcoidosis, Crohn's, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, primary biliary cholangitis
  • Foreign-body → suture, talc, keratin, with randomly scattered giant-cell nuclei
Do not confuse a granuloma with granulation tissue (the healing tissue at the base of a wound).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the five cardinal signs of inflammation and their causes?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Redness (rubor) — ↑blood flow (vasodilation)
  • heat (calor) — ↑blood flow
  • swelling (tumor) — ↑vascular permeability → fluid leaks into tissue (exudate)
  • pain (dolor) — mediators (bradykinin, prostaglandins) sensitise nerves
  • loss of function — pain + swelling

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which local and systemic factors delay wound healing?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Local:
  • infection (commonest)
  • poor blood supply or ischaemia
  • necrotic tissue or a foreign body
  • haematoma
  • tension or repeated movement across the wound
  • previous radiotherapy
Systemic:
  • diabetes
  • smoking
  • malnutrition (protein, vitamin C, zinc)
  • obesity
  • older age
  • corticosteroids and other immunosuppressants
  • chemotherapy
  • jaundice and liver disease
  • uraemia
  • malignancy

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: The vascular response: what are the effects of vasodilation and increased vascular permeability?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Vasodilation → ↑blood flow to the area → redness + heat (mediated by histamine, prostaglandins, NO)
  • ↑Vascular permeability → endothelial cells contract → gaps form → fluid + proteins leak out (exudate) → swelling.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: The vascular response: what is stasis and why does it matter?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Stasis is slowed flow (from fluid loss + haemoconcentration) → it lets leucocytes marginate.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does an inflammatory exudate differ from a transudate?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The fluid that leaks out is protein-rich (exudate) — carrying antibodies, complement, and fibrinogen (which forms fibrin to wall off the area) → this distinguishes inflammatory exudate from a simple transudate.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: List the five steps of the cellular response (neutrophil recruitment).
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Margination (slowed flow → neutrophils move to the vessel edge)
  • rolling and adhesion (bind endothelium via selectins then integrins)
  • diapedesis/transmigration (squeeze through the vessel wall into the tissue)
  • chemotaxis (migrate toward the pathogen along a chemical gradient — C5a and IL-8 are the two chemotaxins to know, plus bacterial peptides)
  • phagocytosis (engulf and destroy, aided by opsonisation)

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which cell arrives first in acute inflammation, and which takes over later?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Neutrophils arrive first (acute inflammation), then macrophages later (clean-up + chronic); this is why the FBC shows neutrophilia in acute bacterial infection.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is opsonisation?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Coating the pathogen with antibody/complement → makes phagocytosis far more efficient ('opsonins' = 'to prepare for eating').

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Histamine: source and action (and what blocks it)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Source: mast cells
  • Action: vasodilation + ↑permeability (early) — antihistamines block it.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Prostaglandins: source and action (and what blocks them)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Source: from arachidonic acid (COX)
  • Action: vasodilation, pain, fever — NSAIDs block COX.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Leukotrienes: source and action (and what blocks them)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Source: from arachidonic acid (lipoxygenase)
  • Action: bronchoconstriction, ↑permeability — leukotriene antagonists (in asthma).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6): source and action?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Source: macrophages
  • Action: the systemic response — fever, acute-phase proteins; TNF/IL-6 = biologic drug targets.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Bradykinin and complement in inflammation: source and actions?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Bradykinin (source: plasma kinin system) → pain, vasodilation and increased permeability. Complement (source: plasma):
  • C3a and C5a are anaphylatoxins → mast cell degranulation
  • C5a is also the main neutrophil chemotaxin
  • C3b is the opsonin that coats the microbe for phagocytosis
  • C5b–9 is the membrane attack complex

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do NSAIDs and corticosteroids act on inflammation, and what are the key harms of each?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
NSAIDs block COX → ↓prostaglandins → anti-inflammatory, analgesic and antipyretic. Harms:
  • GI ulceration and bleeding (PPI cover if at risk)
  • AKI and fluid retention (avoid in renal impairment, heart failure and hypovolaemia; beware NSAID + ACE inhibitor + diuretic)
  • bronchospasm in aspirin-sensitive asthma
  • cardiovascular risk
  • avoid in the third trimester (BNF)
Steroids suppress inflammation broadly, including ↓phospholipase A₂ → ↓the whole arachidonic acid pathway (both prostaglandins and leukotrienes). Harms:
  • hyperglycaemia
  • hypertension
  • Cushingoid features
  • osteoporosis
  • gastric ulceration
  • mood change
  • cataracts
  • delayed wound healing
  • and infection risk with masking of its signs
— never stop long-term steroids abruptly (HPA suppression); increase the dose in illness and give a steroid card (BNF).Note paracetamol is antipyretic and analgesic but not anti-inflammatory.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Drug-target payoff: how do biologics act, and give examples of their use.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Biologics (anti-TNF, anti-IL-6) block specific cytokines — used in rheumatoid arthritis and IBD.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: The systemic response: how does fever arise, and what are the acute-phase proteins?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Fever: pyrogenic cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α) → hypothalamus → ↑PGE₂ → ↑temperature set point, which is why paracetamol and NSAIDs, which block prostaglandin synthesis, are antipyretic. Acute-phase proteins:
  • the liver produces CRP, fibrinogen and ferritin (IL-6-driven)
  • albumin is a negative acute-phase protein and falls.
CRP is the clinical inflammatory marker.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: The systemic response: what are leucocytosis and malaise/anorexia due to?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Leucocytosis: ↑white cell production (neutrophilia in bacterial infection)
  • Malaise/anorexia: cytokine effects.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Compare CRP and ESR: what they measure, and how fast each rises and falls.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• CRP is a liver-made acute-phase protein driven by IL-6: it rises within about 6 hours, peaks at 24–48 hours and falls fast — so it tracks the illness in near real time and is the marker for monitoring response to treatment
  • ESR measures how fast red cells settle, reflecting plasma fibrinogen and immunoglobulins: it rises over days and can stay raised for weeks after recovery — better for chronic or smouldering inflammation (giant cell arteritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, myeloma).
ESR is also raised by anaemia, pregnancy, older age and a paraprotein, so it is the less specific of the two.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: At its extreme, what does the systemic inflammatory response become?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Sepsis — life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. SIRS (deranged temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate and white cell count) is the older, non-specific concept: trauma, burns, pancreatitis and surgery all cause it without infection, so it is no longer used to define sepsis.The UK screening tool is NEWS2.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the possible outcomes of acute inflammation?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Resolution (the cause is cleared → tissue returns to normal — the ideal)
  • chronic inflammation (if unresolved → shifts to macrophages + lymphocytes → ongoing tissue damage + repair)
  • fibrosis/scarring (repair with fibrous tissue if tissue can't regenerate)
  • abscess (a localised collection of pus — dead neutrophils + debris)

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the high-yield picture of chronic inflammation, and what does it underlie?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Chronic inflammation is macrophage + lymphocyte-driven (not neutrophils), with simultaneous tissue destruction + repair (fibrosis) → it underlies TB, rheumatoid arthritis, IBD, atherosclerosis, and chronic infection → often with granuloma formation (organised macrophages — TB, sarcoid, Crohn's).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Compare wound healing by primary and by secondary intention.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Primary intention: a clean wound with apposed edges (sutured incision, clean laceration) — minimal granulation tissue, epithelium bridges within about 48 hours, fast healing, fine linear scar, low infection risk
  • Secondary intention: a wound left open (tissue loss, drained abscess cavity, contaminated or infected wound, pressure ulcer) — the defect fills from the base with granulation tissue and epithelialises inwards, healing slowly over weeks to months with wound contraction, a larger scar and higher infection risk
  • Delayed primary (tertiary) closure: leave a contaminated wound open, then close it a few days later once clean.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the phases of wound healing, and what is granulation tissue?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Haemostasis (clot) → inflammation (neutrophils then macrophages clear debris) → proliferation → remodelling. Granulation tissue is the proliferative-phase tissue — new capillaries, fibroblasts and loose collagen — the red, bumpy tissue at the base of an open wound (not to be confused with a granuloma).In remodelling, type III collagen is replaced by type I and the scar strengthens over months but never regains full tensile strength.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: When does a raised CRP NOT mean bacterial infection?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Always consider it. CRP marks inflammation from any cause — surgery, trauma, burns, myocardial infarction, VTE, pancreatitis, an autoimmune flare, malignancy — and cannot distinguish bacterial from viral. Equally, a normal CRP does not exclude infection: it takes about 6 hours to rise, and is blunted by corticosteroids, anti-IL-6 biologics and liver failure.Never rule out sepsis on a CRP — sepsis is a clinical diagnosis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the two linked ideas of this topic — define HCAIs and infection control.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: HCAIs (healthcare-associated/nosocomial infections) are acquired ≥48h after admission (not incubating on arrival); infection control is the measures that prevent them. The ≥48-hour rule is the working definition — a surgical site infection is attributed for up to 30 days after surgery, or 90 days if an implant was left in place.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the organising principle of infection control, and the single most effective intervention?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The organising principle is the chain of infection: every infection follows a predictable chain, and breaking any single link prevents transmission. The single most effective intervention is hand hygiene.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the definition threshold for a healthcare-associated infection (HCAI)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: An HCAI is acquired ≥48h after admission — the working rule. Device- and procedure-related infections have longer attribution windows: a surgical site infection counts for up to 30 days after surgery, or 90 days if an implant was left in place, and C. difficile can present after discharge yet still be healthcare-associated.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: List the six links in the chain of infection.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• 1. Infectious agent (the pathogen)
  • 2. Reservoir (where it lives)
  • 3. Portal of exit (how it leaves)
  • 4. Mode of transmission (contact/droplet/airborne/vehicle)
  • 5. Portal of entry (how it enters)
  • 6. Susceptible host (the patient at risk).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Chain of infection: how do you break the infectious agent and reservoir links?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Infectious agent (the pathogen) → antimicrobials, sterilisation
  • Reservoir (people, equipment, water) → cleaning, decontamination.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Chain of infection: how do you break the portal of exit and mode of transmission links?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Portal of exit (secretions, blood, faeces) → respiratory hygiene, cover wounds
  • Mode of transmission (contact/droplet/airborne/vehicle) → hand hygiene, PPE, isolation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Chain of infection: how do you break the portal of entry and susceptible host links?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Portal of entry (wounds, lines, mucosa) → aseptic technique, catheter care
  • Susceptible host (the patient at risk) → vaccination, treating comorbidity, nutrition.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Name the four transmission routes and give examples of each.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Contact (direct/indirect — MRSA, C. diff)
  • droplet (large particles, settle quickly — influenza, COVID, pertussis, meningococcus)
  • airborne (small particles, stay suspended — TB, measles, varicella)
  • vehicle/vector (food, water, blood).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the standard precautions applied to every patient, always?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Hand hygiene (the foundation)
  • PPE (gloves, apron, mask, eye protection as risk dictates)
  • sharps safety (never re-sheathe; dispose at the point of use into a sharps bin; the user disposes of their own sharp — and know the sharps-injury drill: bleed and wash, report to occupational health the same day, risk assess the source, HIV PEP within 72 hours if indicated)
  • respiratory hygiene ('catch it, bin it, kill it')
  • safe waste + linen disposal
  • cleaning + decontamination of equipment and environment
  • aseptic technique for invasive procedures.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the WHO '5 Moments for Hand Hygiene'?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• 1. Before touching a patient
  • 2. Before a clean/aseptic procedure
  • 3. After body-fluid exposure risk
  • 4. After touching a patient
  • 5. After touching patient surroundings.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Soap and water vs alcohol gel: what is the key distinction (the classic exam point)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Alcohol gel for most situations, BUT soap and water (not alcohol gel) for C. difficile — alcohol does not kill spores — and for norovirus, a non-enveloped virus with no lipid envelope for alcohol to disrupt. The two fail alcohol for different reasons. Also use soap and water whenever hands are visibly soiled, because alcohol gel does not remove dirt or organic matter.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What does 'bare below the elbows' refer to?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
The UK dress code that makes effective hand hygiene possible:
  • short sleeves or sleeves rolled above the elbow
  • no wristwatch
  • no rings other than a plain band
  • no bracelets
  • nails short, clean and free of polish, gel or false nails
  • cuts and abrasions covered with a waterproof dressing.
The areas most often missed are the thumbs, fingertips, between the fingers and the wrists.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Transmission-based precautions: what organisms require CONTACT precautions and what measures?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
For
  • MRSA
  • C. diff
  • VRE
  • norovirus and RSV.
Measures:
  • gloves + disposable apron (a fluid-repellent gown if there is extensive contact or splash risk)
  • single room
  • dedicated equipment.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Transmission-based precautions: what organisms require DROPLET precautions and what measures?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
For
  • influenza
  • COVID-19
  • pertussis
  • meningococcus.
Measures:
  • surgical mask
  • single room.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Transmission-based precautions: what organisms require AIRBORNE precautions and what measures?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
For
  • TB
  • measles and varicella.
Measures:
  • fit-tested FFP3 respirator plus eye protection
  • negative-pressure single room with the door closed
  • and a surgical mask on the patient if they must leave the room.
Staff should ideally be immune (measles/varicella).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which combinations of precautions apply to pulmonary TB, to chickenpox, and to C. diff?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Pulmonary/laryngeal TB = airborne + standard — TB is not spread by contact or fomites, so contact precautions are added only for a draining extrapulmonary lesion
  • Chickenpox and disseminated shingles = airborne + contact, because the vesicle fluid is infectious
  • C. diff = contact + standard.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: C. difficile as an HCAI: cause/association and key prevention.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Antibiotic-associated (the 4 Cs — clindamycin, cephalosporins, co-amoxiclav, ciprofloxacin), spore-forming, toxin-mediated. Prevention:
  • stewardship (the root cause)
  • isolate in a single room with en-suite as soon as it is suspected
  • soap-and-water hand hygiene
  • gloves + apron
  • chlorine-based environmental cleaning.
Treat with oral vancomycin first-line and fidaxomicin second-line (metronidazole is no longer first-line), and stop the causative antibiotic.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: MRSA as an HCAI: cause/association and key prevention.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Colonisation → infection; lines and wounds. Prevention:
  • contact precautions (single room, gloves + apron, dedicated equipment)
  • risk-based screening (high-risk units, elective surgical pre-assessment, previously positive patients) with a nose swab plus other sites
  • and decolonisation — nasal mupirocin plus an antiseptic body wash for 5 days, then re-screen.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: CAUTI and CLABSI: their associations and key prevention.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: CAUTI (urinary catheters): insert only for a valid documented indication; aseptic insertion, sterile closed drainage, bag below bladder level, daily meatal hygiene, review daily and remove early. No prophylactic antibiotics, no routine washouts, and do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria. CLABSI (central venous catheters): insertion bundle = maximal sterile barriers, chlorhexidine-in-alcohol prep, ultrasound, avoid the femoral site; maintenance bundle = scrub the hub, aseptic non-touch technique, intact dressing, minimise accesses, review daily and remove early.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: SSI and HAP/VAP: their associations and key prevention.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
SSI (surgery):
  • antibiotic prophylaxis within 60 minutes before incision (a single dose for most cases)
  • clippers not razors and only if hair removal is needed
  • chlorhexidine-alcohol skin prep
  • normothermia
  • glycaemic control
  • dressing left intact for 48 hours.
HAP/VAP (ventilation, aspiration):
  • head of bed 30–45°
  • daily sedation hold with assessment of readiness to extubate
  • subglottic secretion drainage
  • oral care (cross-ref respiratory).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Norovirus as an HCAI: cause/association and key prevention.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Faecal-oral, causes outbreaks (wards/cruise). Prevention:
  • soap & water
  • ward closure
  • isolation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: MRSA in focus: mechanism, screening, decolonisation, and treatment.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Staph aureus resistant to β-lactams via altered PBP2a. Screen the high-risk, not everyone (high-risk units, elective pre-op, previously positive) — nose swab plus groin/perineum and any wound or catheter urine → decolonise for 5 days (nasal mupirocin + chlorhexidine or octenidine body wash) → re-screen. Contact precautions throughout. Treat infection, not colonisation, with vancomycin/teicoplanin/linezolid.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: C. difficile in focus: pathogenesis and the '4 Cs' high-risk antibiotics.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Antibiotic use → loss of gut flora → toxin-producing C. diff overgrowth → pseudomembranous colitis. The '4 Cs' high-risk antibiotics:
  • clindamycin
  • cephalosporins
  • co-amoxiclav
  • ciprofloxacin.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: C. difficile in focus: management.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Isolate in a single room with en-suite as soon as it is suspected; soap-and-water hand hygiene, gloves + apron, chlorine-based cleaning, until 48 hours symptom-free. Oral vancomycin first-line, fidaxomicin second-line (metronidazole is no longer first-line); IV vancomycin does not work because the drug must reach the bowel lumen. Stop the offending antibiotic, and avoid loperamide and other antimotility agents — risk of toxic megacolon.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the system-level (organisational) prevention measures for HCAIs?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Care bundles (CLABSI, CAUTI, ventilator bundles)
  • mandatory HCAI surveillance reporting of MRSA and MSSA bacteraemia, C. difficile infection and Gram-negative bacteraemias (E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas aeruginosa) (UKHSA), plus hand-hygiene and bundle compliance audits
  • statutory notification of notifiable diseases to the local UKHSA health protection team on clinical suspicion, without waiting for the laboratory
  • antimicrobial stewardship and environmental cleaning
  • isolation facilities (side rooms, negative pressure)
  • staff health — hepatitis B and annual influenza vaccination, documented MMR and varicella immunity with non-immune staff excluded from measles and chickenpox cases, and staff off work until 48 hours symptom-free after diarrhoea, vomiting or fever
  • outbreak management
  • and Aseptic Non-Touch Technique (ANTT) for invasive procedures.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why is antimicrobial stewardship described as core infection control?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Antimicrobial stewardship is core infection control because it prevents C. diff and resistance.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What steps does outbreak management involve?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Recognise (two or more linked cases, or more cases than expected) → isolate or cohort affected patients and staff → convene an outbreak control team with IPC, microbiology, management and, where relevant, UKHSA → agree a case definition and keep a line list → restrict admissions, transfers and visiting, closing bays or the ward if needed → reinforce hand hygiene and PPE with enhanced/terminal cleaning using the correct agent (chlorine-based for C. diff and norovirus) → exclude affected patients and staff until 48 hours symptom-free → notify UKHSA where notifiable → declare the outbreak over and debrief.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is immunodeficiency, and what does it lead to?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A missing or defective component of the immune system → recurrent, severe, unusual, or persistent infections.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the single organising principle of immunodeficiency?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The deficient component predicts the infection pattern — work out which arm has failed, and you predict the bug.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the top-level fork of immunodeficiency, and which is commoner?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Primary (genetic/intrinsic) vs secondary (acquired) — secondary is far commoner.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the four functional arms that can fail in immunodeficiency?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Humoral (B-cell/antibody)
  • cell-mediated (T-cell)
  • phagocyte
  • and complement.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Humoral (B-cell/antibody) deficiency: characteristic infections and the clue.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Encapsulated bacteria — H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis ('SHiN'). Clue: recurrent sinopulmonary infections, after 6 months of age.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: T-cell (cell-mediated) deficiency: characteristic infections and the clue.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
'HIV-type' opportunists —
  • viruses
  • fungi (PCP/candida)
  • intracellular bacteria (TB)
  • protozoa
Clue: severe/atypical viral + fungal infections.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Phagocyte deficiency: characteristic infections and the clue.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Catalase-positive bacteria (Staph aureus) + fungi (Aspergillus). Clue: abscesses, osteomyelitis, in childhood.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Complement deficiency: characteristic infection and the clue.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Neisseria (recurrent meningococcal). Clue: recurrent meningococcaemia.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Give examples of primary vs secondary immunodeficiency.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Primary (intrinsic/genetic): the named syndromes —
  • XLA
  • DiGeorge
  • CGD
  • SCID
Secondary (acquired, far commoner):
  • HIV — the commonest cause in UK practice, with protein-energy malnutrition the commonest worldwide
  • drugs mapped to the arm they knock out — corticosteroids and calcineurin inhibitors (T-cell), rituximab (anti-CD20 → B-cell/antibody), cytotoxic chemotherapy (neutropenia → phagocyte), TNF-α inhibitors (T-cell/granuloma, so screen for TB before starting), eculizumab (terminal complement → meningococcal risk), natalizumab
  • malignancy (myeloma, leukaemia/lymphoma, CLL)
  • protein loss (nephrotic syndrome, protein-losing enteropathy)
  • malnutrition
  • asplenia/hyposplenism
  • diabetes
  • extremes of age

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: State the MHC 'Rule of 8'.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Class I (HLA-A/B/C, all nucleated cells) → CD8 + NK; CD8 × MHC I = 8
  • Class II (HLA-DQ/DR/DP, APCs + B-cells only) → CD4; CD4 × MHC II = 8.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Compare the TH1 and TH2 pathways.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• TH1 (cell-mediated): IL-12 → TH1 → IFNγ → macrophage activation → IL-1/6/8, TNFα
  • TH2 (humoral): IL-4 → TH2; IL-4 → IgE + B-cell proliferation, IL-5 → IgA + eosinophils, IL-10 → inhibits TH1.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Summarise complement function (C3a/C4a/C5a, C3b, C5a, C5b–9) and the three pathways.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• C3a/C4a/C5a = anaphylatoxins (mast cell degranulation)
  • C3b = opsonisation (splenic phagocytosis)
  • C5a = neutrophil chemotaxis
  • C5b–9 = membrane attack complex (kills Neisseria) — note C5a is a soluble anaphylatoxin and is not part of the MAC
Three activating pathways converge on C3 → C5: classical (antibody bound to antigen, IgM > IgG), lectin (mannose-binding lectin on microbial sugars) and alternative (spontaneous C3 tick-over, antibody-independent).Low C4 with normal C3 suggests classical-pathway consumption (active SLE, hereditary angioedema); low C3 with normal C4 suggests alternative-pathway consumption.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: X-Linked Agammaglobulinaemia (XLA/Bruton's): defect, presentation, and infection pattern.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• BTK mutation → absent B-cells + absent antibodies
  • presents after 6 months (as maternal IgG wanes)
  • recurrent URTI/LRTI with encapsulated organisms

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Common Variable Immune Deficiency (CVID): how does it differ from XLA, and what are its risks?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Like XLA but less severe (low rather than absent antibodies) and it affects adults. Recurrent sinopulmonary infection leading to bronchiectasis, plus granulomatous and GI/diarrhoeal disease; increased risk of autoimmune disease and lymphoma.Treated with immunoglobulin replacement.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Selective IgA Deficiency: how common is it, what infections, and what transfusion caution applies?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• The most common primary immunodeficiency
  • GI/respiratory infections (especially Giardia and Cryptosporidium)
  • often asymptomatic
There is a small risk of anaphylaxis to blood products, confined to those who have anti-IgA antibodies — routine IgA screening before transfusion is not required, but after a previous severe reaction use IgA-deficient or washed components and discuss with the transfusion laboratory.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Infection risk by antibody type: what do IgG and IgA deficiency predispose to?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• IgG deficiency → encapsulated bacteria (H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis)
  • IgA deficiency → GI/respiratory (Giardia, Cryptosporidium).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion): mechanism, features, and mnemonic.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Failure of development of the 3rd/4th pharyngeal pouches → thymic aplasia (↓T-cells) + hypoparathyroidism (↓PTH → hypocalcaemia); also cleft palate, conotruncal cardiac defects. CATCH-22:
  • Cardiac
  • Abnormal facies
  • Thymic aplasia
  • Cleft palate
  • Hypocalcaemia
  • 22q11.2
Tetany/hypocalcaemia at birth + cardiac defect → think DiGeorge.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the secondary causes of T-cell deficiency, and the infections to think of?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Secondary:
  • HIV/AIDS (destroys CD4+ — the commonest acquired T-cell deficiency)
  • natalizumab (blocks T-cell extravasation)
  • cytotoxics
Infections (think HIV):
  • bacteria (Mycoplasma, TB, Salmonella, Listeria)
  • viruses (herpesviruses — VZV, HSV, CMV, HHV8, EBV; HPV)
  • fungi (Candida, Pneumocystis jirovecii/PCP, Histoplasma)
  • protozoa (Cryptosporidium, Toxoplasma)

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD): defect, organisms, presentation, and diagnosis.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Commonly X-linked, though autosomal recessive forms occur
  • loss of NADPH oxidase → no respiratory burst → can't kill catalase-positive organisms (especially Staph aureus and Aspergillus)
  • presents before age 5 with osteomyelitis, abscesses and sepsis
Diagnosis: NBT (nitroblue tetrazolium) test fails to turn blue, or DHR flow cytometry.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Chédiak-Higashi and Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency: defects and features.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Chédiak-Higashi: lysosomal defect → dysfunctional phagocytosis + NK/CD8 dysfunction → partial albinism and peripheral neuropathy, with giant granules in neutrophils on the blood film as the exam handle; pancytopenia develops in the accelerated phase
  • Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency: CD18 mutation → impaired phagocyte migration → delayed umbilical cord separation, recurrent bacterial infections without pus, and a markedly raised neutrophil count — the neutrophils are made but cannot leave the vessel.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Complement deficits: what results from a terminal (C5–C9/MAC) defect and from C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Terminal (C5–C9/MAC): recurrent Neisseria (meningococcal/gonococcal) — Neisseria have a thin cell wall and are killed mainly by direct MAC-mediated lysis, so losing the terminal pathway removes the main defence against them. Manage with
  • MenACWY and MenB vaccination
  • antibiotic prophylaxis
  • a febrile-illness plan and family screening
C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency: hereditary angioedema — recurrent non-itchy angioedema, no urticaria, often with abdominal pain, and a low C4 even between attacks. It is bradykinin-mediated, so adrenaline, antihistamines and steroids do not work — treat an acute attack with C1 esterase inhibitor concentrate or icatibant, airway first.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Complement deficits: what results from early complement (C1/C2/C4) deficiency and C3 deficiency?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Early complement (C1/C2/C4): SLE-like autoimmunity + encapsulated bacteria
  • C3 deficiency: severe recurrent bacterial infections.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: SCID (Severe Combined Immunodeficiency): defect, causes, presentation, and management.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Failure of both B and T cells — the 'bubble baby'. Causes: X-linked common gamma chain mutation (commonest), adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency. Presents in infancy —
  • failure to thrive
  • persistent diarrhoea
  • chronic candidiasis
  • severe infections
  • disseminated infection from live vaccines (BCG, rotavirus)
A paediatric emergency → stem cell transplant. Avoid all live vaccines and use irradiated, CMV-negative blood products.Newborn blood spot screening for SCID is being evaluated in England rather than offered routinely across the UK (UK NSC), so a normal newborn screen does not exclude it.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Ataxia Telangiectasia: inheritance, gene, mnemonic, and features.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Autosomal recessive, ATM gene
  • mnemonic 'AAA' — Ataxia + oculocutaneous telangiectasia (dilated capillaries, not angiomas) + Antibodies low (IgA, IgG subclasses, IgE)
  • lymphopenia
  • a raised alpha-fetoprotein is the classic supporting test
  • increased leukaemia/lymphoma
  • high radiation sensitivity

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome: inheritance, mnemonic, and features.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: X-linked; 'WATER' — Wiskott (thrombocytopenia, characteristically with small platelets, which is what separates it from ITP) + Atopy (eczema) + T-cell dysfunction + Elevated IgE/A + Recurrent pyogenic infections (IgM/G low).Eczema + thrombocytopenia + infections in a male = WAS.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Hyper-IgM Syndrome: defect and consequences.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• CD40L mutation → no class switching → IgM only (absent IgG/A/E)
  • susceptible to PCP and Cryptosporidium.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Hyper-IgE Syndrome (Job's): features and mnemonic.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Raised IgE + eosinophilia → atopy, weak bones (pathological fractures), cold Staph abscesses (no inflammatory signs). Mnemonic FATED —
  • coarse Facies
  • cold Abscesses
  • retained primary Teeth
  • raised IgE
  • Dermatological/eczema

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Asplenia/hyposplenism: what does the spleen clear, what are the causes, and what is the key risk?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The spleen clears encapsulated organisms → asplenia (post-splenectomy, sickle cell autosplenectomy, coeliac) → risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI) with encapsulated bacteria (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, N. meningitidis).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Asplenia/hyposplenism: blood film clue and management.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Blood film clue: Howell-Jolly bodies. Management:
  • vaccination — pneumococcal, Hib, MenACWY, MenB and annual influenza, given at least 2 weeks before a planned splenectomy or from about 2 weeks after an emergency one
  • antibiotic prophylaxis with phenoxymethylpenicillin (a macrolide such as erythromycin or clarithromycin if penicillin-allergic), offered lifelong after splenectomy and especially important in those at continued high risk
  • a patient alert card, a rescue antibiotic supply, travel and animal-bite advice, and prompt medical assessment of any fever — OPSI can kill within hours

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: When should immunodeficiency be suspected (the 'SPUR' mnemonic plus extras)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
SPUR:
  • Severe
  • Persistent
  • Unusual (opportunistic organisms/sites)
  • Recurrent
  • plus failure to thrive
  • family history
  • and infection from live vaccines.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which tests assess humoral immunity in an immunodeficiency workup?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Immunoglobulins (IgG/A/M) + electrophoresis assess humoral immunity
  • specific antibody responses to vaccines assess humoral function.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which tests assess T-cell/combined, complement, and phagocyte function?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Lymphocyte subsets (CD4/CD8/B/NK) → T-cell/combined
  • complement (CH50, C3, C4) → complement
  • neutrophil function (NBT/DHR) → phagocyte (CGD)

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the management principles for immunodeficiency?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Prompt treatment + prophylactic antibiotics
  • immunoglobulin replacement — intravenous (IVIg) or subcutaneous (SCIg) home therapy — for antibody deficiencies
  • vaccination, but avoid live vaccines in T-cell/combined defects
  • stem cell transplant for SCID
  • specialist immunology referral
And know the emergency: any patient on anticancer treatment with a temperature above 38°C has neutropenic sepsis until proved otherwise and needs empirical IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, without waiting for the neutrophil count (NICE).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do hypersensitivity and autoimmunity both represent the immune system attacking the wrong target?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Hypersensitivity = an excessive/inappropriate immune response
  • autoimmunity = loss of self-tolerance so the immune system attacks the host.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What classification is used for hypersensitivity reactions, and how many types are there?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The Gell and Coombs classification. The classical scheme has four types (I–IV); some texts add a fifth for receptor-stimulating or receptor-blocking antibodies (Graves', myasthenia gravis), which the four-type scheme places within Type II.If a question offers only four types, put Graves' and MG in Type II.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Type I hypersensitivity: name, mechanism, and key examples.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Immediate/allergic. Mechanism: IgE cross-links → mast cell/basophil degranulation → histamine/leukotriene. Examples:
  • anaphylaxis
  • atopy
  • asthma
  • allergic rhinitis
  • urticaria
  • angioedema

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Type II hypersensitivity: name, mechanism, and key examples.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Antibody-mediated (cytotoxic). Mechanism: IgG/IgM vs cell-surface/matrix antigen → destruction. Examples:
  • AIHA
  • Goodpasture's (collagen IV)
  • pemphigus (desmosomes)
  • pemphigoid (hemidesmosomes)

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Type III hypersensitivity: name, mechanism, and key examples.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Immune complex. Mechanism: antigen-antibody complexes deposit → inflammation. Examples:
  • SLE
  • post-strep GN
  • serum sickness
  • extrinsic allergic alveolitis
  • membranous nephropathy

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Type IV hypersensitivity: name, mechanism, and key examples.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Delayed (cell-mediated). Mechanism: T-cells (no antibody) + granuloma formation. Examples:
  • contact dermatitis
  • coeliac
  • MS
  • sarcoidosis
  • Crohn's
  • TB/Mantoux

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Type V hypersensitivity: name, mechanism, and key examples.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Receptor stimulation (a subset of II). Mechanism: antibody stimulates/blocks a receptor. Examples:
  • Graves' (TSH receptor)
  • myasthenia gravis (ACh receptor)

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the ABCD(E) mnemonic for hypersensitivity, the core split, and the timing of each type?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
ABCD(E):
  • Allergic (I)
  • antibody/B cytotoxic (II)
  • immune Complex (III)
  • Delayed (IV)
  • receptor (V)
Core split: I–III + V = antibody-mediated; IV = T-cell-mediated/delayed (no antibody). Timing:
  • Type I seconds to 30 minutes
  • Type II hours to days
  • Type III about 4–10 days (serum sickness — the Arthus reaction is the local form at 4–12 hours)
  • Type IV 48–72 hours, which is why the Mantoux and patch tests are read at 48–72 hours.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which Gell and Coombs type are Graves'/MG, coeliac/Crohn's/MS/sarcoidosis, and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Graves' and myasthenia gravis = Type V where a fifth type is used, otherwise Type II
  • Coeliac, Crohn's, MS and sarcoidosis = Type IV (T-cell-mediated)
  • Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis = Type III (immune complex).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the Type I mechanism in depth, and which look-alike reactions are NOT IgE-mediated?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Prior sensitisation leaves allergen-specific IgE bound to mast cells and basophils; on re-exposure the allergen cross-links that IgE → degranulation → histamine, tryptase, leukotrienes and prostaglandins → vasodilatation, increased permeability and bronchospasm within minutes. Examples:
  • allergic rhinitis and atopy
  • food and drug allergy
  • allergic asthma
  • urticaria/angioedema
  • anaphylaxis
Not everything that looks allergic is IgE-mediated — aspirin/NSAIDs, opioids, radiocontrast and rapid vancomycin infusion cause direct (non-IgE) mast cell activation; the picture and the emergency treatment are the same.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Anaphylaxis can be allergic or non-allergic — what is the difference, and does it change treatment?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Allergic anaphylaxis is immune-mediated, usually IgE cross-linking on mast cells. Non-allergic anaphylaxis is direct, non-IgE mast cell activation — radiocontrast, NSAIDs, opioids, some neuromuscular blockers. They are clinically indistinguishable and the emergency treatment is identical: IM adrenaline first.The older term 'anaphylactoid' is no longer used.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does anaphylaxis present, and how is it diagnosed?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Anaphylaxis = acute onset with life-threatening airway (swelling, hoarseness, stridor), breathing (wheeze, hypoxia) or circulation (hypotension, collapse) compromise, usually — but not always — with skin/mucosal changes (urticaria, angioedema). Skin changes alone, with no A/B/C compromise, are an allergic reaction, not anaphylaxis. Diagnosis is clinical: never delay IM adrenaline for a test. Serum mast cell tryptase confirms retrospectively on timed samples — as soon as feasible after treatment has started, 1–2 h after onset, and a baseline at least 24 h later; a normal tryptase does not exclude anaphylaxis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the management of anaphylaxis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
IM adrenaline 1:1000 into the anterolateral thigh is the key intervention — adult and over-12s 500 mcg (0.5 mL), 6–12 y 300 mcg, 6 months–6 y 150 mcg, under 6 months 100–150 mcg — repeated after 5 minutes if there is no improvement; stop the trigger but never delay adrenaline to do it. Lie the patient flat with the legs raised (sit up only if breathing is the dominant problem; never sit or stand them up).
  • High-flow oxygen
  • IV fluids
  • salbutamol for wheeze
Antihistamines and steroids are NOT first-line — a non-sedating oral antihistamine only after stabilisation for residual skin symptoms, and steroids are no longer routinely recommended (Resuscitation Council UK). Refractory (persisting after 2 IM doses) → senior and critical care help, IV fluids and a specialist-only IV adrenaline infusion.
  • Then observe for a biphasic reaction (2, 6 or 12 hours by severity)
  • prescribe two adrenaline auto-injectors with training
  • and refer to a specialist allergy service.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Angioedema: how do you tell histamine-mediated from bradykinin-mediated, and how does each change treatment?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Histamine-mediated angioedema comes with urticaria and itch and responds to antihistamines, with IM adrenaline if there is airway, breathing or circulatory compromise. Bradykinin-mediated angioedema has no urticaria and no itch and does not reliably respond to adrenaline, antihistamines or steroids — the two causes are ACE-inhibitor angioedema (stop the ACE inhibitor permanently, never re-challenge) and C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency (hereditary, or acquired with autoimmune/lymphoproliferative disease). Screen with a persistently low C4 plus a low C1-esterase inhibitor level. Acute attack: C1-esterase inhibitor concentrate or icatibant (a bradykinin B2-receptor antagonist). Prophylaxis: tranexamic acid, danazol or C1-esterase inhibitor.If the airway is threatened and the diagnosis is uncertain, still give IM adrenaline.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is urticaria managed?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Transient itchy wheals, each lesion lasting under 24 hours; acute under 6 weeks, chronic 6 weeks or more.
  • Remove the trigger
  • regular non-sedating (second-generation) H1 antihistamine first-line
  • if inadequate, up-dose the antihistamine up to four times the standard dose (± montelukast as an add-on)
  • then omalizumab (anti-IgE) for refractory chronic spontaneous urticaria
  • then ciclosporin under specialist care

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the core defect in autoimmunity?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Loss of self-tolerance.
  • Central tolerance deletes self-reactive T-cells in the thymus (and self-reactive B-cells in the marrow)
  • peripheral tolerance holds the escapees in check with regulatory T-cells, anergy and deletion.
Autoimmunity is both nets failing in a genetically susceptible person, usually with an environmental trigger.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the contributors to autoimmunity (genetic, infection, cancer, and demographic)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Genetic — strong HLA associations; autoimmunity clusters in families and within the same patient (e.g. type 1 diabetes with coeliac and autoimmune thyroid disease)
  • Infection (molecular mimicry) — a microbial antigen resembles a self-antigen so the response cross-reacts with host tissue: rheumatic fever after Strep pyogenes (the flagship), Guillain-Barré syndrome after Campylobacter, reactive arthritis after gut or genital infection, cold AIHA after Mycoplasma
  • Cancer (paraneoplastic) — MG ↔ thymoma, Lambert-Eaton ↔ small cell lung cancer, dermatomyositis; lymphoma → AIHA/ITP/pemphigus
  • Female preponderance in most systemic autoimmunity

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the organising fork for autoimmune diseases (organ-specific vs systemic)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Organ-specific (Hashimoto's, T1DM, MG, Graves') vs systemic/multisystem (SLE, RA, systemic sclerosis, vasculitis).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Autoantibodies by function: what are receptor antibodies (Type V) and their diseases?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Receptor antibodies (Type V):
  • Graves' (anti-TSH receptor)
  • MG (anti-ACh receptor)
  • Lambert-Eaton (anti-VGCC)

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Autoantibodies by function: what are destructive antibodies and 'marker' antibodies?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Destructive antibodies:
  • AIHA
  • ITP (also CLL/SLE)
  • SLE
  • Goodpasture's
  • pemphigus/pemphigoid
'Marker' antibodies (less directly pathogenic):
  • pernicious anaemia
  • PBC
  • PSC
  • autoimmune hepatitis
  • ANCA vasculitis — GPA (cANCA), microscopic polyangiitis & eGPA (pANCA).
Note: polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) is characteristically ANCA-NEGATIVE.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which antibodies are associated with SLE (screening and specific)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• ANA — SLE (screening), other connective tissue disease
  • Anti-dsDNA / anti-Smith — SLE (specific).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which diseases are associated with anti-CCP/rheumatoid factor, anti-TPO/anti-thyroglobulin, and anti-TSH receptor?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Anti-CCP / rheumatoid factor — rheumatoid arthritis
  • Anti-TPO / anti-thyroglobulin — Hashimoto's (+ Graves')
  • Anti-TSH receptor — Graves'.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which diseases are associated with anti-ACh receptor and anti-GBM (collagen IV)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Anti-ACh receptor — myasthenia gravis
  • Anti-GBM (collagen IV) — Goodpasture's.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which diseases are associated with cANCA (anti-PR3) and pANCA (anti-MPO)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• cANCA (anti-PR3) — GPA (Wegener's)
  • pANCA (anti-MPO) — microscopic polyangiitis and eosinophilic GPA, though pANCA is positive in only about a third of eosinophilic GPA, so a negative ANCA does not exclude it.
Polyarteritis nodosa is characteristically ANCA-negative.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which diseases are associated with anti-TTG/anti-endomysial, anti-mitochondrial (AMA), and anti-smooth muscle?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Anti-TTG / anti-endomysial — coeliac
  • Anti-mitochondrial (AMA) — PBC
  • Anti-smooth muscle — autoimmune hepatitis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which diseases are associated with anti-centromere and anti-Scl-70?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Anti-centromere / anti-Scl-70 — limited / diffuse systemic sclerosis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: HLA associations: what diseases are linked to HLA-B27 and HLA-DR3?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• B27 — ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, seronegative arthritis, IBD-associated
  • DR3 — T1DM, Hashimoto's, Graves', myasthenia gravis, SLE.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: HLA associations: what diseases are linked to HLA-DR4 and HLA-DQ2/DQ8?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• DR4 — T1DM, rheumatoid arthritis
  • DQ2/DQ8 — coeliac disease.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: HLA associations: which diseases are linked to HLA-Cw6 and HLA-DR2/DR15?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Cw6 — psoriasis
  • DR2/DR15 — multiple sclerosis (and Goodpasture's).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Exam pearl: which paraneoplastic autoimmune associations should you know?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• MG ↔ thymoma
  • Lambert-Eaton ↔ small cell lung cancer.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the mandatory first step in every febrile traveller from an endemic area?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Malaria must be excluded in EVERY febrile traveller from an endemic area — it's the one that kills fast.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the three questions that drive the differential in a febrile returning traveller?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• WHERE did they travel (geography → which diseases are endemic)
  • WHEN (incubation period)
  • WHAT exposures (water, food, sexual, insect bites, animals, healthcare).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Exposure mapping: what should a mosquito bite and fresh water make you think of?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Mosquito bite → malaria, dengue, chikungunya, Zika, yellow fever
  • Fresh water → schistosomiasis, leptospirosis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Exposure mapping: what do unpasteurised dairy/animals and contaminated food/water suggest?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Unpasteurised dairy / animals → brucellosis
  • Contaminated food/water → typhoid, hepatitis A/E, travellers' diarrhoea.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Exposure mapping: what do a tick bite, sexual contact, and caves/birds/farms suggest?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Tick bite → Rickettsia, Lyme
  • Sexual contact → HIV, hepatitis B, gonorrhoea
  • Caves/birds/farms → histoplasmosis, Q fever, avian flu.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Geography: what diseases should Sub-Saharan Africa and South/SE Asia make you think of?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Sub-Saharan Africa → malaria (falciparum), HIV, schistosomiasis, rickettsia
  • South / SE Asia → typhoid, dengue, malaria (vivax), hepatitis A/E.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Geography: what diseases should South America and the Middle East make you think of?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• South America → dengue, yellow fever, leptospirosis
  • Middle East → brucellosis, MERS.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which traveller fevers are notifiable?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Notifiable traveller fevers include
  • malaria
  • enteric fever (typhoid/paratyphoid)
  • viral haemorrhagic fever
  • measles
  • brucellosis
  • typhus
  • yellow fever
  • rabies
  • tetanus
  • and TB.
Notify the local health protection team (UKHSA) on SUSPICION — the legal duty does not wait for laboratory confirmation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the critical 'stop and isolate' step for VHF risk assessment?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Fever (or fever in the last 24 h) within 21 days of leaving a VHF area PLUS a risk exposure — contact with a case or their body fluids, basic rural conditions in a Lassa area, caves/bats/primates, tick or animal-blood contact in Crimean-Congo areas, or healthcare/laboratory work — or unexplained bleeding. Isolate immediately in a side room with PPE and contact the local health protection team (UKHSA) and the infection consultant BEFORE sending samples, so the laboratory can be warned. Malaria screening still goes ahead under those precautions — it is the commonest and fastest-killing diagnosis in this group. Notifiable.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Define pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO).
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Fever >38.3°C on several occasions
  • persisting ≥3 weeks
  • undiagnosed after appropriate investigation — 3 outpatient visits or 3 days of inpatient investigation
(the original criterion was 1 week as an inpatient).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the categories of PUO causes and their approximate proportions?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Infection (TB, endocarditis, occult abscess, EBV, CMV, HIV, typhoid)
  • malignancy (lymphoma, leukaemia, RCC, HCC)
  • non-infectious inflammatory (SLE, RA, adult-onset Still's disease, giant cell arteritis)
  • miscellaneous (drug fever, VTE/PE, thyroid disease, factitious).
In industrialised practice infection and non-infectious inflammatory disease each account for roughly a fifth to a third, malignancy around 10–15%, and up to about half remain undiagnosed — many settling spontaneously. Infection predominates in the developing world.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Outline the investigation approach to PUO.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• History (travel, sexual contacts, animal exposure, occupation, medications)
  • blood cultures (×3, different sites) + thick/thin blood films
  • FBC, CRP, LFTs, U&E, LDH, ferritin
  • serology (HIV, EBV, CMV, hepatitis, syphilis, Brucella, Leishmania)
  • CXR, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis
  • echocardiogram (endocarditis).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Incubation <1 week: which diseases should you think of?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Meningococcus
  • diphtheria
  • influenza
  • scarlet fever
  • dengue (4–7 days).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Incubation 1–2 weeks: which diseases should you think of?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Malaria
  • dengue
  • chikungunya
  • typhoid
  • measles
  • rickettsia
  • leptospirosis.
But malaria breaks the bands — falciparum can present up to about 6 months after return and vivax/ovale a year or more later, so a long interval never excludes it.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Incubation 2–3 weeks and >3 weeks: which diseases should you think of?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
2–3 weeks:
  • mumps
  • rubella
  • chickenpox
  • brucellosis (5–30 days).
>3 weeks:
  • infectious mononucleosis
  • CMV
  • viral hepatitis
  • HIV seroconversion (2–4 weeks, so it straddles the bands)
  • TB
  • amoebic liver abscess
  • schistosomiasis (Katayama)
  • visceral leishmaniasis
  • rabies (weeks–months).
Malaria breaks the bands — falciparum up to about 6 months and vivax/ovale a year or more, so a long interval never excludes it.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Malaria: which species is most common and severe, the vector, and typical symptoms?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Plasmodium falciparum is most common and severe; the vector is the Anopheles mosquito. Symptoms:
  • fever
  • sweating
  • headache
  • vomiting
  • pallor
  • jaundice
  • hepatosplenomegaly.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Malaria: investigations and treatment for severe and uncomplicated disease.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Investigation: urgent thick and thin blood films (thick = detect, thin = speciate and quantify). ONE NEGATIVE FILM DOES NOT EXCLUDE MALARIA — three negatives over three consecutive days are needed (repeat at 12–24 h, then a further 24 h). Rapid antigen tests are an adjunct, never a replacement. Severe malaria: IV artesunate first-line (IV quinine only if artesunate is not immediately available), managed in HDU/ICU with regular glucose and cautious fluids, followed by a full oral course. Admit every case of falciparum. Uncomplicated falciparum: oral artemether-lumefantrine.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Malaria: how do vivax/ovale differ from falciparum regarding relapse, and how is this managed?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Vivax/ovale have dormant liver hypnozoites → relapse → add primaquine (check G6PD first); falciparum has no hypnozoite stage (no relapse).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Dengue fever: vector, classic triad, symptom range, and treatment.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Aedes mosquito, tropical infection. Classic triad: fever + rash + bone pain ('breakbone fever'). Course: febrile phase (days 1–3), then a critical phase AS THE FEVER FALLS (days 3–7) — deterioration happens at defervescence, not at the peak. Warning signs (admit and observe):
  • abdominal pain or tenderness
  • persistent vomiting
  • mucosal bleeding
  • fluid accumulation
  • lethargy or restlessness
  • tender hepatomegaly
  • and a rising haematocrit with a rapidly falling platelet count.
Treatment: supportive with careful fluid balance — avoid aspirin and NSAIDs, use paracetamol. No antivirals.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Chikungunya: vector, incubation, defining feature, and treatment.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Aedes mosquito; incubation 1–12 days. Defining feature: severe polyarthralgia (can persist months). Fever + rash. Treatment: supportive — paracetamol first; withhold NSAIDs until dengue has been excluded, since the two co-circulate, share the same mosquito and look identical early, and NSAIDs are unsafe in dengue. NSAIDs and physiotherapy help the prolonged arthralgia once dengue is excluded.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Rickettsia (African tick typhus): features, hallmark sign, and treatment.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Non-specific:
  • fever
  • headache
  • rash (petechial/maculopapular)
  • myalgia.
Hallmark: black eschar at the bite site. Treatment: doxycycline (azithromycin if pregnant).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Enteric fever (typhoid/paratyphoid): organism, symptoms, investigation, and treatment.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Salmonella typhi/paratyphi, after South/SE Asia travel. Symptoms:
  • fever
  • headache
  • relative bradycardia
  • constipation then diarrhoea
  • dry cough
  • rose spots on the abdomen.
Investigation: blood cultures (positive in week 1). Treatment: ceftriaxone (IV) or azithromycin (oral) first-line — fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin) resistance is now high (including XDR strains), so cipro only for confirmed-sensitive isolates. Vaccine not 100% effective.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Schistosomiasis: source, features, malignancy association, and treatment.
