conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Tropical parasitic flukes from fresh water. Eosinophilia + swimmer's itch. Katayama fever (acute); chronic: hepatic fibrosis, bladder cancer (squamous cell). Urine/stool microscopy shows eggs (if <2 months: serology). Treatment: praziquantel (repeat in 2 months — only kills adults).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Leptospirosis (Weil's disease): exposure, phases, features of severe disease, and treatment.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Fresh water exposure. Biphasic illness: initial septicaemic phase (fever, headache, myalgia) then immune phase. Severe (Weil's):
  • jaundice
  • conjunctival suffusion
    •
  • renal failure
  • haemorrhage.
Treatment: doxycycline/amoxicillin (mild) or IV penicillin (severe).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Brucellosis: setting, incubation, features, investigation, and treatment.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
High prevalence in farming/animal-human contact areas or from eating unpasteurised food. Incubation 5–30 days.
  • Fever
  • weight loss
  • night sweats
  • lymphadenopathy.
Important cause of PUO. Investigation: blood cultures (gold standard) plus serology. Treatment: doxycycline for 6 weeks, combined with either rifampicin for the full 6 weeks or an aminoglycoside (gentamicin) for the first 1–2 weeks only. Notifiable.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Amoebic liver abscess: organism, route, features, investigation, and treatment.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Entamoeba histolytica (faeco-oral). Single mass usually in the right lobe — 'anchovy sauce' contents.
  • Fever
  • RUQ pain
  • hepatomegaly.
Amoebic dysentery: profuse bloody diarrhoea. Investigation: ultrasound plus serology. Treatment: oral metronidazole (tissue amoebicide), followed by a luminal amoebicide — paromomycin in the UK, as diloxanide furoate is no longer available — to clear gut carriage and prevent relapse. Drainage is reserved for a large abscess, one at risk of rupture, or failure to respond.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Tetanus: setting, risk factors, progression, diagnosis, and treatment.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Commonest where vaccine coverage is low — the vaccine is highly effective, so it is coverage rather than availability that is the issue. Risk factors: wounds contaminated with soil, manure or dirt, especially deep puncture wounds with devitalised tissue (rust itself is not the risk; the soil on the object is). Prodromal malaise + fever → trismus (lockjaw), risus sardonicus, muscle spasms, opisthotonus and dysphagia → respiratory failure. Diagnosis is clinical. Treatment: ICU admission, human tetanus immunoglobulin, wound debridement, metronidazole, and benzodiazepines (± magnesium) for spasms, in a quiet darkened environment. Tetanus does not produce immunity — vaccinate after recovery. Notifiable.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Viral haemorrhagic fever (Ebola, Lassa, Marburg): features, incubation, and the isolation imperative.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Fever + bleeding + organ failure after travel to West/Central Africa (incubation up to 21 days). The isolation imperative: isolate + urgent specialist/public-health involvement BEFORE routine bloods — don't delay. Notifiable. (Yellow fever is a related mosquito-borne VHF — vaccine-preventable.)

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which infections cause chronic disease via HPV, EBV, and HTLV-1?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• HPV (16, 18) → cervical + anal + oropharyngeal cancer
  • HPV (6, 11) → genital warts
  • EBV → nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Burkitt's lymphoma (Africa), Hodgkin's lymphoma
  • HTLV-1 → adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which infections cause chronic disease via H. pylori, schistosomiasis, and hepatitis B + C?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• H. pylori → gastric cancer + MALT lymphoma
  • Schistosomiasis → squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder
  • Hepatitis B + C → hepatocellular carcinoma.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Exam pearl: what are the severe features of malaria, and how quickly can falciparum be fatal?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Always suspect malaria in any febrile returning traveller. Falciparum can be fatal within 24–48 hours, so send urgent thick and thin films — a positive result should reach you within about 4 hours. ONE NEGATIVE FILM NEVER EXCLUDES MALARIA — three negative films over three consecutive days are required. Severe features:
  • impaired consciousness or seizures (cerebral malaria)
  • respiratory failure
  • shock
  • acidosis
  • AKI
  • hypoglycaemia
  • severe anaemia
  • bleeding/DIC
  • jaundice
  • haemoglobinuria
  • or parasitaemia >2% in a non-immune patient.
Severe malaria = IV artesunate in HDU/ICU; admit every falciparum case; malaria is notifiable.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Exam pearl: what are the distinctive analgesia and features points for dengue and typhoid?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Dengue: AVOID aspirin and NSAIDs — paracetamol only. The danger window is the critical phase as the fever settles (days 3–7), not the fever peak; warning signs are
  • abdominal pain
  • persistent vomiting
  • mucosal bleeding
  • fluid accumulation
  • lethargy
  • tender hepatomegaly
  • and a rising haematocrit with falling platelets.
Typhoid: rose spots on the abdomen in week 2 plus relative bradycardia (pulse–temperature dissociation); watch for intestinal perforation and GI haemorrhage in week 3.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Exam pearl: what clinical clues point to schistosomiasis and leptospirosis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Schistosomiasis: eosinophilia + travel to Africa/Middle East/SE Asia + water exposure; Katayama fever at 4–8 weeks post-exposure. Leptospirosis: distinctive features are conjunctival suffusion (red eyes without discharge) + jaundice + renal failure; associated with water sports/occupational exposure.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the orienting framework for grouping antibiotic classes?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Every class is grouped by where it acts; the mechanism and the side-effect/resistance logic follows from that.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which antibiotic classes act on cell wall synthesis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Penicillins
  • cephalosporins
  • carbapenems (β-lactams)
  • and glycopeptides (vancomycin — a non-β-lactam).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which antibiotics inhibit protein synthesis at the 30S ribosome, and what mnemonic helps?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Aminoglycosides and tetracyclines — remember 'buy AT 30' (A = aminoglycosides, T = tetracyclines at 30S).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which antibiotics inhibit protein synthesis at the 50S ribosome?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Macrolides
  • lincosamides (clindamycin)
  • chloramphenicol
  • and linezolid.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which antibiotics act on DNA gyrase/topoisomerase, RNA polymerase, and nucleic acid/DNA damage?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• DNA gyrase/topoisomerase — fluoroquinolones
  • RNA polymerase — rifampicin
  • Nucleic acid/DNA damage — metronidazole, nitrofurantoin.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which antibiotics act on folate synthesis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Trimethoprim + sulfamethoxazole (sequential blockade), and sulfonamides.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which antibiotics are bactericidal versus bacteriostatic, and when is bactericidal preferred?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Cidal: β-lactams, vancomycin, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, metronidazole
  • Static: macrolides, tetracyclines, clindamycin, trimethoprim.
Prefer bactericidal in serious infection / immunocompromise / endocarditis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How are Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria distinguished structurally?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Gram-positive: thick peptidoglycan, no outer lipid membrane
  • Gram-negative: thin peptidoglycan + outer lipid membrane.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Give examples of Gram-positive organisms by morphology.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Cocci: Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, Enterococcus
  • Rods: Corynebacterium, Listeria, Bacillus, Nocardia
  • Anaerobes: Clostridium, Lactobacillus, Actinomyces, Propionibacterium.
Mycobacteria are often grouped here but do NOT Gram stain reliably — their waxy mycolic-acid wall means they are identified by acid-fast (Ziehl-Neelsen) staining.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Give examples of Gram-negative and atypical organisms.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Gram-negative: Neisseria (meningitidis, gonorrhoeae), H. influenzae, E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Moraxella catarrhalis
  • Atypicals: Legionella, Chlamydia, Mycoplasma, Coxiella burnetii — Mycoplasma has no cell wall, and the others are intracellular and/or lack classical peptidoglycan, so all of them fail to respond to β-lactams.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is MRSA, by what mechanism is it resistant, and what are the treatment options?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Staph aureus resistant to beta-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems) via altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a). Treatment:
  • doxycycline
  • clindamycin
  • vancomycin
  • teicoplanin
  • linezolid.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do penicillins (beta-lactams) work, and what are their key side effects?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Inhibit cell wall synthesis by blocking transpeptidation; bactericidal. Examples: amoxicillin, flucloxacillin, piperacillin-tazobactam. Side effects:
  • allergy (from rash to anaphylaxis)
  • cholestatic jaundice/hepatitis with co-amoxiclav and with flucloxacillin — often delayed, sometimes appearing after the course has finished
  • hypokalaemia and a large sodium load with piperacillin-tazobactam
  • and the classic rash when amoxicillin is given in EBV.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do glycopeptides (vancomycin) work, and what are their key side effects?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Inhibit cell wall synthesis by a non-beta-lactam mechanism — binding D-Ala-D-Ala; Gram-positive cover only. Side effects: nephrotoxicity (monitor U&Es), ototoxicity, and the vancomycin infusion reaction (formerly "red man syndrome") — flushing and itch from rapid infusion causing histamine release. It is NOT an allergy: slow the infusion rather than labelling the patient allergic. IV vancomycin requires pre-dose (trough) level monitoring.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do aminoglycosides work, and what are their key cautions?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Inhibit protein synthesis (30S ribosome); e.g. gentamicin. Cautions:
  • contraindicated in myasthenia gravis (blocks NMJ)
  • dose by ideal body weight in obese patients.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do tetracyclines work, what are their key side effects, and what are they used for?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Inhibit protein synthesis (30S ribosome); bacteriostatic; e.g. doxycycline. Side effects: photosensitivity, oesophagitis (take upright with water), and teeth discolouration/enamel hypoplasia — avoid in pregnancy, breastfeeding and children under 12. Absorption is reduced by antacids, calcium, iron and dairy. Used for atypicals, Rickettsia, Chlamydia, Lyme disease and brucellosis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do macrolides work, and what are their key side effects?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Inhibit protein synthesis (50S ribosome — block translocation); bacteriostatic; e.g. clarithromycin, erythromycin, azithromycin. Side effects:
  • QTc prolongation and torsades
  • cholestatic jaundice
  • GI upset (erythromycin is a motilin agonist).
Clarithromycin and erythromycin are P450 inhibitors: they raise statin levels (withhold simvastatin for the duration of the course) and also raise warfarin, digoxin and colchicine levels. Azithromycin has far fewer interactions. Useful in penicillin allergy and for atypical cover.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do lincosamides (clindamycin) work, what is their main risk, and what are they used for?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Inhibit protein synthesis (50S ribosome). Main risk: C. diff infection (highest risk). Used for
  • anaerobic infections
  • dental abscesses
  • and bone/joint infections.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do fluoroquinolones work, and what are their key side effects?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Inhibit DNA gyrase/topoisomerase; bactericidal, oral with excellent bioavailability; e.g. ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin. They are RESTRICTED (MHRA) — prescribe only when other recommended antibiotics are inappropriate, and never for mild or self-limiting infection. Counsel about
  • tendinitis and tendon rupture (stop at the first tendon pain)
  • aortic aneurysm and dissection
  • peripheral neuropathy
  • and CNS/mental-health effects including a lowered seizure threshold.
Also C. diff risk, photosensitivity and QTc prolongation. Avoid in epilepsy, myasthenia gravis and pregnancy.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do folate antagonists (trimethoprim, co-trimoxazole) work, and what are they used for?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Inhibit folate synthesis (sequential blockade). Nitrofurantoin is now first-line for uncomplicated lower UTI (NICE); trimethoprim is a second choice only where local resistance is known to be low. Co-trimoxazole (trimethoprim + sulfamethoxazole) = PCP treatment/prophylaxis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the key side effects of trimethoprim and of sulfonamides?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Trimethoprim is a folate antagonist → teratogenic (1st trimester) + hyperkalaemia + raised creatinine
  • Sulfonamides → Stevens-Johnson, and haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does metronidazole work, what does it cover, and what is its classic side effect?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Bactericidal vs anaerobes + protozoa — Giardia, amoebiasis, trichomonas, bacterial vaginosis, dental and intra-abdominal/pelvic abscesses — by causing DNA damage. Note it is NO LONGER first-line for C. difficile (that is oral vancomycin). Classic side effect: disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol; also peripheral neuropathy with prolonged courses.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is nitrofurantoin used, and what are its key cautions?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Concentrated in urine → uncomplicated LOWER UTI only (it does not reach kidney tissue, so it is no use in pyelonephritis).
  • Avoid at term (neonatal haemolysis)
  • in G6PD deficiency
  • and if eGFR is below 45 — it will not concentrate in the urine and toxicity rises.
Long-term prophylaxis risks pulmonary fibrosis, hepatotoxicity and peripheral neuropathy.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the true rate of penicillin–cephalosporin cross-reactivity, and what is the rule in true anaphylaxis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Much lower than the old "10%" teaching: roughly 1–2% with cephalosporins and under 1% with carbapenems, and it is side-chain dependent rather than class-wide. Most reported "penicillin allergy" is actually intolerance (nausea, diarrhoea, a non-specific rash) — take a careful history and delabel where appropriate, because a false label leads to broader, more toxic and less effective antibiotics. In true anaphylaxis to penicillin, avoid ALL β-lactams and use a non-β-lactam (e.g. a macrolide, doxycycline, vancomycin or teicoplanin depending on the infection).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: First-line antibiotic(s) for MRSA and for Pseudomonas.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• MRSA: vancomycin, teicoplanin, linezolid, doxycycline
  • Pseudomonas: piperacillin-tazobactam, ciprofloxacin, ceftazidime, meropenem, gentamicin.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: First-line antibiotic(s) for anaerobes, atypicals, ESBL, and C. diff.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Anaerobes: metronidazole, co-amoxiclav, clindamycin
  • Atypicals (Legionella/Mycoplasma/Chlamydia): macrolides, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones (β-lactams useless — no cell wall, or intracellular)
  • ESBL: meropenem (carbapenem)
  • C. diff: oral vancomycin first-line, fidaxomicin second-line.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the atypicals reasoning step for antibiotic choice?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: β-lactams fail against atypicals for two reasons — Mycoplasma has NO cell wall at all, while Legionella, Chlamydia and Coxiella are intracellular and/or lack classical peptidoglycan, and β-lactams penetrate cells poorly. So reach for agents that get inside cells: protein-synthesis inhibitors (macrolides, tetracyclines) or a quinolone.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Resistance mechanism — altered target: what does it involve, with examples?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
A mutation in the target site:
  • RNA polymerase (rifampicin)
  • DNA gyrase (ciprofloxacin)
  • 30S ribosome (streptomycin)
  • and altered PBP in MRSA.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Resistance mechanism — enzymatic inactivation: what does it involve, and how is it overcome?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Beta-lactamase destroys the beta-lactam ring (penicillinase, ESBLs); aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes also occur. Overcome with combinations such as co-amoxiclav = amoxicillin + clavulanate (a beta-lactamase inhibitor).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Resistance mechanisms — efflux pumps and alternative target/reduced permeability: describe each.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Efflux pumps: active transport pumps the antibiotic back out of the cell (affects tetracyclines, quinolones, beta-lactams, macrolides; common in Pseudomonas). Reduced permeability: loss of outer membrane porins keeps the drug out. Biofilm on prostheses and catheters shields organisms, giving chronic, hard-to-treat infection. Note that vancomycin resistance in VRE — D-Ala-D-Ala changing to D-Ala-D-Lac — is target modification, not an alternative pathway. Resistance spreads mainly by horizontal gene transfer: conjugation, transformation and transduction.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: On what shared principle do all antifungals act, and why?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: They all act on fungal cell wall/membrane synthesis, because fungi have ergosterol (not cholesterol).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Azoles: mechanism, key interaction issue, and drugs of choice for Candida and Aspergillus.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Inhibit ergosterol synthesis (lanosterol 14α-demethylase); they are P450 inhibitors → many drug interactions.
  • Fluconazole for Candida
  • voriconazole for Aspergillus.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Polyenes (amphotericin B, nystatin): mechanism, key toxicity, and role.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Bind ergosterol → pore formation → membrane leak → cell death. Amphotericin B is highly nephrotoxic with electrolyte imbalances; reserve for life-threatening infections.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Echinocandins (micafungin, caspofungin): mechanism, use, and toxicity compared to amphotericin.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Inhibit beta-glucan synthesis → cell wall formation. Good for invasive Candida/Aspergillus; less toxic than amphotericin.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Exam pearl: what is the C. diff risk hierarchy, and the current first-line treatment?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The high-risk antibiotics are the "4 Cs" — clindamycin, cephalosporins, co-amoxiclav and ciprofloxacin. Clindamycin carries the highest risk per exposure, while cephalosporins and co-amoxiclav cause the most cases because they are prescribed so much more. First-line treatment is ORAL vancomycin (it must reach the bowel lumen — IV vancomycin does not work), with fidaxomicin second-line if vancomycin fails or on recurrence (NICE). Metronidazole is no longer first-line.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Exam pearl: what monitoring and cautions apply to gentamicin?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Gentamicin is dosed once daily by weight on a nomogram (ideal body weight in obesity). Monitoring is the PRE-DOSE (trough) level, taken before the second dose — a high trough means accumulation, so lengthen the interval rather than cutting the dose. Peak levels are only needed in divided-dose (endocarditis synergy) regimens. Monitor U&Es for nephrotoxicity (usually reversible) and ask about hearing loss, tinnitus and balance — ototoxicity may be permanent, so stop if it develops. Avoid in myasthenia gravis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Exam pearl: what is the fluconazole + warfarin interaction?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Fluconazole causes CYP450 inhibition → ↑warfarin levels → bleeding risk. Always check P450 interactions with azoles.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Exam pearl: how are ESBL-producing organisms and increasing CRE treated?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: ESBL-producing organisms (Klebsiella, E. coli) are resistant to all penicillins and cephalosporins → treat with meropenem (a carbapenem).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why is the cell membrane described as a selective barrier, and what does this control create?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It controls what enters and leaves the cell, and this control creates the ion gradients that underlie the resting membrane potential (the electrical charge across the membrane) essential for all excitable tissue.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the organising principle of the cell membrane's transport?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The membrane is selectively permeable, using different transport mechanisms for different substances; the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase sets up ion gradients that (with the membrane's K⁺ permeability) create the resting membrane potential — the foundation for nerve, muscle, and cardiac action potentials.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe the basic structure of the cell membrane.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A phospholipid bilayer (hydrophilic heads out, hydrophobic tails in) with embedded proteins (channels, transporters, receptors).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: State the permeability principle of the lipid bilayer — what crosses freely and what is blocked?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The lipid bilayer lets small, lipid-soluble (non-polar) molecules cross freely (O₂, CO₂, steroids, lipid-soluble drugs), but blocks large or charged/polar molecules (ions, glucose) → these need transport proteins.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the consequence of the membrane's selective permeability?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It allows the cell to maintain a different internal environment from the outside, including the ion gradients that create the membrane potential.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Simple diffusion: is it passive or active, which direction does it move, and give examples.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Passive (no ATP)
  • moves down the gradient
  • examples are O₂, CO₂, and lipid-soluble molecules crossing the bilayer directly.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Facilitated diffusion: is it passive or active, which direction, and give examples.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Passive
  • moves down the gradient
  • examples are glucose (GLUT) and ions through channels — via a protein.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Osmosis: is it passive or active, which direction does water move, and via what?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Passive
  • water moves down its osmotic gradient
  • via aquaporins.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Primary active transport: what energy source does it use, which direction, and give examples.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Active — uses ATP directly
  • moves against the gradient
  • examples are Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase, Ca²⁺ ATPase, and the proton pump.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Secondary active transport: what energy source does it use, which direction, and give examples.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Active — uses an ion gradient rather than ATP directly
  • moves against the gradient
  • examples are glucose-Na⁺ cotransport (SGLT) and Na⁺/H⁺ exchange.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Summarise the passive-vs-active transport distinction.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Passive = down the gradient, no energy (diffusion, facilitated diffusion, osmosis)
  • Active = against the gradient, needs energy (directly as ATP, or borrowed from an ion gradient).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Explain the high-yield mechanism of secondary active transport with an example.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It doesn't use ATP directly — it uses the energy stored in an ion gradient (usually the Na⁺ gradient made by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump) to move something else against its gradient, e.g. SGLT (glucose rides in on the Na⁺ gradient).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What does the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump per ATP, and what gradients does this maintain?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It pumps 3 Na⁺ OUT and 2 K⁺ IN per ATP (against their gradients), maintaining high Na⁺ outside and high K⁺ inside — the fundamental cellular ion gradients. It is found in every cell.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the three main 'payoffs' of the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• 1) It sets up the gradients for the resting membrane potential and all action potentials
  • 2) it powers secondary active transport (the Na⁺ gradient drives glucose/amino acid uptake)
  • 3) it's electrogenic (3 out, 2 in → net loss of positive charge → contributes slightly to the negative resting potential).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why is the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase described as electrogenic?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It pumps 3 positive ions out for every 2 in, causing a net loss of positive charge, which contributes slightly to the negative resting potential.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the clinical link between digoxin and the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Digoxin inhibits the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase in cardiac muscle → ↑intracellular Na⁺ → ↑intracellular Ca²⁺ (via Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchange) → ↑contractility (positive inotrope).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: At rest, what is the inside of the cell relative to the outside, and what are the typical values?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The inside is negative relative to the outside — about −70 mV in neurons and about −90 mV in cardiac/skeletal muscle.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What three factors contribute to the resting membrane potential and how?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• 1) Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase — sets up the ion gradients (high K⁺ in, high Na⁺ out)
  • 2) K⁺ leak channels — the membrane is most permeable to K⁺ at rest, so K⁺ leaks out down its gradient, leaving the inside negative
  • 3) large intracellular anions — proteins/phosphates (negative, can't leave) add to the negativity.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why is the resting potential set mainly by potassium?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Because the membrane is most permeable to K⁺ at rest, the resting potential sits close to the K⁺ equilibrium potential (about −90 mV). K⁺ leaking out is what makes the inside negative.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is an equilibrium potential, and what gives it?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Each ion has an equilibrium potential — the voltage at which its electrical and chemical gradients balance. The Nernst equation gives it; the resting potential is a weighted average dominated by the most permeable ion (K⁺).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is the resting potential the starting point for an action potential?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A stimulus depolarises the membrane toward threshold → voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open → the action potential fires.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Explain the high-yield electrolyte link: how does hyperkalaemia affect the resting membrane potential and excitability?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Hyperkalaemia (↑extracellular K⁺) → ↓the K⁺ gradient → depolarises the resting potential → initially more excitable, then (sustained) inactivates Na⁺ channels → inexcitable → cardiac arrest.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does hypokalaemia affect the membrane, and what is the risk?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Hypokalaemia hyperpolarises the membrane → arrhythmia risk.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why are potassium disorders considered cardiac emergencies?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Because they directly alter the resting membrane potential of excitable tissue.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do SGLT2 inhibitors and local anaesthetics act, in terms of membrane transport?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• SGLT2 inhibitors block Na⁺-glucose cotransport (secondary active transport) in the kidney
  • Local anaesthetics block voltage-gated Na⁺ channels → no action potential.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do oral rehydration therapy and diuretics relate to membrane transport?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Oral rehydration therapy: glucose-Na⁺ cotransport (SGLT) drives water absorption
  • Diuretics: act on tubular transporters (NKCC2, NCC, ENaC).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does cerebral/cellular oedema relate to membrane transport?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It results from osmotic water movement.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do cells communicate, and what is the basis of coordinated body function?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Cells communicate via chemical signals (hormones, neurotransmitters, local mediators) that bind receptors and trigger a response — the basis of coordinated body function.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the organising principle of cell signalling?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Signalling depends on where the receptor is, which is determined by whether the signal molecule is water-soluble (can't cross the membrane → surface receptors) or lipid-soluble (crosses the membrane → intracellular receptors). The receptor type then determines the speed and mechanism of the response.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Classify the four types of chemical signalling by distance, with where the signal travels and an example of each.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Endocrine — via the blood to distant targets (hormones: insulin, thyroid, cortisol)
  • Paracrine — to nearby cells by local diffusion (local mediators: histamine, prostaglandins)
  • Autocrine — back to the same cell (growth factors, some immune signals)
  • Neuronal/synaptic — across a synapse (neurotransmitters).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What common principle unites endocrine and neuronal signalling, and how do they mainly differ?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The same principle (signal → receptor → response) operates whether the signal travels body-wide (endocrine) or just across a synapse (neuronal) — they differ mainly in distance and speed.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Water-soluble signals: give examples, state whether they cross the membrane, and where their receptors are.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Examples: peptide hormones (insulin, ADH, most), catecholamines, neurotransmitters.
  • They cannot cross the membrane (polar).
  • Their receptors are at the cell surface (membrane receptors).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Lipid-soluble signals: give examples, state whether they cross the membrane, and where their receptors are.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Examples: steroid hormones (cortisol, aldosterone, sex steroids), thyroid hormone, vitamin D.
  • They can cross the membrane (lipophilic).
  • Their receptors are intracellular (cytoplasm/nucleus).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Compare the mechanism, speed, and duration of water-soluble versus lipid-soluble signals.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Water-soluble: act via second messengers; fast (seconds–minutes); short duration.
  • Lipid-soluble: directly alter gene transcription; slow (hours — needs new protein synthesis); long duration.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: State the whole cell-signalling framework in one linked sentence.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Water-soluble → surface receptor → second messenger → fast, short
  • lipid-soluble → intracellular receptor → gene transcription → slow, long.
This single divide explains why adrenaline acts in seconds but cortisol/thyroid hormone take hours.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the transport corollary for lipid-soluble hormones in the blood?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Lipid-soluble hormones (steroids, thyroid) are carried bound to plasma proteins in the blood (they're not water-soluble), and only the free fraction is active (e.g. free T4).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why must water-soluble signals use surface receptors and second messengers?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Water-soluble signals can't enter the cell, so they bind surface receptors that relay the signal inward via second messengers.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs): what is their mechanism and give examples.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: They activate a G-protein → second messengers (cAMP, IP₃/Ca²⁺). Examples: adrenergic, muscarinic, and many hormones — the biggest drug-target family.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Receptor tyrosine kinases: what is their mechanism and give examples.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The receptor has enzyme activity → a phosphorylation cascade. Examples: insulin, growth factors.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Ligand-gated ion channels: what is their mechanism and give examples.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The receptor is an ion channel → it opens on binding. Examples: nicotinic ACh (NMJ), GABA-A.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Name the major second messengers and their sources.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• cAMP (from GPCRs via adenylyl cyclase) — the classic
  • IP₃ + DAG → ↑intracellular Ca²⁺ (another major pathway)
  • Ca²⁺ itself (a key intracellular signal).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Explain the high-yield amplification point of second-messenger signalling.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: One hormone molecule → activates many G-proteins → each makes many cAMP → each activates many enzymes → a cascade that massively amplifies a tiny signal (which is why hormones work at nanomolar concentrations).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do lipid-soluble signals act via the slow (intracellular) pathway?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Lipid-soluble signals (steroids, thyroid hormone, vitamin D) cross the membrane and bind intracellular receptors (cytoplasm/nucleus); the hormone-receptor complex acts as a transcription factor → binds DNA → alters gene expression → new protein synthesis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the consequences of the intracellular gene-transcription pathway in terms of speed and duration?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It is slow (hours–days — takes time to make new proteins) but produces lasting effects — which is why steroid effects (cortisol, aldosterone) build up over hours and persist.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the steroid pharmacology link arising from the intracellular pathway?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It explains why therapeutic steroids take time to work and why they have widespread effects (altering transcription across many tissues).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Define an agonist and an antagonist in receptor pharmacology, with an example of each.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Agonist — binds and activates the receptor (mimics the natural signal), e.g. salbutamol (β2 agonist).
  • Antagonist — binds and blocks the receptor (no activation), e.g. β-blockers, antihistamines.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Define a partial agonist and the competitive vs non-competitive distinction.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Partial agonist — activates, but sub-maximally, e.g. buprenorphine.
  • Competitive vs non-competitive — reversible (surmountable) vs not — relevant to overdose/reversal.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the key receptor-pharmacology point about how most drugs work?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Most drugs work by mimicking (agonist) or blocking (antagonist) endogenous signalling → knowing the receptor and its second-messenger system predicts the effect.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does chronic overstimulation versus chronic blockade affect receptors, and what is a clinical consequence?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Chronic overstimulation → downregulation/desensitisation; chronic blockade → upregulation — which is why abruptly stopping β-blockers causes rebound tachycardia.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Cell signalling explanation: why are some hormones fast and others slow?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Peptide/catecholamine hormones use surface receptors → act in seconds
  • steroid/thyroid hormones use intracellular receptors → act over hours.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does insulin act at the receptor level, and what does it recruit?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Insulin acts via a receptor tyrosine kinase → GLUT4, producing metabolic effects (cross-ref glucose homeostasis).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does cholera toxin cause disease at the signalling level?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It locks the G-protein 'on' → ↑↑cAMP → massive secretory diarrhoea (a signalling disease).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does cell signalling relate to cancer?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Many oncogenes are mutated signalling proteins (growth factor receptors).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is body water distributed, and what drives water movement between compartments?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Body water is distributed between compartments (inside vs outside cells, and within the extracellular space); water moves between them by osmosis — driven by solute concentrations.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the organising principle of body fluid compartments?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Total body water splits into intracellular and extracellular compartments, kept separate by cell membranes; water moves freely between them by osmosis (following solutes), while the solutes that can't cross determine where water goes. Sodium is the main extracellular solute (so it governs extracellular volume), and osmosis explains fluid shifts, oedema, and IV fluid behaviour.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is total body water as a fraction of body weight, and what is the '60-40-20 rule'?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Total body water is about 60% of body weight. The 60-40-20 rule:
  • total body water ~60%
  • intracellular fluid (ICF) ~40%
  • extracellular fluid (ECF) ~20% of body weight.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What fraction of total body water is intracellular versus extracellular (the key split)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Two-thirds intracellular, one-third extracellular. Of the ECF: three-quarters interstitial + one-quarter plasma.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Break down the ECF: what percentage of body weight and fraction of ECF are interstitial fluid and plasma?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Interstitial (between cells) ~15% of body weight (~¾ of ECF)
  • plasma (intravascular) ~5% of body weight (~¼ of ECF).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the two barriers separating the fluid compartments, and what crosses each?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• The cell membrane separates ICF from ECF (water crosses freely, solutes selectively).
  • The capillary wall separates plasma from interstitium (water + small solutes cross, proteins mostly don't).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What determines where water goes between compartments?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Water follows osmotically active solutes — but which compartment a solute is confined to determines where it pulls water.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which compartment is sodium confined to, what confines it there, and what does it govern?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Sodium is confined to the extracellular compartment (pumped out by Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase) and governs ECF volume (it's the main extracellular osmole).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which compartments are potassium and plasma proteins (albumin) confined to, and what do they govern?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Potassium is confined to the intracellular compartment and governs the ICF.
  • Plasma proteins (albumin) are confined to plasma (can't cross the capillary) and govern plasma volume via oncotic pressure.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Explain the high-yield 'sodium = volume' point.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Because sodium is the main extracellular solute, total body sodium determines ECF volume — so sodium = volume. Add sodium → hold water in the ECF → ↑volume; lose sodium → lose ECF volume.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the corollary distinguishing control of water balance from control of sodium?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Water balance (osmolality) is controlled by ADH
  • sodium (volume) is controlled by aldosterone/RAAS.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Define osmosis in terms of solute and water concentration.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Osmosis is water moving across a semipermeable membrane from low solute (high water) → high solute (low water) concentration → water follows solute.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Define osmolality and give its normal range.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Osmolality is the concentration of osmotically active particles (mainly Na⁺, glucose, urea in the ECF); normal is about 285–295 mOsm/kg.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is tonicity, and why is it the clinically useful concept?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Tonicity is the effective osmolality — how a solution affects cell volume.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the effect on cells of an isotonic solution, and give an example.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: No net water movement (cells stay the same) — e.g. 0.9% saline.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the effect on cells of a hypotonic solution, and give an example.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Water moves into cells → cells swell (can lyse) — e.g. giving too much free water.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the effect on cells of a hypertonic solution, and give an example.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Water moves out of cells → cells shrink — e.g. hypernatraemia.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do changes in ECF osmolality shift water, and why is hyponatraemia dangerous?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Changes in ECF osmolality shift water in or out of cells. Hyponatraemia (low ECF osmolality) → water moves into cells → cellular swelling (dangerous in the brain → cerebral oedema); hypernatraemia → cells shrink.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is an effective versus ineffective osmole, with examples?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Urea crosses membranes freely so it's an ineffective osmole (doesn't shift water); Na⁺ and glucose are effective osmoles (they do shift water) — which is why hyperglycaemia causes hyponatraemia by pulling water out of cells.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: IV fluids: where does 0.9% saline / Hartmann's distribute, and what is it used for?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: 0.9% saline / Hartmann's (isotonic crystalloid) stays in the ECF (¼ intravascular, ¾ interstitial); used for volume resuscitation and replacement.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: IV fluids: where does 5% dextrose distribute, and what is it used for?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The glucose is metabolised → leaves free water → distributes across all compartments (mostly into cells); used for free water replacement (rarely for resuscitation — little stays intravascular).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: IV fluids: where do colloids/albumin distribute, and what is their use?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: They stay intravascular (large molecules); limited use for plasma volume.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the high-yield point comparing isotonic crystalloids and 5% dextrose for resuscitation?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Isotonic crystalloids expand the ECF (good for resuscitation, though only ¼ stays intravascular)
  • 5% dextrose gives free water (spreads everywhere, a poor volume expander — and giving too much → hyponatraemia/cellular swelling).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Fluid shifts: what happens in dehydration?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: ECF volume loss → ↑osmolality (if water is lost) → water shifts out of cells.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Fluid shifts: what causes oedema (excess interstitial fluid)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Excess interstitial fluid from
  • ↑hydrostatic pressure (heart failure)
  • ↓oncotic pressure (hypoalbuminaemia)
  • ↑permeability (sepsis)
  • or lymphatic block
— a Starling-force imbalance.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Fluid shifts: describe the water movement in hyponatraemia versus hypernatraemia.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Hyponatraemia: ↓ECF osmolality → water into cells → cerebral oedema.
  • Hypernatraemia: ↑ECF osmolality → water out of cells → cellular shrinkage.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is third-spacing?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Fluid shifts into a non-functional compartment (e.g. bowel in obstruction, ascites).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why must hyponatraemia be corrected slowly?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Because ↓osmolality → cellular swelling → cerebral oedema, but correcting too fast risks osmotic demyelination.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Clinically, how does hyperglycaemia cause hyponatraemia?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Glucose (an effective osmole) pulls water out of cells → dilutional hyponatraemia.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Define homeostasis.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment despite external changes — the fundamental organising principle of all physiology.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the organising principle of homeostasis, and what three components make up its control systems?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The body keeps regulated variables (temperature, pH, glucose, ions, blood pressure, osmolality) within narrow ranges using negative feedback control systems — a sensor, control centre, and effector. This framework makes every regulatory system an instance of the same logic, and disease is often a failure of homeostasis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which systems regulate temperature, blood glucose, and pH?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Temperature — hypothalamus (thermoregulation)
  • blood glucose — insulin/glucagon (glucose homeostasis)
  • pH — lungs + kidneys (acid-base).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which systems regulate ions, osmolality/water, blood pressure/volume, and O₂/CO₂?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Ions (Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺) — kidneys + hormones (electrolyte handling, calcium homeostasis)
  • osmolality/water — ADH + thirst
  • blood pressure/volume — baroreceptors + RAAS
  • O₂/CO₂ — respiratory control.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is a set point, and what corrects deviations from it?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Each regulated variable has a set point (the target value) and a control system that corrects deviations — every regulatory system is one of these.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is negative feedback, and how does it act on the variable?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Negative feedback is where the response opposes the change, pulling the variable back toward the set point. Almost all homeostasis works this way.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Name the three components of a feedback loop and their roles, using temperature as the example.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Sensor (receptor) — detects the change (thermoreceptors)
  • control centre — compares to the set point and coordinates the response (hypothalamus)
  • effector — produces the corrective response (sweating/shivering, vasodilation/constriction).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Explain the logic of a negative feedback loop step by step.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A deviation from the set point → detected → triggers a response that opposes/reverses the deviation → the variable returns toward normal → the response switches off. The response counteracts the stimulus (hence 'negative').

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Give the high-yield universality point — how blood glucose and blood pressure illustrate the same negative-feedback structure.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
The same structure runs every regulatory system:
  • ↑blood glucose → (sensor: β-cells) → insulin → (effector: cells take up glucose) → glucose falls
  • ↑BP → (baroreceptors) → ↓sympathetic → ↓BP
  • ↑cortisol → suppresses CRH/ACTH
— all the same negative-feedback logic.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is positive feedback, and what is it used for (in contrast to negative feedback)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Positive feedback amplifies the change (the response reinforces the stimulus) → not for maintaining stability, but for driving a process rapidly to completion.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe the amplifying loop of the LH surge → ovulation as a positive-feedback example.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Oestrogen peak → ↑LH → more oestrogen → ovulation (cross-ref menstrual cycle).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Give the amplifying loops for blood clotting and labour/uterine contractions.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Blood clotting: activated factors activate more factors (the cascade).
  • Labour/uterine contractions: contractions → ↑oxytocin → stronger contractions → delivery.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is the action potential upstroke an example of positive feedback?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Depolarisation → opens Na⁺ channels → more depolarisation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the key distinction between negative and positive feedback, and which loops are the classic positive-feedback exceptions?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Negative feedback = stability (the norm)
  • positive feedback = amplification to an endpoint (the rare exceptions).
The few positive-feedback loops — the LH surge, clotting, labour, and the AP upstroke — are worth knowing precisely because they're exceptions.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is feedforward control, with examples?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Feedforward control is where the body anticipates a change before it happens (e.g. the cephalic phase of digestion — seeing food triggers acid/insulin release before eating; the anticipatory ↑heart rate before exercise) → it prepares in advance rather than just correcting after.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How can set points be reset, using fever as the example?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Set points can be reset: in fever, infection resets the hypothalamic temperature set point higher (via pyrogens) → the body actively defends the new higher temperature (which is why you shiver with a fever).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Explain 'disease as failure of homeostasis' with the examples of diabetes, hypertension, and heart failure.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Many diseases are a breakdown of homeostatic control:
  • diabetes = failure of glucose homeostasis
  • hypertension = dysregulated BP control
  • heart failure = maladaptive compensation (RAAS activation worsens congestion).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which homeostatic failures underlie acid-base disorders and fluid/electrolyte disorders?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Acid-base disorders = failure of pH regulation
  • fluid/electrolyte disorders = failure of osmotic/volume/ion regulation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Explain the high-yield maladaptive-compensation point using heart failure.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Sometimes the homeostatic response itself becomes harmful — e.g. in heart failure, RAAS activation (a normal 'low perfusion' response) causes fluid retention that worsens the failure → a homeostatic loop turned pathological.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does drug logic relate to homeostasis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Many drugs support or replace a failed homeostatic mechanism (e.g. insulin, antihypertensives).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is genetics, in terms of storage, expression, and inheritance?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Genetics is the molecular basis of inheritance — how information is stored (DNA), expressed (→ protein), and passed on — and how variations cause inherited disease.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the organising principle of genetics?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Genetic information flows DNA → RNA → protein (the central dogma); it's packaged into chromosomes and inherited in predictable patterns (dominant, recessive, X-linked); mutations disrupt this and cause disease. Recognising the inheritance pattern predicts recurrence risk and which relatives are affected.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe the three steps of the central dogma (DNA to protein).
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• DNA — the stored code (in the nucleus), organised into genes on chromosomes.
  • Transcription — DNA → mRNA (in the nucleus).
  • Translation — mRNA → protein (at the ribosome, using the genetic code — codons).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the key concept linking genes, DNA sequence, and disease?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Genes code for proteins; the sequence of DNA bases → the sequence of amino acids → the protein's structure/function → so a mutation in the DNA → an altered protein → disease.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How many chromosomes do humans have, and how are they arranged?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Humans have 46 (23 pairs) — 22 autosomal pairs + 1 sex pair (XX female, XY male); one of each pair comes from each parent.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Define gene and allele.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Gene — a segment of DNA coding for a protein.
  • Allele — a version of a gene (one from each parent).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Define genotype and phenotype.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Genotype — the genetic makeup.
  • Phenotype — the observable trait/expression.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Define homozygous and heterozygous.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Homozygous — two identical alleles.
  • Heterozygous — two different alleles (a 'carrier' if recessive).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Define dominant and recessive.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Dominant — expressed even with one copy.
  • Recessive — expressed only with two copies.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Autosomal dominant inheritance: state the rule, examples, and key features.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Rule: one copy → affected; 50% risk to offspring; affects every generation.
  • Examples: Huntington's, familial hypercholesterolaemia, ADPKD, Marfan's, neurofibromatosis.
  • Key features: vertical transmission; both sexes; often later-onset.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Autosomal recessive inheritance: state the rule, examples, and key features.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Rule: two copies needed; carriers unaffected; 25% risk if both parents are carriers.
  • Examples: cystic fibrosis, sickle cell, thalassaemia, most metabolic disorders.
  • Key features: can skip generations; consanguinity increases risk.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: X-linked recessive inheritance: state the rule, examples, and key features.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Rule: on the X; males affected (only one X), females usually carriers.
  • Examples: haemophilia A/B, Duchenne muscular dystrophy, G6PD deficiency, red-green colour blindness.
  • Key features: no male-to-male transmission; affects mostly males.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: X-linked dominant inheritance: state the rule and key feature.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Rule: on the X, one copy is enough (rarer).
  • Key feature: affected males → all daughters affected.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Mitochondrial inheritance: state the rule, an example, and key features.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Rule: inherited only from the mother (mitochondria come from the egg).
  • Example: mitochondrial myopathies.
  • Key features: maternal inheritance, affects both sexes (all her children can be affected; affected fathers don't pass it on).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Pattern-recognition payoff: what are the hallmarks of autosomal dominant vs autosomal recessive inheritance?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Autosomal dominant: affects every generation (vertical), 50% risk — e.g. Huntington's.
  • Autosomal recessive: skips generations, carriers common, 25% risk if both parents are carriers — e.g. CF, sickle cell.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Pattern-recognition payoff: what are the hallmarks of X-linked recessive and mitochondrial inheritance?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• X-linked recessive: mostly males affected, no male-to-male transmission, females carriers — e.g. haemophilia, DMD.
  • Mitochondrial: only from the mother (all her children can be affected; affected fathers don't pass it on).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is a point mutation, with a classic example?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A single-base change — e.g. sickle cell (a single base → a single amino acid change in β-globin).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is a frameshift mutation and its effect?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: An insertion or deletion that shifts the reading frame → major disruption.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is a trinucleotide repeat expansion, with examples and its characteristic feature?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Repeated sequences expand → Huntington's (CAG), fragile X, Friedreich's ataxia; the characteristic feature is anticipation (the disease worsens/appears earlier each generation).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are chromosomal mutations, with examples?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Whole-chromosome abnormalities →
  • Down syndrome (trisomy 21)
  • Turner's (45,X)
  • Klinefelter's (47,XXY).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Explain the high-yield sickle cell point.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A single point mutation in β-globin → the disease — the classic example of how one base change → one amino acid change → an abnormal protein.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Explain the high-yield concept of anticipation.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: In trinucleotide repeat disorders (e.g. Huntington's), the repeat expands each generation → the disease appears earlier and more severe in successive generations.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Define penetrance and expressivity.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Penetrance — the proportion with the genotype who show the phenotype (incomplete penetrance = not everyone with the gene is affected).
  • Expressivity — how severely the phenotype shows (variable expressivity = different severity).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Define codominance, with an example.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Codominance is where both alleles are expressed — e.g. ABO blood groups.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is polygenic/multifactorial inheritance, with examples?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Many genes + environment (e.g. diabetes, hypertension, most common diseases) — not simple Mendelian.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is pharmacogenomics, with examples?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Genetic variation in drug handling (e.g. fast/slow acetylators, CYP polymorphisms) — cross-ref drug biotransformation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does recognising the inheritance pattern help in genetic counselling?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The pattern predicts recurrence risk — recognising the inheritance pattern predicts which relatives are affected and the risk to offspring.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the first division of immunity, and how do the two arms differ?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Innate (born with it, non-specific, immediate, no memory) vs adaptive (acquired, specific, slower first time but has memory).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is herd immunity, which type of immunity produces it, and who does it protect?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
When enough of a population is immune, transmission chains break and the unimmunised are protected indirectly. Only active immunity — vaccination or infection — creates it; passive antibody protects only the recipient. The threshold rises with transmissibility: measles, the most transmissible, needs roughly 95% two-dose coverage. It protects those who cannot be vaccinated —
  • infants too young for the schedule
  • the pregnant
  • and the significantly immunosuppressed.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the defining trade-off between active and passive immunity?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Active = slow onset but long-lasting (memory)
  • passive = immediate but short-lived (no memory).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the components of innate vs adaptive immunity?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Innate:
  • granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils)
  • APCs (dendritic cells, macrophages)
  • NK cells
  • complement
Adaptive:
  • T-cells
  • B-cells

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do innate and adaptive immunity differ in response speed and recognition?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Innate: nonspecific, rapid; recognises PAMPs via TLRs
  • Adaptive: specific, slow first time and faster on re-exposure; uses T-cell + B-cell receptors.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which immune arm has memory, and what does this underpin?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Adaptive immunity has memory (innate does not) — this is the basis of vaccination.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the mechanism of active vs passive immunity?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Active: the host's own immune system is stimulated → makes its own antibodies + memory cells
  • Passive: pre-formed antibodies are given to the host.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Compare active and passive immunity by onset, duration and memory.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Active: slow onset (days-weeks), long-lasting (memory), memory = yes
  • Passive: immediate onset, short-lived (antibodies degrade, no memory), memory = no.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Give examples of active vs passive immunity.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Active:
  • infection
  • vaccination
Passive:
  • placental IgG
  • breast-milk IgA
  • immunoglobulin injection

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: In one line, when should passive immunity be used?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Active is slow but durable; passive is instant but temporary — so use passive when you need protection NOW and there's no time to mount a response.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the examples in the NATURAL row of the active/passive × natural/artificial 2×2?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Natural active: infection → immune response + memory
  • Natural passive: placental transfer (IgG) to fetus; breast milk (IgA) to neonate.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the examples in the ARTIFICIAL row of the active/passive × natural/artificial 2×2?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Artificial active: vaccination. Artificial passive: immunoglobulin administration —
  • anti-tetanus Ig
  • anti-rabies Ig
  • hepatitis B Ig
  • anti-D
  • antivenom
  • monoclonal antibodies

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is active immunity generated, and what does it prime?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Generated by infection (natural) or vaccination (artificial)
  • both prime B/T cells to produce antibodies + memory cells → a faster, stronger response on re-exposure.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do live attenuated and killed/inactivated vaccines differ in the immunity they produce?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Live attenuated: better cell-mediated immunity, and the mucosally given ones (oral rotavirus, oral typhoid, nasal influenza) also produce mucosal IgA
  • Killed/inactivated: mainly systemic IgG rather than mucosal IgA.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do live attenuated and killed/inactivated vaccines differ in dosing?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Live attenuated: often a single priming dose is enough and no adjuvant is needed — though the UK schedule still gives two doses of MMRV/varicella and two oral rotavirus doses
  • Killed/inactivated: a primary course plus boosters, and usually — but not always — adjuvanted (IPV and standard inactivated influenza are not).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the key caveat for live attenuated vs killed/inactivated vaccines?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Live attenuated: may cause mild disease; avoid in immunocompromise and pregnancy
  • Killed/inactivated: safe in pregnancy and in immunocompromise, although the antibody response may be blunted in significant immunosuppression.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Give examples of live attenuated vs killed/inactivated vaccines.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Live attenuated:
  • MMR/MMRV
  • varicella
  • BCG
  • oral rotavirus
  • live attenuated nasal influenza
  • yellow fever
  • oral typhoid
Killed/inactivated/subunit:
  • IPV
  • DTaP
  • hepatitis B
  • pneumococcal
  • HPV
  • injectable influenza
  • meningococcal
The UK shingles vaccine is recombinant and NOT live.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the principle of passive immunity, and what role does it serve?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It gives instant protection when there's no time to wait for an active response — a bridge, not a long-term solution.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the forms of natural passive immunity?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Placental IgG — the only immunoglobulin that crosses the placenta, transferred mainly in the third trimester by active transport, so preterm babies get less; it wanes by around 6 months, leaving a window of susceptibility before the infant's own schedule takes over
  • And breast-milk IgA — mucosal protection of the gut and airway, which is not absorbed systemically.
This is why the pertussis and RSV vaccines in pregnancy are timed to load the fetus before delivery.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the clinical uses of artificial passive immunity?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Post-exposure prophylaxis — human tetanus immunoglobulin for a high-risk tetanus-prone wound, rabies immunoglobulin, hepatitis B immunoglobulin — plus anti-D (prevents rhesus sensitisation), antitoxins/antivenoms, and monoclonal antibodies (nirsevimab for RSV in high-risk infants, which has replaced palivizumab in the UK).Note VZIG has been withdrawn in the UK: varicella post-exposure prophylaxis is now antiviral-first, oral aciclovir days 7–14 after exposure (UKHSA).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the limitation of passive immunity?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• It wears off as antibodies degrade
  • no memory — so it doesn't protect against future exposures.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the key facts and clinical relevance of IgG?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Most abundant
  • the only Ig that crosses the placenta
  • main secondary-response antibody
  • long-lived
Clinical relevance:
  • natural passive immunity to the neonate
  • basis of therapeutic Ig
  • IgG = past infection

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the key facts and clinical relevance of IgA?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Found in
  • mucosal secretions
  • breast milk
  • gut/respiratory linings
Clinical relevance:
  • mucosal defence
  • natural passive immunity via breast milk
  • IgA deficiency → GI/resp infections (Giardia, Cryptosporidium)

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the key facts and clinical relevance of IgM?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Largest (pentamer)
  • first antibody in the primary response
  • can't cross the placenta
Clinical relevance: acute/recent infection marker (IgM = current infection).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the key facts and clinical relevance of IgE?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Binds mast cells/basophils. Clinical relevance:
  • type I hypersensitivity (allergy)
  • anaphylaxis
  • parasites

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the key facts and clinical relevance of IgD?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Mostly on the naïve B-cell surface. Clinical relevance:
  • B-cell activation
  • minor role

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What two anchors tie the immunoglobulin classes to the active/passive topic?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• IgG crosses the placenta + IgA in breast milk = the natural passive box
  • IgM-vs-IgG = recent-vs-past infection (ties to hepatitis serology + autoimmune liver notes).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What does IgG deficiency predispose to?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Encapsulated bacteria risk (H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are interleukins, and which IL causes fever as an endogenous pyrogen?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Interleukins = cytokines (chemical messengers between immune cells). IL-1 is an endogenous pyrogen → fever.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the one thing to remember for IL-2 and IL-6?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• IL-2: T-cell proliferation
  • IL-6: acute-phase response + fever (drives CRP).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the one thing to remember for IL-4 and IL-5?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• IL-4: IgE class switch + B-cell proliferation (Th2/allergy)
  • IL-5: IgA class switch + eosinophil growth (allergy, parasites).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the one thing to remember for IL-8 and IL-10?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• IL-8: neutrophil chemotaxis
  • IL-10: inhibits the Th1/inflammatory response (anti-inflammatory).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the grouping logic for the high-yield interleukins?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Fever (1, 6)
  • recruit/activate a specific cell (2→T-cells, 5→eosinophils, 8→neutrophils)
  • drive allergy (4, 5)
  • switch off (10)

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How do Th1 and Th2 responses differ?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Th1 = cell-mediated (IL-12 → IFN-γ)
  • Th2 = humoral (IL-4).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is antimicrobial stewardship (AMS)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The coordinated effort to promote and monitor the responsible use of antimicrobials to preserve their future effectiveness — a public-health and patient-safety strategy, not a clinical condition.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the driving problem AMS addresses, and why does it matter?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) — already responsible for over a million deaths worldwide each year and projected to rise substantially by 2050, driven substantially by inappropriate antibiotic use.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the logical chain that organises antimicrobial stewardship?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Antibiotic exposure exerts selection pressure → resistance and collateral harm (C. difficile, MRSA) → so use is governed by stewardship goals → delivered in practice through Start Smart, Then Focus → underpinned by understanding how bacteria become resistant.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the goals of stewardship (promoting judicious antibiotic use)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Reduce inappropriate use
  • improve patient outcomes
  • increase guideline adherence
  • decrease resistance
  • and reduce healthcare costs.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the conceptual heart of AMS — the balance it strikes?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Safeguard the quality of care for the patient in front of you while protecting antibiotics for future patients — the individual-vs-population tension is the conceptual heart.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the drivers of antimicrobial resistance?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Over-prescribing (including for viral infections)
  • broad-spectrum use when narrow would do
  • inadequate dosing/duration and poor adherence
  • and agricultural antibiotic use / global spread.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the consequences of antibiotic overuse?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Untreatable infections
  • longer admissions
  • higher mortality
  • reliance on toxic/last-line agents.
Two distinct harms: selection of resistant organisms (MRSA, ESBL producers) and destruction of protective gut flora allowing C. difficile overgrowth — C. difficile is collateral damage to the microbiome, not a resistance mechanism. The high-risk "4 Cs" for C. difficile are clindamycin, cephalosporins, co-amoxiclav and ciprofloxacin.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the underlying principle linking antibiotic exposure to resistance, and the resulting goal?
