conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Every antibiotic exposure exerts selection pressure favouring resistant organisms — so the goal is 'the right drug, for the right bug, at the right dose, for the right duration'.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the two phases of Start Smart, Then Focus?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Phase 1, Start Smart, at initiation: only start with clinical evidence of infection, take cultures where possible without delaying treatment, follow local guidelines, and document indication, drug, dose, route, duration or review/stop date and allergy status
  • Phase 2, Then Focus: an antibiotic review at 48–72 hours with a documented decision — one of five outcomes.
It is the UK two-phase model (UKHSA / NICE) applied to every antibiotic prescription.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What does Phase 1 — Start Smart (at initiation) involve?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Don't start without clinical evidence of infection (avoid treating contamination, colonisation or viral illness — the classic trap is asymptomatic bacteriuria, which is not treated unless there are urinary symptoms, pregnancy being the main exception)
  • take cultures before starting where possible (especially blood cultures), but never delay antibiotics for cultures in septic shock, neutropenic sepsis or suspected meningococcal disease
  • follow local prescribing guidelines (reflecting local resistance patterns)
  • document indication, drug, dose, route, duration or a review/stop date, and allergy status
  • consider severity, immunocompromise, resistance risk, and prior antibiotic exposure.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What does Phase 2 — Then Focus involve, and when is it done?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Review the diagnosis and continuing need at 48–72 hours (current UK wording asks for an active review within 24–72 hours), and document a clear plan as one of five defined outcomes — stop, switch, change, continue or OPAT.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the five outcomes of the antibiotic review at 48–72 h?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Stop (no evidence of infection → cease)
  • Switch (IV → oral when stable)
  • Change (de-escalate to a narrower-spectrum agent, or broaden if needed, per culture results)
  • Continue (document review date)
  • OPAT (outpatient parenteral antibiotic therapy).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the pivotal AMS action at the focus stage?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: De-escalation — empirical broad-spectrum → narrow targeted once sensitivities return.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the 'right' mnemonic for practical stewardship?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Right drug, dose, route, duration, for the right diagnosis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What practical stewardship measures relate to route and duration of antibiotics?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
IV-to-oral switch (IVOS) as soon as criteria are met — it reduces line infections, length of stay and cost. Review every patient on IV antimicrobials within 48 hours and daily thereafter, and switch when the patient is Afebrile and haemodynamically stable, Clinically improving with falling inflammatory markers, Eating and drinking with an absorbing gut, and has no Deep-seated infection ("ACED"). Deep-seated infections needing specialist advice before any switch:
  • bloodstream infection
  • endocarditis
  • meningitis and other CNS infection
  • osteomyelitis
  • septic arthritis
  • empyema
  • undrained abscess and necrotising soft-tissue infection.
Also use the shortest effective duration — the old "always finish the course" dogma is dropped where evidence supports shorter courses.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What do stewardship rules say about spectrum, restricted agents and fluoroquinolones?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Use the narrowest effective spectrum. Reserve restricted agents (carbapenems, piperacillin-tazobactam, glycopeptides) via local restriction/approval. Systemic fluoroquinolones are nationally restricted (MHRA): prescribe one only when other recommended antibiotics are inappropriate — because they have failed, will not work because of resistance, or are unsafe for that patient — and never for a mild or self-limiting infection, because of rare but disabling and potentially irreversible tendon, aortic, neurological and mental-health effects.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What practical stewardship measures relate to cultures and biomarkers?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Take cultures before antibiotics where possible, but never delay treatment for them in septic shock, neutropenic sepsis or suspected meningococcal disease. Biomarkers such as procalcitonin can support a decision to stop antibiotics earlier where available — they support, and never override, clinical judgement.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Who makes up an AMS team, and what organisational measures support stewardship?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• AMS teams (microbiologist + antimicrobial pharmacist, supported by infection specialists, infection prevention and control nurses and a clinical lead)
  • local guidelines
  • audit/feedback
  • prescriber education
  • ward rounds.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which stewardship measures act on prescriber behaviour and the patient record?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Educate the public and prescribers that antibiotics do not treat viral infections
  • use delayed (back-up) prescriptions in primary care
  • and check and challenge penicillin-allergy labels — around 1 in 10 patients carries one but the large majority are not truly allergic, and a false label pushes patients onto broader, more toxic, less effective agents with more MRSA and C. difficile.
Refer for assessment and delabelling where the story is not consistent with true allergy.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the 'altered target' mechanism of resistance, with examples?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Altered target:
  • altered PBP2a in MRSA (so all β-lactams fail)
  • RNA polymerase (rifampicin)
  • DNA gyrase (ciprofloxacin)
  • 30S ribosome (streptomycin)
  • and D-Ala-D-Ala → D-Ala-D-Lac in VRE.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: By what mechanism is MRSA resistant to β-lactams, and how is that mechanism classified?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: MRSA acquires an altered penicillin-binding protein, PBP2a, which β-lactams cannot bind — so all β-lactams fail. This is classified as an altered-target mechanism, the same category as altered DNA gyrase (ciprofloxacin), altered RNA polymerase (rifampicin) and the D-Ala-D-Ala → D-Ala-D-Lac change in VRE.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the 'drug modification / breakdown' mechanism of resistance, with examples?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Drug modification / breakdown:
  • β-lactamases (penicillins)
  • aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the 'efflux pumps' mechanism of resistance, with examples?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Efflux pumps:
  • tetracyclines
  • quinolones
  • β-lactams.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why is MRSA the archetype of resistance, and how is it treated?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Staph aureus resistant to β-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems) via an altered penicillin-binding protein, PBP2a — an altered-target mechanism → treated with
  • doxycycline
  • clindamycin
  • vancomycin
  • teicoplanin
  • or linezolid.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO), and how should it be conceptualised?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Not a disease but a diagnostic problem: a prolonged fever that remains undiagnosed despite a proper initial workup. The topic is about a structured approach to a defined differential, not a single condition.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is 'the spine' of the approach to PUO?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Define it → place the patient in the right sub-type → work through the four cause-buckets → investigate in a staged, history-led way.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the decisive feature of PUO, and why does it narrow the causes?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The precise definition (Petersdorf & Beeson) — the '3 weeks + appropriate investigation' criterion separates true PUO from an ordinary acute fever and narrows the likely causes.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the Petersdorf & Beeson criteria for PUO (temperature, duration, investigation)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Temperature: >38.3°C on several occasions
  • Duration: fever persisting ≥3 weeks
  • Investigation: no diagnosis despite appropriate workup — originally 1 week inpatient, now revised to 3 outpatient visits or 3 days of inpatient / intensive ambulatory investigation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why does the '≥3 weeks + investigated' criterion matter?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: By definition these patients have already resisted classification on baseline investigation, so the differential is a specific (often smaller, often serious) set — most self-limiting viral fevers have resolved or declared themselves by 3 weeks.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the Classic sub-type of PUO, and its dominant causes?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Patient: immunocompetent, no specific risk factors. Dominant causes: the full four-bucket differential.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the Healthcare-associated (nosocomial) sub-type of PUO, and its dominant causes?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Patient: inpatient, fever developing in hospital. Dominant causes:
  • line/catheter sepsis
  • C. diff
  • drug fever
  • VTE/PE
  • sinusitis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the Immunocompromised / neutropenic sub-type of PUO, and its dominant causes?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Patient: chemotherapy, immunosuppression. Dominant causes: opportunistic infection (bacterial; fungal — Candida/Aspergillus). Treat as neutropenic sepsis until proven otherwise — temperature ≥38°C (or other signs of significant sepsis) with neutrophils ≤0.5 × 10⁹/L means empirical IV broad-spectrum antibiotics WITHIN 1 HOUR (NICE). This is the opposite of the methodical classic-PUO workup; never apply the ≥3-week rule to a neutropenic patient.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the HIV-associated sub-type of PUO, and its dominant causes?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Patient: known/suspected HIV. Dominant causes:
  • opportunistic infections (TB, MAC, PCP, CMV)
  • HIV itself
  • lymphoma.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why establish the PUO sub-type first?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It reshapes the differential and the urgency — neutropenic PUO is an emergency; classic PUO is a methodical workup.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the Infection bucket of PUO causes?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
A large group (especially in the developing world):
  • TB (especially miliary/extrapulmonary — the classic PUO cause)
  • occult abscess (subphrenic, pelvic, dental)
  • infective endocarditis
  • osteomyelitis
  • HIV
  • EBV/CMV
  • brucellosis
  • hidden empyema.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the Malignancy bucket of PUO causes?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Lymphoma (the classic)
  • leukaemia
  • renal cell carcinoma
  • hepatocellular carcinoma
  • atrial myxoma.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the Non-infectious inflammatory bucket of PUO causes?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Predominates in the developed world:
  • adult-onset Still's disease (young adult, quotidian spiking fever, evanescent salmon-pink rash, arthralgia, sore throat, neutrophilia, markedly raised ferritin, ANA and RF negative)
  • giant cell arteritis / PMR (anyone over 50)
  • SLE
  • vasculitides
  • IBD (can present as isolated PUO).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the Miscellaneous bucket of PUO causes?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Drug fever
  • VTE/PE
  • hyperthyroidism / subacute thyroiditis
  • factitious fever
  • familial Mediterranean fever
  • sarcoidosis.
DRUG FEVER: suspect it in anyone on a new or long-standing drug — the patient often looks well for the height of the fever, and eosinophilia or a rash may be present but are often absent. Culprits: beta-lactams, sulfonamides, anticonvulsants, allopurinol, antituberculous drugs, NSAIDs, heparin. Stopping the drug is the diagnostic test — the fever usually settles within 48–72 hours. FACTITIOUS FEVER: a high reading in a well-looking patient with no rigors or sweats, no rise in pulse or respiratory rate, no diurnal variation and a normal CRP/ESR — confirm with supervised temperature measurement.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the reality of PUO outcomes by geography and overall?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Infection predominates in developing nations, non-infectious inflammatory disease in industrialised nations — and a large proportion (up to ~half in some series) remain undiagnosed despite full workup (many resolve spontaneously, a reassuring point).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the classic don't-miss trio in PUO?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• TB
  • lymphoma
  • and giant cell arteritis.
GCA is the sight-threatening one: think of it in ANY patient over 50 with PUO, headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication or a very high ESR/CRP — start high-dose steroids on suspicion, BEFORE the biopsy (oral prednisolone 40–60 mg daily; IV methylprednisolone plus same-day ophthalmology if there are visual symptoms), with biopsy ideally within 1 week and not beyond 2 weeks of starting steroids. A negative biopsy does not exclude GCA.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the highest-yield step in PUO assessment, and what should the history cover?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
History is the highest-yield step:
  • fever pattern/duration
  • travel (malaria, typhoid, TB)
  • animal/occupational exposure (brucellosis, Q fever)
  • sexual history (HIV)
  • drug history (drug fever)
  • TB risk/contacts
  • weight loss / night sweats (B symptoms → lymphoma/TB)
  • joint/skin/eye symptoms (connective tissue)
  • family history (FMF)
  • recent surgery/lines (nosocomial).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why is repeated, thorough examination essential in PUO?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A meticulous, repeated examination is essential — new signs (a murmur, lymphadenopathy, a rash, temporal artery tenderness, splenomegaly) often emerge over time and provide the diagnostic lead.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the red flags in PUO?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Weight loss + night sweats (malignancy/TB)
  • new murmur (endocarditis)
  • localising signs
  • immunocompromise/neutropenia (urgent).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the first-line (baseline) investigations in PUO?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
First check the fever is documented on a chart by staff. Then:
  • FBC + film
  • U&E
  • LFT
  • CRP/ESR
  • ferritin
  • blood cultures (×3 from 3 different sites, before antibiotics)
  • urinalysis + culture
  • CXR
  • HIV test
  • autoantibodies (ANA, ANCA, RF — low-titre positives are common and non-specific, and endocarditis and lymphoma can themselves produce them)
  • TFTs
  • LDH
  • blood film for malaria if travel.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the second-line (directed) investigations in PUO?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• CT chest/abdomen/pelvis (occult abscess, lymphadenopathy, malignancy)
  • echocardiography (endocarditis — TTE → TOE, and a normal TTE does not exclude it)
  • viral serology (EBV, CMV, hepatitis)
  • TB workup — sputum ×3 for AFB and culture, CT chest, and tissue for culture and histology
  • tumour markers.
Two caveats: a negative IGRA does not exclude active TB and a normal CXR does not exclude miliary or extrapulmonary TB. For culture-negative endocarditis, the usual reason is antibiotics given before cultures — if the patient is stable, discuss stopping them and re-culturing; otherwise send serology for Coxiella burnetii, Bartonella and Brucella.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the third-line (specialist) investigations in PUO?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• PET-CT (increasingly useful for occult malignancy/inflammation/infection)
  • biopsy (lymph node, bone marrow, temporal artery, liver)
  • invasive imaging.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the governing principle of investigating PUO?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Investigate logically and in a directed way — let history and examination steer the next test rather than ordering everything at once. Avoid empirical 'blind' antibiotics/steroids unless the patient is unstable, as they obscure the diagnosis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the fundamental management principle of PUO?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Treat the underlying cause once found — PUO itself isn't treated, the diagnosis is.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: When should blind empirical treatment be avoided in PUO, and what are the exceptions?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Avoid blind empirical treatment (antibiotics or steroids) in the stable patient — it masks the picture. Exceptions:
  • neutropenic/immunocompromised (empirical IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour)
  • clinical instability or sepsis
  • and strong suspicion of giant cell arteritis — urgent steroids to prevent blindness, started BEFORE the temporal artery biopsy, which follows within 1–2 weeks and stays informative for some weeks after steroids are begun.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the appropriate approach in the stable, improving PUO patient who remains undiagnosed?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A significant proportion resolve spontaneously undiagnosed — careful follow-up rather than ever-more-invasive testing is appropriate in the stable, improving patient.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the two linked jobs of travel medicine?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The pre-travel consultation (risk assessment, vaccines, advice) and specifically malaria prophylaxis (the most examinable part).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the ABCD organising framework for malaria prophylaxis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Awareness of risk
  • Bite prevention
  • Chemoprophylaxis
  • Diagnose promptly (treat any fever after travel as malaria until proven otherwise).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the single most important safety message in malaria prophylaxis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: No prophylaxis is 100% effective — any fever during or after travel to an endemic area is malaria until proven otherwise, and bite avoidance matters as much as the drugs.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What does the risk assessment in a pre-travel consultation cover?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Destination
  • rural vs urban
  • duration
  • season
  • activities
  • accommodation
  • plus patient factors (age, pregnancy, immunosuppression, comorbidities, current meds).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What travel vaccines are considered in a pre-travel consultation?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Routine boosters + destination-specific —
  • hepatitis A
  • typhoid
  • yellow fever (certificate may be legally required for entry, and becomes valid 10 days after vaccination)
  • rabies
  • Japanese encephalitis
  • cholera
  • meningococcal ACWY (e.g. Hajj).
Yellow fever and oral typhoid are LIVE — contraindicated in significant immunosuppression and in pregnancy; the rest are non-live. A pre-travel rabies course does not remove the need for urgent assessment after a bite, but it means only two further doses and no immunoglobulin.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What general advice is given in a pre-travel consultation, and what is the commonest cause of traveller death?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Food/water hygiene (travellers' diarrhoea)
  • sun/heat
  • accident/road-traffic risk (the commonest cause of preventable death in young travellers — cardiovascular events cause most deaths abroad overall)
  • STI/blood-borne risk
  • travel insurance.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What does bite avoidance (the 'B', which applies to all) involve?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Anopheles bites from dusk to dawn — that is when the precautions matter. DEET 20–50% on exposed skin, reapplied as directed (50% DEET is first-line and safe in pregnancy and in infants over 2 months); apply sunscreen first, then repellent.
  • Cover up after dusk
  • sleep under an insecticide (permethrin)-treated bed net
  • permethrin-treated clothing
  • air-conditioned or screened rooms.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What organism causes malaria, how is it transmitted, and which species is the deadly one?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Caused by Plasmodium (mosquito-borne, Anopheles); five species, but P. falciparum is the deadly one (cerebral malaria, the bulk of travel deaths).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which malaria species have a dormant liver stage, and why does this matter?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: P. vivax and P. ovale have a dormant liver stage (hypnozoites) → they can relapse months later even after correct prophylaxis (the key to understanding primaquine).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why are standard prophylactic drugs called 'suppressive', and what follows from this?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Chloroquine, mefloquine and doxycycline are "suppressive" — they act on the blood stage, not the liver — so they must be continued for 4 weeks after leaving, to kill parasites emerging from the liver. Atovaquone-proguanil is the exception: it also kills the pre-erythrocytic liver stage ("causal" prophylaxis), so it stops 1 week after leaving. No prophylactic drug kills hypnozoites, which is why vivax and ovale can still relapse.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone): dosing, timing, side effects and notes.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: 250/100 mg, one tablet daily with food; start 1–2 days before, stop 1 week after leaving. Best tolerated overall; GI upset. Shortest post-travel course because it also acts on the liver stage; expensive; good for short trips. Absorption depends on fat, so take it with food or a milky drink. Not for prophylaxis if eGFR/creatinine clearance is below 30 mL/min (proguanil accumulates → pancytopenia) (BNF).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe doxycycline: dosing, timing, side effects and contraindications.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: 100 mg daily; start 1–2 days before, continue 4 weeks after leaving. GI upset, pill oesophagitis, photosensitivity (warn about high-factor sunscreen and sun avoidance), Candida vaginitis. Cheapest; contraindicated in pregnancy and children under 12; take with food and stay upright.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe mefloquine (Lariam): dosing, timing, side effects and contraindications.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: 250 mg once weekly, same day each week; start 2–3 weeks before, continue 4 weeks after leaving. Neuropsychiatric side effects — vivid or abnormal dreams, insomnia, anxiety, depression, and rarely psychosis or seizures. Contraindicated in convulsions/epilepsy and in any current or previous psychiatric disorder (depression, anxiety, psychosis, schizophrenia). (MHRA) reactions may persist for months or years after stopping — issue the patient alert card, and tell the traveller to stop it and seek medical advice if neuropsychiatric symptoms develop. Starting early allows tolerability to be checked before departure.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe chloroquine (± proguanil): dosing, timing, side effects and notes.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Chloroquine 310 mg base once weekly PLUS proguanil 200 mg once daily — only the chloroquine is weekly. Start 1 week before, continue 4 weeks after leaving. GI upset; retinopathy with long-term high cumulative dose. Only for the few remaining chloroquine-sensitive areas, so rarely recommended.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the '4 weeks after' vs '1 week after' rule for malaria prophylaxis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Only atovaquone-proguanil stops at 1 week (it hits the liver stage); the suppressive agents (doxycycline, mefloquine, chloroquine) need 4 weeks to cover emerging blood-stage parasites.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the selection logic for choosing a malaria chemoprophylaxis agent?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Atovaquone-proguanil and doxycycline are first-choice for most (best tolerated); mefloquine's neuropsychiatric profile makes it the one to avoid in psychiatric/epilepsy history, but its weekly dose suits long trips. Choice also depends on
  • the resistance pattern of the destination
  • cost
  • pregnancy
  • and tolerability.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is malaria prophylaxis approached in pregnancy?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Malaria is more severe in pregnancy, so advise against travel to a malarious area. If travel is unavoidable:
  • mefloquine may be used, including in the first trimester where falciparum risk is high
  • chloroquine + proguanil (with folic acid 5 mg daily) where appropriate
  • doxycycline is contraindicated
  • atovaquone-proguanil is not recommended unless there is no suitable alternative.
Where mefloquine resistance is documented there is no safe effective regimen — advise against travel (UKHSA).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the role of primaquine in relapse prevention, and what must be checked first?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Primaquine is the only drug acting on liver hypnozoites — used as presumptive anti-relapse therapy after significant exposure (P. vivax / ovale); must check G6PD first (primaquine → haemolysis in G6PD deficiency).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is malaria prophylaxis managed in children, the immunocompromised, and long-term travellers?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Individualised, specialist advice. Three groups to flag:
  • VFR travellers (visiting friends and relatives) are the biggest group of imported UK malaria cases — they often skip pre-travel advice and assume they are still immune, but semi-immunity is lost after a year or two living in the UK (UKHSA)
  • Asplenic or hyposplenic travellers are at high risk of severe malaria
  • Adherence is the commonest reason prophylaxis fails — same time each day or week, complete the full post-travel course, and if a dose is missed take it as soon as remembered without doubling up.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the 'D' (diagnose promptly) can't-miss rule for malaria?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Any febrile illness during or up to a year after travel to an endemic area = malaria until excluded.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is malaria diagnosed, and what is needed to exclude it?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Thick and thin blood films (thick = detect parasites, thin = speciate + quantify) — three films to exclude — repeat at 12–24 h and again 24 h later; one negative film never excludes malaria; rapid antigen tests are an adjunct.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why is falciparum malaria significant, and what is its public-health status?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Falciparum is a medical emergency → urgent treatment. Malaria is a notifiable disease.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is infective diarrhoea (gastroenteritis), and what is the examined skill?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: GI infection causing diarrhoea ± vomiting — mostly self-limiting and managed with rehydration. The skill examined is recognising the specific organisms by their clinical signatures and knowing the few that change management.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is Fork 1 (bloody vs non-bloody) in infective diarrhoea?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Inflammatory / invasive (bloody) vs secretory / watery (non-bloody).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is Fork 2 (antibiotics or not) — the highest-yield rule in infective diarrhoea?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Never give antibiotics if E. coli O157 (Shiga-toxin) is possible — they increase HUS risk.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the source, incubation and signature feature of Campylobacter?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Source: undercooked poultry, travellers' diarrhoea. Incubation 2–5 days. Bloody diarrhoea. Signature: severe abdo pain (mimics appendicitis); Guillain-Barré + reactive arthritis sequelae. It is the commonest bacterial cause.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the source, incubation and signature feature of E. coli O157 (STEC)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Source: undercooked beef, unpasteurised milk, petting farms. Incubation typically 3–4 days (range 1–14). Bloody diarrhoea. Signature: Shiga toxin → HUS; antibiotics AND antimotility agents both increase HUS risk.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the source, incubation and signature feature of Salmonella?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Source: eggs, poultry, raw food. Incubation 6–72 h (usually 12–72 h). ± bloody diarrhoea. Signature: can cause bacteraemia; reactive arthritis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the source, incubation and signature feature of Shigella?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Source: faecal-oral, contaminated water. Incubation 1–2 days. Bloody diarrhoea. Signature: Shiga toxin in S. dysenteriae type 1 only → HUS; S. sonnei, the usual UK isolate, does not produce it.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the source, incubation and signature feature of Staph aureus (toxin)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Source: reheated / handled food. Incubation 1–6 h (fast). Watery diarrhoea. Signature: rapid-onset vomiting (preformed enterotoxin).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the source, incubation and signature feature of Bacillus cereus?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Source: reheated rice. Incubation 1–5 h (emetic). Watery diarrhoea. Signature: the 'fried rice' vomiting.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the source, incubation and signature feature of C. difficile?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Source: post-antibiotics. Incubation variable. Profuse watery diarrhoea (blood uncommon). Signature: pseudomembranous colitis; treat with oral vancomycin first-line, fidaxomicin second-line.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the source, incubation and signature feature of Norovirus?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Source: outbreaks (cruise ships, wards). Incubation 24–48 h. Watery + vomiting. Signature: highly contagious. It is the commonest viral cause.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the source, incubation and signature feature of Rotavirus?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Source: faecal-oral spread, typically children under 5 in nurseries. Incubation 1–2 days. Watery diarrhoea. Signature: vaccine-preventable.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the source, incubation and signature feature of Giardia?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Source: travel, contaminated water. Incubation 1–3 weeks. Chronic, non-bloody, fatty diarrhoea. Signature: malabsorption / steatorrhoea → metronidazole.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the two timing extremes worth holding in infective diarrhoea, and what does bloody diarrhoea imply?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Very fast (1–6 h) = preformed toxin (Staph aureus, Bacillus cereus). Bloody = invasive (Campylobacter, E. coli O157, Salmonella, Shigella).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe Campylobacter in detail — type, presentation and incubation.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• A Gram-negative, curved/spiral rod
  • the commonest bacterial cause of gastroenteritis in the UK
  • from undercooked poultry, untreated water, unpasteurised milk
  • a common cause of travellers’ diarrhoea
Incubation 2–5 days, resolving over 3–6 days. Bloody diarrhoea with abdominal pain that can mimic appendicitis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: When are antibiotics used for Campylobacter, and what is first-line? What are its sequelae?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Antibiotics are not routine — most cases are self-limiting. Treat if severe (high fever, bloody stools, high-output diarrhoea, or symptoms worsening or lasting more than a week) or high-risk (immunocompromised/HIV, pregnancy, frail elderly). Clarithromycin is first-line, or azithromycin; they work best started within the first ~3 days. Ciprofloxacin is NOT a reliable choice — UK Campylobacter fluoroquinolone resistance is high, and systemic fluoroquinolones are restricted anyway (MHRA). In bloody diarrhoea, withhold antibiotics until E. coli O157 has been excluded.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does E. coli O157:H7 (STEC) cause its key complication?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It produces Shiga toxin → abdominal cramps, bloody diarrhoea, vomiting. The toxin binds Gb3 receptors on (mainly renal) endothelium, causing endothelial injury and microthrombi that mechanically shear red cells — a MICROangiopathic haemolytic anaemia — producing haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS: MAHA + thrombocytopenia + AKI). Avoid antibiotics (they increase HUS risk).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is THE RULE for E. coli O157, and what is its source?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Antibiotics increase the risk of HUS → avoid antibiotics if E. coli O157 is possible (the single most-tested fact in this topic). Source: undercooked beef, unpasteurised dairy, petting farms.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the HUS triad, and how common is it in O157 infections?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: AKI + microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia + thrombocytopenia — commonest in children under 5. It complicates a minority of STEC infections: classically of the order of 10–15% of infected children, and far fewer across all ages. The clotting screen is NORMAL, which distinguishes it from DIC.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Describe Salmonella gastroenteritis — source, incubation, presentation and antibiotic approach.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: From eggs, poultry, raw foods; incubation 6–72 h; watery (± bloody) diarrhoea, cramps, fever, vomiting. Usually self-limiting: antibiotics do NOT shorten uncomplicated illness and may prolong faecal carriage, so treat with rehydration alone. Reserve antibiotics for severe or invasive disease and high-risk patients (infants, frail elderly, immunocompromised, prosthetic material, sickle cell disease).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is Salmonella gastroenteritis distinct from typhoid / enteric fever?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Typhoid / enteric fever (Salmonella Typhi or Paratyphi) is a systemic illness — a returning traveller, typically from South Asia, with fever and headache, constipation before diarrhoea, relative bradycardia and rose spots. It is always treated with antibiotics and is notifiable. A small minority become chronic carriers, the organism persisting in the gallbladder (associated with gallstones) and shed in stool long after recovery. This is distinct from the gastroenteritis caused by non-typhoidal Salmonella.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What should the history cover in infective diarrhoea?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Onset/duration
  • blood in stool
  • vomiting
  • food / travel / contact history
  • antibiotic use (C. diff)
  • immunosuppression

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the main thing that matters on clinical assessment of infective diarrhoea, and what are its signs?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Assess dehydration — the priority assessment in the unwell patient:
  • dry mucous membranes
  • reduced skin turgor
  • tachycardia
  • hypotension
  • reduced urine output
  • prolonged CRT

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the red flags in infective diarrhoea?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Bloody diarrhoea, high fever
  • signs of HUS (reduced urine / pallor / bruising)
  • severe dehydration / shock, immunocompromise, recent hospital / antibiotics (C. diff)

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Do most cases of infective diarrhoea need investigation, and when is stool MC&S indicated?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Most cases need no investigation — it is self-limiting and a clinical diagnosis. Stool MC&S (+ ova/cysts/parasites) if:
  • bloody diarrhoea
  • systemically unwell
  • immunocompromised
  • recent travel
  • suspected outbreak
  • or symptoms >7 days

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What targeted investigations are used in infective diarrhoea (Shiga-toxin, C. diff, bloods)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Stool Shiga-toxin / E. coli O157 testing if bloody (it informs the no-antibiotics decision); C. diff toxin if recent antibiotics; bloods if unwell — and repeat them in suspected STEC: FBC (HUS — anaemia + thrombocytopenia, film for schistocytes), U&E (AKI and dehydration), CRP, cultures if septic. A normal clotting screen distinguishes HUS from DIC.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the mainstay of management for infective diarrhoea?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Rehydration — oral rehydration solution first-line; IV fluids if severe dehydration / shock / vomiting.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the supportive management of infective diarrhoea, and which agents must be avoided?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Antiemetics if needed. Avoid antimotility agents (loperamide) in bloody / inflammatory diarrhoea, in suspected C. difficile, and in anyone who could have E. coli O157 — risk of toxic megacolon and prolonged toxin exposure. In suspected STEC, antibiotics AND antimotility agents are both avoided because each increases the risk of HUS.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Summarise the selective antibiotic approach in infective diarrhoea.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Not routine — most are self-limiting; antibiotics can prolong carriage or precipitate HUS. Avoid entirely if E. coli O157 possible (raises HUS). Consider for:
  • severe campylobacter/shigella
  • systemically unwell
  • immunocompromised
  • specific organisms (giardia → metronidazole, C. diff → vancomycin/fidaxomicin)

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the public-health measures for infective diarrhoea?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Notify on clinical SUSPICION — do not wait for the stool result. The notifiable entries are food poisoning, infectious bloody diarrhoea, haemolytic uraemic syndrome and enteric fever; notification goes to the local UKHSA health protection team. Infection control: isolate, hand hygiene — alcohol gel is ineffective against C. diff and norovirus, so use soap and water. Exclusion from work, school or nursery until 48 h symptom-free; for E. coli O157 and enteric fever, risk groups (food handlers, care staff, under-5s at nursery) also need negative stool samples before returning.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the complications of infective diarrhoea?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• HUS (E. coli O157 / STEC — the can’t-miss: no antibiotics, no loperamide; Shigella dysenteriae type 1 rarely)
  • Guillain-Barré and reactive arthritis (post-campylobacter)
  • dehydration / AKI / shock
  • bacteraemia (Salmonella)
  • toxic megacolon
  • post-infectious IBS
  • C. difficile colitis

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is meningococcal disease, and what organism causes it?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Invasive infection with Neisseria meningitidis (a Gram-negative diplococcus) — a medical emergency.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What distinguishes meningococcal meningitis from meningococcal septicaemia?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Meningococcal meningitis: N. meningitidis infects the meninges + CSF → the meningitic picture. Meningococcal septicaemia: the bacteria invade the bloodstream → non-blanching rash + shock — the more lethal form.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the single most important action for suspected meningococcal disease in the community?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Give IV or IM benzylpenicillin (under 1 year 300 mg, 1–9 years 600 mg, 10 years and over 1.2 g) and arrange immediate transfer — but giving it must never delay the transfer.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Contrast meningococcal meningitis and septicaemia by site and dominant features.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Meningitis: site is meninges + CSF; dominant features are headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, fever. Septicaemia: site is the bloodstream; dominant features are a non-blanching petechial/purpuric rash and shock.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Contrast the key danger of meningococcal meningitis vs septicaemia.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Meningitis: raised ICP, neuro damage. Septicaemia: septic shock, DIC, Waterhouse-Friderichsen.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What causes the non-blanching rash in meningococcal disease, and what is the key caveat about its absence?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It is caused by the septicaemia. It can be absent in meningococcal disease — its absence never excludes the diagnosis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the bacterial causes of meningitis by age group?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Neonates → Group B Strep, E. coli, Listeria
  • Children/adults → N. meningitidis, S. pneumoniae
  • Aged 60 and over, immunocompromised or pregnant → add Listeria cover

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the viral causes of meningitis, and how do they compare in frequency and severity?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Enteroviruses, HSV, VZV — viral is the commonest overall and usually milder.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Which two organisms are the big bacterial causes of meningitis in the immunocompetent child/adult?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Meningococcus + pneumococcus.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the classic triad of the meningitic picture, and how sensitive is it?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Fever + neck stiffness + altered mental status — all three are present in fewer than half of cases, so its absence never excludes it. Nearly all patients have at least two of headache, fever, neck stiffness and altered mental state. Other features: photophobia, vomiting.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the meningism signs Kernig's and Brudzinski's?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Kernig's: pain on knee extension with the hip flexed
  • Brudzinski's: involuntary hip/knee flexion on neck flexion

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the features of the septicaemic picture?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Non-blanching petechial/purpuric rash (the glass/tumbler test — doesn’t fade under pressure)
  • cold peripheries
  • limb pain
  • and signs of shock (tachycardia, hypotension, prolonged CRT)
Beware: the rash may start as a blanching, maculopapular, "viral-looking" rash and only later become petechial — recheck it, and undress the patient to look everywhere.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does meningococcal disease present atypically in babies / young children?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Non-specific: fever, lethargy, poor feeding, bulging fontanelle, high-pitched cry, hypotonia, seizures — easily missed.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the red flags for raised ICP that contraindicate a lumbar puncture?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Reduced/fluctuating GCS
  • focal neurology
  • seizures
  • papilloedema
  • and bradycardia + hypertension

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What blood investigations are used in meningococcal disease, and which is the key confirmatory test?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Cultures
  • meningococcal PCR (key confirmatory test — remains positive after antibiotics)
  • FBC
  • U&E
  • CRP
  • glucose
  • clotting (DIC)
  • lactate
  • ABG

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: When should a lumbar puncture be done in suspected meningitis, and when is it contraindicated?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: LP + CSF analysis ideally before antibiotics, but never delay antibiotics in an acutely unwell patient. Contraindicated if raised ICP / shock / coagulopathy (do CT + treat first).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: On CSF analysis, how do bacterial and viral meningitis differ in appearance and cell type?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Bacterial: cloudy/turbid appearance with markedly raised neutrophils. Viral: clear appearance with raised lymphocytes.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: On CSF analysis, how do bacterial and viral meningitis differ in protein and glucose?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Bacterial: high protein, low glucose (CSF:plasma <½). Viral: normal/mildly raised protein, normal glucose.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why do bacterial and viral meningitis produce their characteristic CSF patterns, and what is the TB/fungal pattern?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Bacteria release proteins and consume glucose (→ high protein, low glucose); the immune system sends neutrophils to bacteria and lymphocytes to viruses. TB/fungal meningitis: lymphocytes + high protein + low glucose.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the community / pre-hospital management of suspected bacterial meningitis or meningococcal disease?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Strongly suspected meningococcal disease: IV or IM benzylpenicillin (under 1 year 300 mg, 1–9 years 600 mg, 10 years and over 1.2 g), or ceftriaxone, at the earliest opportunity — but it must NEVER delay transfer. Withhold it only for a known severe (anaphylactic) allergy. For suspected bacterial meningitis without meningococcal features, give pre-hospital antibiotics only if transfer is significantly delayed.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the mainstay empirical hospital antibiotic for meningococcal disease, and when is amoxicillin added?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime) — a third-generation cephalosporin — is the mainstay at any age. Add IV amoxicillin for Listeria cover: babies under 3 months (automatic), adults 60 and over, pregnancy, and the immunocompromised — cephalosporins do not cover Listeria.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: When is vancomycin added to empirical hospital treatment for meningitis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: If there is a risk of penicillin- or cephalosporin-resistant pneumococcus: travel outside the UK in the last 6 months, or prolonged or multiple antibiotic exposure.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the role of dexamethasone in bacterial meningitis, and when is it given?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: In bacterial meningitis it reduces neurological complications, especially hearing loss, with the greatest benefit in pneumococcal disease — given with or just before the first antibiotic dose in anyone over 3 months. It is NOT routinely given in meningococcal disease (NICE), where it has been associated with higher mortality. Antibiotics are never delayed to give it.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What does supportive management of meningococcal disease involve, and what is the antibiotic duration?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Treat septic shock (Sepsis Six, fluids, vasopressors)
  • manage raised ICP
  • correct DIC
Duration: IV ceftriaxone reviewed at 5 days — stop if recovered, otherwise seek infection specialist advice (contrast: pneumococcal 10 days, Listeria 21 days).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What public-health step must not be forgotten in meningococcal disease?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It is a notifiable disease: notify the proper officer of the local authority — in practice the local UKHSA health protection team — by telephone the same day, on clinical SUSPICION. Never wait for laboratory confirmation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Who needs contact prophylaxis in meningococcal disease, and why?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Close contacts — those with prolonged, close contact in a household-type setting in the 7 days before onset (household members, partners and kissing contacts, students sharing a hall kitchen) — need post-exposure prophylaxis to eradicate nasopharyngeal carriage. Transient contact does not qualify: most classmates, colleagues and healthcare staff need nothing.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the first-line agent for contact prophylaxis in meningococcal disease, and who coordinates it?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Ciprofloxacin, a single oral dose, first-line at any age including pregnancy: 12 years and over 500 mg, 5–11 years 250 mg, under 5 years 125 mg; rifampicin is the alternative. Give it ideally within 24 hours of the case being diagnosed. The index case needs it too before discharge unless treated with ceftriaxone. UKHSA coordinate contact tracing and prophylaxis, and offer contacts vaccination where the serogroup is vaccine-preventable.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the acute complications of meningococcal disease?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Septic shock + DIC
  • Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome (bilateral adrenal haemorrhage → adrenal failure)
  • raised ICP / cerebral oedema, seizures, death

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the chronic / sequelae of meningococcal disease?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Sensorineural hearing loss (commonest — every patient needs a formal hearing assessment, ideally before discharge and within 4 weeks of being well enough to test)
  • neurodevelopmental delay, epilepsy, focal neurology
  • limb / digit loss (purpura fulminans / ischaemia)

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is meningococcal disease prevented?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Vaccination: MenB in infancy and MenACWY for teenagers and university entrants — the separate Hib/MenC dose has been withdrawn from the UK schedule, and MenC protection now comes from the adolescent MenACWY programme. Plus chemoprophylaxis for close contacts. No vaccine covers every serogroup, so vaccination never excludes the diagnosis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the Sepsis-3 definition of sepsis, and why is it a time-critical emergency?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. It is not the infection itself but the body's damaging reaction to it. In septic shock and high-risk sepsis, delay to effective antibiotics costs lives — but in lower-risk patients the priority is to clarify the diagnosis and target the therapy rather than reflexively giving broad-spectrum cover (NICE).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is 'the spine' of the sepsis approach?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Recognise early → stratify the risk with NEWS2 → deliver the Sepsis Six with the urgency that risk demands (within 1 hour if high risk) → identify and control the source.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the sepsis severity ladder?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Infection → sepsis (organ dysfunction) → septic shock (refractory hypotension + raised lactate).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is septic shock defined under Sepsis-3?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Sepsis with persisting hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP ≥65 plus lactate >2 despite adequate fluid resuscitation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is bacteraemia, and how does it differ from sepsis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Bacteria in the blood — distinct from sepsis, as it may be transient or harmless.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the status of SIRS in the Sepsis-3 era?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: SIRS — temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate and white cell count derangement — was the pre-Sepsis-3 basis for defining sepsis. It was abandoned because it is non-specific (trauma, burns, pancreatitis and surgery all trigger it without infection) and insensitive (patients can have organ dysfunction from infection without meeting two criteria). It is not the UK screening tool — NEWS2 is. The same reform retired the term "severe sepsis".

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Outline the early pathophysiology of sepsis from infection to cytokine storm.
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Infection → release of pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) → massive innate immune activation → cytokine storm (the dysregulation).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why does sepsis produce a 'warm' distributive shock?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: The cytokine storm causes widespread vasodilation + capillary leak (NO-mediated) → distributive ('warm') shock.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How does sepsis progress to multi-organ dysfunction at the microvascular level?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Microvascular thrombosis + endothelial injury → tissue hypoperfusion → lactate rises (anaerobic metabolism) → multi-organ dysfunction. It can also cause DIC (consumption of clotting factors), AKI, ARDS and encephalopathy.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Who is vulnerable to sepsis (risk factors)?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Extremes of age (very young, elderly)
  • immunocompromise (chemotherapy, steroids, diabetes, HIV, asplenia)
  • indwelling devices (lines, catheters)
  • recent surgery / instrumentation
  • pregnancy / peripartum
  • IVDU and chronic disease

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Is sepsis a clinical or test-based diagnosis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Sepsis is a clinical diagnosis — no single test rules it in or out. A normal lactate, a normal temperature and a low qSOFA all fail to exclude it.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What tool is used to screen for and stratify sepsis risk in UK adults, and what are its limits?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: NEWS2 — the UK standard track-and-trigger score for adults aged 16 or over in acute hospital, acute mental health and ambulance settings (NICE). It is more sensitive than qSOFA and it sets the urgency of antibiotics (NEWS2 ≥7 high risk, 5–6 moderate, 1–4 lower). Limits: it is not validated in pregnancy, in under-16s, or on end-of-life pathways, and a worrying patient with a low score still needs review.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the qSOFA criteria, and what is its current role?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: A quick bedside score — GCS <15, RR ≥22, SBP ≤100 mmHg — one point each; ≥2 flags a higher risk of a poor outcome, which is not the same as NICE’s "high risk" category. It is no longer used as the screening tool (less sensitive than early warning scores) and a low qSOFA does not exclude sepsis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What does the SIRS score assess?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Temp, HR, RR and WCC derangement (the older criteria).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the red flags that prompt urgent action in sepsis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Altered mentation
  • SBP ≤90 (or a drop >40 from baseline)
  • RR ≥25
  • SpO₂ needing O₂
  • lactate >2
  • reduced urine output
  • mottled/ashen skin
  • non-blanching rash

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the Sepsis Six, and how quickly must it be delivered?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: "Take 3, give 3" — TAKE blood cultures, lactate and urine output; GIVE oxygen, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and IV fluids. Timing is risk-based (NICE): within 1 hour for high-risk sepsis or septic shock (NEWS2 ≥7 or a red-flag criterion); within 3 hours for moderate risk (NEWS2 5–6); within 6 hours for lower risk (NEWS2 1–4). Ensure a senior clinician attends the high-risk patient.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the three 'GIVE' components of the Sepsis Six?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: 1. Oxygen — target 94–98% (88–92% if at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure). 2. IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (empirical, per local guidelines). 3. IV fluids — isotonic crystalloid 250 mL over 10–15 min, reassess after each bolus, up to 1000 mL then senior advice (NICE). In pregnancy 500 mL over under 15 min; in under-16s 10 mL/kg (max 250 mL).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the three 'TAKE' components of the Sepsis Six?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: 1. Blood cultures (before antibiotics — but never delay antibiotics for them in a shocked patient). 2. Lactate (venous or arterial gas). 3. Urine output — measure it, catheterise only if needed, aim >0.5 mL/kg/h. The revised bundle also requires a senior clinician to attend and ongoing monitoring.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: Why is antibiotic timing the single most important intervention, and how does this interact with blood cultures?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Give broad-spectrum antibiotics immediately, ideally within 1 hour, for septic shock or high-likelihood sepsis. Take blood cultures before antibiotics where possible — but do not delay antibiotics for them in shock.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How should fluids be used in sepsis resuscitation?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Use dynamic measures to guide resuscitation; reassess after each bolus — avoid both under- and over-resuscitation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is source control, and why are antibiotics alone sometimes insufficient?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Antibiotics alone are not enough if there is a focus of infection that needs physical removal or drainage. Source control is the definitive step — a collection of pus under pressure will not clear with antibiotics alone.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the source control for an abscess, and for an obstructed + infected kidney?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Abscess → drainage (radiological or surgical). Obstructed + infected kidney → nephrostomy / stent.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the source control for ascending cholangitis, and for an infected line/device?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Ascending cholangitis → ERCP biliary decompression. Infected line / device → remove it.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the source control for necrotising fasciitis / perforation, and for an empyema?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Necrotising fasciitis / perforation → urgent surgical debridement / repair. Empyema → chest drain.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the overarching principle of source control?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Find the source and control it — the same logic as the cholangitis and infected-stone notes.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How should a patient be reassessed after the Sepsis Six?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Repeat the lactate after resuscitation (within about an hour) and reassess observations, conscious level and urine output. Not improving, lactate not clearing, or persisting hypotension → escalate to senior and critical care; if there is no response within 1 hour of the first antibiotic, a consultant should attend in person (NICE).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is septic shock managed when hypotension is fluid-refractory?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Fluid-refractory hypotension → vasopressors (noradrenaline first-line) to maintain MAP ≥65.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: When and how are antibiotics de-escalated in sepsis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: Review the antibiotic at 48–72 hours against the cultures, sensitivities and the clinical response: de-escalate from empirical broad-spectrum to the narrowest effective agent, switch IV to oral once the patient is improving and able to absorb, and set a stop date. If cultures are negative but the patient has clearly improved, review whether antibiotics are still needed at all.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: How is organ dysfunction treated in sepsis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
Treat organ dysfunction:
  • AKI (may need RRT)
  • ARDS (ventilation)
  • and DIC

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What are the complications of sepsis, including long-term?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back:
• Septic shock
  • multi-organ dysfunction (AKI, ARDS, hepatic, encephalopathy)
  • DIC
  • death
Long-term: post-sepsis syndrome (physical / cognitive impairment).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.front: What is the significance of a lactate >2 in sepsis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.back: It marks tissue hypoperfusion, upgrades a moderate-risk patient to high risk, and is the threshold in the septic shock definition. Over 4 mmol/L demands urgent senior and critical care input. Repeat the lactate after resuscitation — clearance tracks the response. It is not specific to sepsis, and a normal lactate does not exclude it.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 33-year-old man with advanced HIV (CD4 40) is being treated for cryptococcal meningitis with liposomal amphotericin B and flucytosine. On day 3 he remains drowsy with severe headache and new diplopia; the CSF opening pressure at diagnosis was 38 cmH₂O. Which additional measure is most important?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Raised intracranial pressure is the hallmark of cryptococcal meningitis and the main cause of early death and cranial nerve palsies; it is relieved by repeated therapeutic LPs, not by drugs. Dexamethasone does not treat this pressure and worsens outcomes in cryptococcal disease. Switching to fluconazole abandons effective induction therapy (fluconazole is for consolidation and maintenance). Antiretrovirals are essential but are optimised once the infection is controlled, since starting them too early risks IRIS. Shunting is reserved for pressure that persists despite repeated LPs.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 28-year-old man with newly diagnosed HIV (CD4 90) has a 3-week history of dry cough, fever and breathlessness on exertion. His chest is clear, CXR shows bilateral perihilar interstitial shadowing, and on air his SpO₂ is 89% with PaO₂ 7.6 kPa. What is the most appropriate treatment?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Dry cough, exertional desaturation, a clear chest and perihilar infiltrates at CD4 <200 is Pneumocystis pneumonia, treated with high-dose co-trimoxazole. Corticosteroids are added because he is hypoxic (PaO₂ <9.3 kPa or SpO₂ <92% on air), so co-trimoxazole without steroids undertreats him. Voriconazole covers Aspergillus and amphotericin with flucytosine treats cryptococcal meningitis; neither has useful activity against Pneumocystis. Standard pneumonia antibacterials do not cover it either, and the subacute course with a clear chest argues against bacterial pneumonia.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 45-year-old woman with AML has been neutropenic for 14 days. Despite meropenem she develops fever, pleuritic chest pain and haemoptysis, and CT chest shows a nodule surrounded by ground-glass (the halo sign). Which antifungal is first-line?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Neutropenic fever with haemoptysis and a CT halo sign is invasive pulmonary aspergillosis; voriconazole (or isavuconazole) is first-line, with liposomal amphotericin B as an alternative. Fluconazole has no mould activity at all. Echinocandins such as caspofungin are not first-line for Aspergillus and are reserved for salvage or combination use. Griseofulvin and terbinafine treat dermatophyte (skin, hair and nail) infection and have no role in invasive disease.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 54-year-old man with type 1 diabetes is admitted in ketoacidosis and started on a fixed-rate insulin infusion. He has left facial pain, peri-orbital swelling, proptosis and a black necrotic eschar on the hard palate. Liposomal amphotericin B is commenced. Which additional step is most important?
options: Hyperbaric oxygen as the next intervention
Urgent surgical debridement of the sinuses
Intravenous caspofungin as a second agent
A prolonged course of oral fluconazole
Repeat CT sinuses in 48 hours to reassess
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Urgent surgical debridement of the sinuses
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: This is rhino-orbito-cerebral mucormycosis, an angioinvasive mould infection of the diabetic in ketoacidosis. Because the fungus thromboses vessels, antifungal drug does not reach necrotic tissue, so urgent surgical debridement alongside liposomal amphotericin B and correction of the DKA is what changes survival. Fluconazole and echinocandins have no activity against the Mucorales, so neither adding nor substituting them helps. Hyperbaric oxygen is at best adjunctive and does not replace surgery, and waiting to re-image allows intracranial spread within hours to days.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 62-year-old man in ICU after emergency bowel surgery is receiving TPN through a tunnelled central line and has had 10 days of piperacillin-tazobactam. Two sets of blood cultures grow Candida albicans. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Start oral fluconazole and remove the line
Await sensitivities, then remove the line
Start voriconazole and keep the line
Start an echinocandin and remove the line
Start an echinocandin and keep the line
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Start an echinocandin and remove the line
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Candidaemia needs both an effective drug and source control: an echinocandin is first-line and the colonised central line must be removed or replaced, with repeat cultures to document clearance. Starting fluconazole first-line is inadequate because azole resistance is common; fluconazole is a step-down once susceptibility is known. Leaving the line in situ allows persistent candidaemia and seeding whatever drug is chosen, and voriconazole is not the first-line agent here. Delaying treatment until sensitivities return increases mortality in a condition where every hour of untreated candidaemia counts.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 47-year-old woman with AML has been neutropenic for 9 days. She has received meropenem and vancomycin for 5 days but remains febrile at 38.9°C, and examination, cultures and CT have identified no source. What is the most appropriate next step?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Persistent neutropenic fever despite 4–5 days of appropriate broad-spectrum antibacterials is the classic trigger for empirical antifungal therapy, because invasive candidiasis and aspergillosis are the commonest occult causes. Piling on further antibacterials treats an organism that has already failed to respond, and stopping antibacterials in a neutropenic patient risks fulminant Gram-negative sepsis. Antivirals are not indicated without mucocutaneous or organ-specific features. Colony-stimulating factor may shorten neutropenia but does not treat the undiagnosed infection driving the fever.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A neutropenic patient with AML undergoes biopsy of a cavitating lung nodule. Histology shows narrow, septate hyphae branching at acute (~45°) angles, invading blood vessels. Which organism is responsible?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Narrow septate hyphae branching at acute angles, with angioinvasion in a profoundly neutropenic host, are characteristic of Aspergillus. Rhizopus and the other Mucorales give broad, ribbon-like, aseptate hyphae branching at wide (~90°) angles. Candida appears as budding yeasts with pseudohyphae rather than true invasive hyphae, Cryptococcus as an encapsulated yeast with a clear halo on India ink, and Pneumocystis as cysts on silver stain or immunofluorescence, not as hyphae.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 39-year-old woman with relapsed AML develops fever, unilateral facial swelling and black necrotic nasal turbinates. Biopsy shows broad, ribbon-like, aseptate hyphae branching at wide (~90°) angles. Which antifungal should be started?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Broad aseptate hyphae with wide-angle branching identify the Mucorales, which respond only to liposomal amphotericin B (with urgent surgical debridement); antifungals alone are not enough. This is the key reason to separate Mucor from Aspergillus at the microscope: voriconazole and itraconazole have no reliable activity against the Mucorales, and echinocandins such as anidulafungin also lack cover. Flucytosine is used only in combination for cryptococcal meningitis and has no role here.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 51-year-old man with prolonged neutropenia after allogeneic stem cell transplant develops fever and a new lung nodule with a ground-glass halo. Which test is most specific for invasive aspergillosis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Galactomannan is an Aspergillus cell-wall antigen detectable in serum and BAL, and is the specific supporting test in this setting. β-D-glucan is raised in Candida, Aspergillus and Pneumocystis, so it is a broad pan-fungal marker rather than a specific one. Aspergillus IgG reflects chronic or allergic disease and is unhelpful in an acutely immunosuppressed patient who may not mount antibody. Cryptococcal antigen tests for a different organism, and blood cultures are of little use because moulds, unlike Candida, rarely grow from blood.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with suspected invasive fungal infection has a negative serum β-D-glucan. Which pair of pathogens does this result fail to exclude?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: β-D-glucan is a cell-wall component of many fungi and is positive in Candida, Aspergillus and Pneumocystis, so a negative result makes those three unlikely and every option containing them is wrong. The Mucorales do not have significant β-D-glucan in their wall, and the Cryptococcus capsule masks it, so both give false-negative results. A negative β-D-glucan therefore does not exclude mucormycosis or cryptococcal disease, which need histology plus culture and cryptococcal antigen respectively.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 36-year-old man with HIV (CD4 60) has a 2-week history of headache, fever and malaise with no neck stiffness. LP shows an opening pressure of 38 cmH₂O and CSF cryptococcal antigen is positive. Which induction regimen is appropriate?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Cryptococcal meningitis is induced with liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine, then consolidated and maintained on fluconazole. Echinocandins such as caspofungin have no useful activity against Cryptococcus, so any regimen containing one is ineffective however good the partner drug. Fluconazole alone clears the CSF far more slowly than amphotericin-based induction, and voriconazole is an Aspergillus drug not used for this infection. Dexamethasone does not treat the raised intracranial pressure here; repeated therapeutic LPs do.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 68-year-old woman treated for Candida albicans candidaemia has had her central line removed and repeat blood cultures are negative, but she remains intermittently febrile. Which pair of investigations should be arranged to look for deep seeding?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Candidaemia seeds the eye and the heart valves, so dilated fundoscopy for endophthalmitis and an echocardiogram for endocarditis are the two investigations routinely arranged, especially when candidaemia is persistent or fever continues. Options pairing one correct test with bronchoscopy, colonoscopy, ultrasound or cystoscopy look for sites Candida seeds rarely and would miss sight- or life-threatening disease. Candida meningitis is uncommon in adults, so CT head and LP are not routine in this setting.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with candidaemia is started on anidulafungin. What is the mechanism of action of this class of antifungal?
options: Inhibition of fungal DNA and RNA synthesis
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Echinocandins block synthesis of β-1,3-glucan, a structural polysaccharide of the fungal cell wall, which is why they are fungicidal against Candida, well tolerated and free of major CYP450 interactions. Inhibition of ergosterol synthesis (14-α-demethylase) is the azole mechanism, while binding ergosterol to form membrane pores is how amphotericin B works. Interference with DNA and RNA synthesis describes flucytosine. Antifungals in current use do not act by inhibiting fungal protein synthesis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient is to receive a prolonged course of liposomal amphotericin B for an invasive mould infection. Which monitoring is most important during treatment?
options: Full blood count and blood film
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Amphotericin B binds ergosterol but also damages human renal tubules, producing a rising creatinine with renal potassium and magnesium wasting; the liposomal formulation reduces but does not abolish this, so renal function and these electrolytes are checked regularly. Visual disturbance and colour vision change are the classic voriconazole effect, and marrow suppression is the flucytosine problem that mandates blood count monitoring. Azoles, not polyenes, cause CYP450 interactions and QT prolongation, and hepatotoxicity is likewise an azole issue.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 35-year-old man with poorly controlled asthma has recurrent wheeze and brown mucus plugs. Total IgE is 2400 kU/L with eosinophilia, CXR shows fleeting infiltrates and CT shows central bronchiectasis. What is the diagnosis?
options: Aspergilloma in an old TB cavity
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: ABPA is a hypersensitivity response to Aspergillus in asthma or cystic fibrosis, giving wheeze, mucus plugging, a very high IgE with eosinophilia, fleeting infiltrates and central bronchiectasis. Invasive aspergillosis is tissue invasion in a profoundly immunocompromised host and would not present with years of atopic asthma. An aspergilloma is a fungal ball sitting in a pre-existing cavity, and chronic pulmonary aspergillosis causes cavitation and weight loss over months; neither produces this allergic picture. Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis would be expected to cause vasculitic features such as mononeuritis multiplex.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 41-year-old man with newly diagnosed HIV is asymptomatic with a CD4 count of 140 cells/mm³. Antiretroviral therapy is being started. Which additional prophylaxis should he receive?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis against Pneumocystis is indicated once the CD4 count falls below 200 (or with equivalent immunosuppression) and is continued until immune reconstitution on antiretrovirals. Azithromycin prophylaxis is for disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex at a much lower CD4 threshold, around 50. Aciclovir-type prophylaxis is used only for recurrent herpes, not routinely by CD4 count. Fluconazole and posaconazole are antifungal prophylaxis used in prolonged neutropenia, not for HIV, where Aspergillus is not the expected pathogen.
