conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A gardener sustains a deep puncture wound from a soil-contaminated fork. A week later he develops difficulty opening his mouth, a fixed grimace and painful muscle spasms triggered by noise. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: A deep, soil-contaminated puncture wound gives Clostridium tetani spores the anaerobic conditions they need to germinate, and trismus followed by risus sardonicus and stimulus-triggered spasms in a fully conscious patient is diagnostic. Botulism causes a descending flaccid paralysis with pupillary involvement — the opposite of rigidity — and rabies needs an animal exposure and produces hydrophobia rather than lockjaw. A dystonic reaction follows a dopamine-blocking drug and settles with an anticholinergic. Strychnine poisoning produces very similar spasms, but the muscles relax completely between them, whereas tetanus leaves persistent background rigidity.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the mechanism of the tetanus toxin (tetanospasmin)?
options: Irreversibly inhibits acetylcholinesterase at the synapse
Opens voltage-gated sodium channels in motor axons
Blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction
Blocks postsynaptic dopamine receptors in the striatum
Blocks release of inhibitory GABA and glycine
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Blocks release of inhibitory GABA and glycine
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Tetanospasmin travels retrograde up motor axons to the spinal cord, where it stops inhibitory interneurons releasing GABA and glycine; without that inhibition motor neurons fire unopposed, producing rigidity and stimulus-triggered spasms. The instructive contrast is botulinum toxin, which blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction and therefore causes flaccid paralysis — the same bacterial genus, the opposite clinical picture. Cholinesterase inhibition, as in organophosphate poisoning, gives a cholinergic crisis with fasciculation and secretions, and dopamine blockade causes a drug-induced dystonia, which can mimic trismus but follows an antipsychotic rather than a wound.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A seven-day-old baby, born at home in a low-income setting, is brought in unable to feed, with a stiff arched back and spasms triggered by handling. The umbilical stump was cut with an unsterilised blade. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Neonatal tetanus follows contamination of the umbilical stump, classically when the cord is cut with an unsterile blade, and presents in the first two weeks with failure to feed because of trismus, together with rigidity and stimulus-triggered spasms; it remains a major cause of neonatal death where maternal immunisation is unavailable. Infantile botulism causes the opposite tone — a descending flaccid paralysis and a floppy baby. Kernicterus can produce opisthotonus but occurs in a deeply jaundiced infant in the first days of life, and hypocalcaemic tetany causes jitteriness and carpopedal spasm rather than trismus. Group B streptococcal meningitis gives sepsis and a bulging fontanelle, not reflex spasms.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with tetanus is having frequent painful generalised spasms triggered by noise and touch. Which is the single first-line drug for spasm control?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Benzodiazepines are first line because they enhance GABA-ergic inhibition — exactly the transmission tetanospasmin has blocked — and they simultaneously sedate, reducing the reflex spasms provoked by noise, light and touch. Magnesium and intrathecal baclofen are adjuncts reserved for severe or refractory disease in intensive care, and magnesium is used as much for the autonomic instability as for the spasms. Dantrolene acts on skeletal muscle calcium release and belongs to malignant hyperthermia, while phenytoin is an anticonvulsant and these spasms are not seizures. Nursing in a quiet, darkened room, with ventilation if spasms threaten the airway, is part of the same package.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which antibiotic is recommended to eradicate Clostridium tetani in tetanus?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Metronidazole is preferred because it is reliably active against anaerobes including Clostridium tetani and penetrates the devitalised, poorly perfused tissue in which the organism grows; benzylpenicillin is the accepted alternative. Antibiotics only stop further toxin production — they do nothing about toxin already released, which is why debridement and immunoglobulin matter more to the outcome. Gentamicin and ciprofloxacin have essentially no anaerobic activity and vancomycin has no role here; clindamycin, although anti-anaerobic, is not the recommended agent for tetanus.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 40-year-old completed the full UK childhood tetanus course, the last dose at age 14. He now has a deep wound heavily contaminated with manure. In addition to wound cleaning, what tetanus-specific treatment does he need?
options: A reinforcing dose of vaccine alone
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: What matters is not how many doses he has had but how long ago the last one was. He is adequately primed, but the last dose was over 10 years ago, so he needs a reinforcing dose of vaccine — and because heavy contamination with manure makes this a HIGH-RISK tetanus-prone wound, he needs tetanus immunoglobulin as well, at a separate site. Someone whose last dose was within 10 years needs nothing at all, whatever the wound; someone incompletely immunised needs vaccine plus immunoglobulin for any tetanus-prone wound. Assuming that a completed childhood course means nothing is needed is the error to avoid.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A man recovering from clinical tetanus is being prepared for discharge. Why must he still receive a course of tetanus vaccine?
options: Because the vaccine also relieves ongoing spasms
Because immunity from infection lasts only weeks
Because immunoglobulin blunts the response to the toxin
Because the illness itself does not confer immunity
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Because the illness itself does not confer immunity
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The quantity of tetanospasmin needed to cause disease is far smaller than the quantity needed to provoke an antibody response, so a survivor leaves hospital exactly as susceptible as before and needs a full toxoid course. The distinction from the near-miss option matters: immunity after infection is not merely short-lived, it does not develop at all. Tetanus immunoglobulin neutralises circulating toxin and does not meaningfully impair the response to toxoid given at a separate site, and metronidazole has no effect on antibody formation. The vaccine is prophylaxis for the future, not a treatment for current spasms.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with trismus and generalised rigidity is being assessed for tetanus. Which bedside test supports the diagnosis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: In the spatula test, touching the posterior pharynx provokes a reflex masseter spasm so the patient bites down on the spatula, instead of the normal gag and retch — it is specific to tetanus and takes seconds at the bedside. Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs indicate hypocalcaemic tetany, the main mimic of tetanic spasm, and are negative in tetanus. Kernig's sign indicates meningism, and the Tensilon test is used in myasthenia gravis, where the problem is fatigable weakness rather than rigidity. Tetanus remains a clinical diagnosis — there is no reliable confirmatory laboratory test.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A traveller returns from Asia, having been bitten by a stray dog 6 weeks ago. He now has fever, tingling at the healed bite site, agitation and painful throat spasms when trying to drink. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: A dog bite in an endemic area, an incubation of several weeks, prodromal tingling at the healed bite site and then agitation with hydrophobia is the classic sequence of furious rabies. Tetanus after a bite would give trismus and rigidity without agitation or hydrophobia, and botulism causes a descending flaccid paralysis. Cerebral malaria and Japanese encephalitis both cause fever and encephalopathy in a returning traveller, but neither produces bite-site paraesthesia or water-provoked pharyngeal spasm. Once these symptoms appear prophylaxis is no longer an option and the illness is almost always fatal.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A woman was bitten on the hand by a dog while abroad four weeks ago. The wound has healed and she feels completely well. She has never been vaccinated against rabies. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Reassure her; it is now too late
Give prophylaxis only if the dog is traced
Wait until symptoms appear, then treat
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Rabies has an unusually long and variable incubation period — typically weeks to months, and shorter the nearer the bite is to the head — and that is precisely what makes post-exposure prophylaxis effective, because vaccine-induced antibody can be raised before the virus reaches the central nervous system. Prophylaxis should therefore be started however long ago the exposure occurred, provided symptoms have not yet begun; a delay of weeks is not a reason to withhold it. Serology in someone never vaccinated adds nothing and wastes time, and tracing the animal must never delay treatment. Waiting for symptoms is fatal, since established rabies has no effective treatment.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the histological hallmark of rabies?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Negri bodies are eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions within neurons, classically hippocampal pyramidal cells and cerebellar Purkinje cells, and are the histological hallmark of rabies at post-mortem. Councilman bodies are apoptotic hepatocytes seen in viral hepatitis and yellow fever; owl's-eye intranuclear inclusions indicate cytomegalovirus; Auer rods are cytoplasmic rods in acute myeloid leukaemia; and Heinz bodies are denatured haemoglobin within red cells. Antemortem diagnosis does not rely on histology — saliva PCR, nuchal skin biopsy, CSF and serology are used instead, while the virus spreads centrifugally to the salivary glands.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is hydrophobia in rabies?
options: Reflex vomiting whenever fluid is swallowed
A painless inability to swallow from bulbar weakness
Painful pharyngeal spasm on trying to drink
An irrational psychiatric fear of water
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Painful pharyngeal spasm on trying to drink
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Hydrophobia is a violent reflex spasm of the pharynx and larynx provoked by attempting to drink, and later by the sight or sound of water — the patient is thirsty and wants to drink but cannot, so it is not a phobia in the psychiatric sense. A painless inability to swallow from bulbar weakness is a different picture and fits paralytic rabies or Guillain–Barré syndrome. Laryngeal oedema causes continuous stridor rather than intermittent provoked spasm, and vomiting is not the mechanism. Aerophobia — the identical spasm triggered by a draught of air across the face — is its near-pathognomonic companion.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A man attends the emergency department 30 minutes after a stray dog abroad bit his hand, breaking the skin and drawing blood. What is the single most important first step?
options: Infiltrate rabies immunoglobulin around the wound
Give co-amoxiclav and arrange delayed closure
Wash the wound with soap and water for 15 minutes
Close the wound with primary sutures
Give the first dose of rabies vaccine
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Wash the wound with soap and water for 15 minutes
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Immediate, thorough washing with soap and water for about 15 minutes, ideally followed by a virucidal such as povidone-iodine, physically removes and inactivates virus at the inoculation site and by itself substantially reduces the risk of rabies. Vaccine and immunoglobulin are both essential and follow immediately afterwards, but neither substitutes for washing and neither comes first. Primary suturing should be avoided or delayed, because closing the wound drives virus deeper into the tissue. Co-amoxiclav is right for the bacterial risk of a bite but has no effect on rabies.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A bat handler who completed a full course of pre-exposure rabies vaccine two years ago is bitten by a bat and the skin is broken. After the wound has been washed, what rabies-specific treatment does he need?
options: A full primary course of rabies vaccine
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Someone with a documented complete pre-exposure course already has immune memory, so two booster doses of vaccine are enough and immunoglobulin is not indicated — indeed it would blunt the anamnestic response. Immunoglobulin is reserved for people who have never been immunised and have had a highest-risk exposure (saliva in direct contact with broken skin or a mucous membrane, including any direct bat contact), and it is infiltrated into and around the wound rather than into a distant muscle. A fresh primary course is unnecessary in the previously immunised, and doing nothing is wrong: broken skin from a bat always warrants boosting, and no country is considered free of risk from bats.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A man who was bitten by a dog abroad two months ago develops fever and malaise. Which additional feature would most strongly suggest early rabies?
options: A fixed grimace with difficulty opening the mouth
A spreading rash around the healed bite site
Pus discharging from the old bite wound
Itching and tingling at the healed bite site
Tender enlarged lymph nodes in the axilla
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Itching and tingling at the healed bite site
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Paraesthesia, itching or pain at the healed bite site, accompanying fever and malaise, is the classic rabies prodrome and reflects viral replication in the sensory ganglion supplying that dermatome. It is what separates early rabies from the ordinary sequelae of a bite — pus, a spreading rash and tender regional nodes all indicate bacterial wound infection instead. A fixed grimace with trismus after a wound points to tetanus, the other bite-related diagnosis. Once the prodrome gives way to hydrophobia or ascending paralysis the illness is almost always fatal, which is why the prodrome matters.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Paralytic ('dumb') rabies can be mistaken for which condition?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Paralytic rabies produces an ascending flaccid, areflexic weakness that closely mimics Guillain–Barré syndrome and is routinely misdiagnosed as it; the clues are the exposure history, fever at onset and sensory symptoms at the bite site, none of which fit Guillain–Barré. Transverse myelitis gives a sensory level with sphincter involvement, and myasthenia gravis causes fatigable ocular and bulbar weakness with no sensory story. Motor neurone disease evolves over months with mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs, and Lambert–Eaton is proximal, paraneoplastic and shows post-exercise facilitation. Both forms of rabies progress to coma and death within days.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: An 18-year-old woman on day 3 of her period, using a high-absorbency tampon, presents with abrupt fever of 39.4°C, a diffuse blanching sunburn-like rash, vomiting, confusion and a blood pressure of 80/50 mmHg. There is no purpura and no wound or localised soft-tissue pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Abrupt fever, a diffuse macular sunburn-like erythroderma that blanches, hypotension and at least three organ systems (GI, CNS, cardiovascular) in a menstruating tampon user is staphylococcal TSS mediated by TSST-1. Streptococcal TSS is excluded by the absence of a soft-tissue focus or pain out of proportion. Meningococcal septicaemia gives a non-blanching purpuric rash; scarlet fever gives a sandpaper rash with sore throat but not shock; and scalded skin syndrome causes flaccid bullae with superficial shedding in young children, sparing the mucosae, without distributive shock.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: By what mechanism do the toxins of toxic shock syndrome cause shock?
options: Endotoxin activation of host Toll-like receptors
Superantigen bridging of MHC II and the TCR
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Superantigen bridging of MHC II and the TCR
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: TSST-1 and the streptococcal exotoxins are superantigens: they cross-link MHC class II on antigen-presenting cells to the T-cell receptor outside the peptide groove, bypassing antigen processing and activating up to about 20% of all T cells at once, against well under 0.1% for a conventional antigen. The resulting surge of TNF-α, IL-1, IL-2 and IFN-γ causes capillary leak and vasodilation, hence distributive shock. Toll-like receptor activation by endotoxin is Gram-negative sepsis, IgE-mediated degranulation is anaphylaxis, and molecular mimicry of cardiac myosin is rheumatic fever — and the toxins need not invade or lyse endothelium at all.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which toxin mediates classic menstrual staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Menstrual staphylococcal TSS is mediated by TSST-1, a superantigen made by S. aureus colonising the vagina. SPE-A is the corresponding streptococcal superantigen and causes streptococcal TSS, not the menstrual form. Panton–Valentine leukocidin causes necrotising pneumonia and recurrent abscesses, exfoliative toxin cleaves desmoglein to produce scalded skin syndrome, and alpha-haemolysin is a pore-forming cytotoxin — none of the last three is a superantigen.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 34-year-old man with toxic shock syndrome from a necrotising leg infection has blood cultures growing Streptococcus pyogenes. He is on antibiotics and organ support after debridement. Which additional action is required?
options: Start every household contact on flucloxacillin
Send throat swabs from all household contacts
Notify the local health protection team
Place the patient in strict airborne isolation
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Notify the local health protection team
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Invasive group A streptococcal disease is notifiable, so the proper officer / local UKHSA health protection team must be told on clinical suspicion — phoned within 24 hours if urgent and in writing within 3 days. They then assess contacts and decide whether prophylaxis is warranted, which is not a ward-level decision. Routine throat swabbing of contacts is not recommended and flucloxacillin has no role in group A strep prophylaxis; household contacts are instead told what symptoms to watch for. Airborne isolation is not indicated, and vaccinating contacts against varicella does nothing about a strep exposure.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 19-year-old woman is recovering from menstrual staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome and asks how to reduce the chance of it recurring. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: No precautions are needed once she recovers
Stop using tampons and use pads instead
Have a single dose of immunoglobulin now
Take a lifelong low-dose oral antibiotic
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Stop using tampons and use pads instead
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Menstrual staphylococcal TSS recurs if tampon use continues and S. aureus is not eradicated, so patients are usually advised to avoid tampons, caps and diaphragms and to seek advice before using them again. Recovery confers no reliable protection: superantigens bypass antigen processing and do not generate a durable antibody response, which is precisely why recurrence happens. High-absorbency tampons are the original risk factor and changing them more often does not remove it, long-term antibiotics are not indicated, and immunoglobulin is a treatment for acute severe disease rather than prophylaxis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with streptococcal toxic shock syndrome is receiving benzylpenicillin. Which antibiotic should be added specifically to suppress exotoxin production?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Clindamycin binds the bacterial ribosome and halts synthesis of the exotoxins driving the cytokine storm, and that effect does not depend on how fast the organisms are dividing. This matters because at the very high bacterial densities of a necrotising infection the organisms stop dividing and express fewer penicillin-binding proteins, so beta-lactams paradoxically lose potency — that is the Eagle effect, a limitation of penicillin and the reason clindamycin is added, not a property of clindamycin. Metronidazole covers only anaerobes, gentamicin and ciprofloxacin kill without switching off toxin synthesis, and meropenem merely broadens beta-lactam cover while sharing the same high-inoculum weakness.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient has shock, blood cultures positive for group A streptococcus, and severe pain out of proportion to the findings in a swollen leg with dusky skin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Staphylococcal TSS from an occult abscess
Clostridial gas gangrene after penetrating injury
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Pain out of proportion with dusky skin over a swollen limb signals necrotising fasciitis, and a positive blood culture for group A streptococcus in a shocked patient makes streptococcal TSS the diagnosis — note that soft-tissue necrosis is itself one of the defining criteria. Streptococcal TSS is frequently bacteraemic, whereas staphylococcal TSS is toxin-mediated with usually negative cultures. Clostridial gas gangrene follows a penetrating or contaminated injury and grows clostridia, simple cellulitis does not cause disproportionate pain or refractory shock, and extensive venous thrombosis gives a swollen cyanotic limb without fever or positive cultures.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 17-year-old with staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome has had fluid resuscitation and intravenous antibiotics. On examination a tampon is found in situ. Aside from antibiotics and resuscitation, what is the most important immediate intervention?
options: Remove the tampon and culture it
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Remove the tampon and culture it
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Source control stops further toxin production and is the intervention that changes outcome: the tampon comes out immediately and is sent for culture, which also secures the microbiological diagnosis. Imaging adds nothing and delays a bedside action. Immunoglobulin is considered early in severe streptococcal disease but is an adjunct and never a substitute for removing the source. Antiseptic douching does not clear a colonised foreign body and can worsen mucosal injury, and corticosteroids are not established therapy in TSS.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A woman with streptococcal toxic shock syndrome remains in refractory shock on noradrenaline 24 hours after debridement and antibiotics. Which adjunctive treatment specifically targets the circulating superantigen toxin?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Pooled immunoglobulin contains antibodies against the superantigen exotoxins, so it neutralises circulating toxin and blunts T-cell activation — and UK guidance is to consider it early on specialist advice in severe invasive streptococcal infection, not to hold it back as rescue therapy (RCOG). Haemofiltration treats acute kidney injury and does not clear superantigen, and fresh frozen plasma is for coagulopathy. Hydrocortisone may be used for catecholamine-refractory shock of any cause but acts on vascular tone rather than the toxin, and methylene blue is a vasoplegia rescue measure with no antitoxin effect.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 4-year-old is on day 4 of chickenpox. Which new feature should most urgently raise suspicion of invasive group A streptococcal infection?
options: Mild itching relieved by an antihistamine
New high fever with severe focal limb pain
A dry cough with mild coryzal symptoms
Crusting of the earlier vesicular lesions
Fresh crops of vesicles on the trunk and face
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: New high fever with severe focal limb pain
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Chickenpox breaches the skin barrier and is the classic portal for invasive group A streptococcal disease, so a second spike of fever with severe focal pain or rapidly spreading erythema after the initial illness should prompt immediate assessment for necrotising infection and streptococcal TSS, with intravenous antibiotics and urgent surgical review. Continued cropping of vesicles over several days, crusting of older lesions, itch and mild coryzal symptoms are all part of the expected course of uncomplicated varicella.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Twelve days after admission with toxic shock syndrome, a patient who is otherwise improving develops painless peeling of the skin of the palms and soles. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Treat as a new drug reaction
Screen for a second source of infection
Take skin biopsies to exclude vasculitis
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Desquamation of the palms and soles at one to two weeks is part of the natural history of TSS and, being painless with no fever or haemodynamic change, needs only explanation and reassurance. Relapse or a missed second source would present with recurrent fever, rising inflammatory markers and hypotension, not isolated peeling, so neither antibiotic escalation nor a source hunt is warranted. Biopsy adds nothing to a recognised clinical sign, and a drug reaction would be itchy and morbilliform rather than a late palmoplantar peel. The discharge conversation should instead cover recurrence risk.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with toxic shock syndrome deteriorates, with a tense, dusky, exquisitely painful thigh and crepitus. What is the most urgent next step?
options: Escalate antibiotics and admit to intensive care
Bedside incision and drainage in the department
MRI of the limb before any intervention
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Crepitus with pain out of proportion and dusky skin is necrotising infection: the diagnosis is made and treated in theatre, and survival falls with every hour of delay, so urgent exploration and debridement takes precedence. Antibiotics and critical care are necessary but cannot remove necrotic tissue, and admitting without operating is the commonest fatal error here. Imaging must not delay surgery when the picture is this clear, bedside drainage cannot adequately debride fascial planes, and compartment pressures neither confirm nor treat the diagnosis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which pattern of blood results would you most expect in toxic shock syndrome?
options: Raised bilirubin with normal platelets and normal CK
Raised platelets with normal CK and creatinine
Low platelets, raised CK and raised creatinine
Neutropenia with normal CK and creatinine
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Low platelets, raised CK and raised creatinine
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: TSS is defined by involvement of three or more organ systems, so the discriminating finding is the multi-system pattern: thrombocytopenia, a raised CK from myositis and a rising creatinine from acute kidney injury, usually with deranged liver function, a high lactate and features of DIC. No single one of those is specific, which is why the combination is the answer. Isolated hyperbilirubinaemia without cytopenia or rhabdomyolysis suggests a hepatobiliary cause, thrombocytosis is a late reactive change, leukocytosis rather than neutropenia is the rule, and marked eosinophilia points to a drug reaction instead.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with toxic shock syndrome and known MRSA colonisation is already on a beta-lactam and clindamycin. Which agent should be added?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: MRSA needs an agent active against methicillin-resistant staphylococci, and in a shocked patient that means a glycopeptide — vancomycin, or teicoplanin in many UK hospitals — with linezolid as the alternative, which has the added benefit of suppressing toxin synthesis. Every distractor is a real intravenous choice in sepsis, but none covers MRSA: piperacillin–tazobactam, ceftriaxone and meropenem are all beta-lactams, and methicillin resistance is mediated by an altered penicillin-binding protein that defeats the whole class. Gentamicin has unreliable activity against MRSA and is never used as MRSA cover here.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A woman has a temperature of 39.5°C, diffuse macular erythroderma and a systolic blood pressure of 85 mmHg. Which further finding is needed before the recognised criteria for staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome are met?
options: A positive blood culture for S. aureus
Involvement of three or more organ systems
Detection of TSST-1 in a wound swab
Skin peeling of the palms on day one
A rising antibody titre to staphylococcal toxin
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Involvement of three or more organ systems
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The criteria are fever of 38.9°C or above, diffuse macular erythroderma, hypotension, desquamation at one to two weeks, and involvement of at least three organ systems, with no alternative explanation on culture or serology. This patient has the first three, so what is missing is documented multi-system involvement — GI, muscular, mucous membrane, renal, hepatic, haematological or CNS. Blood cultures are usually negative in staphylococcal TSS and are not required; peeling is a late feature and would not appear on day one; and neither toxin detection nor serology forms part of the criteria. Four of the five counts as a probable case, and treatment must not wait for any of them.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with toxic shock syndrome has a blood pressure of 78/40 mmHg and a lactate of 4.5 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate initial resuscitation?
options: Transfuse red cells to raise oxygen delivery
A litre of 5% dextrose over four hours
Start noradrenaline before giving any fluid
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The shock of TSS is distributive, from superantigen-driven capillary leak and vasodilation, so the first move is prompt boluses of balanced crystalloid with reassessment after each, within a sepsis pathway, adding vasopressors and involving critical care if hypotension persists after adequate fluid. Starting a vasopressor before any volume squeezes an underfilled circulation; concentrated albumin is not first-line expansion; 5% dextrose distributes into total body water and does not expand plasma volume; and transfusion is for anaemia or bleeding, not as a resuscitation fluid for vasodilatory shock.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A medical student is asked to explain why antibiotics can kill bacteria without harming human cells. Which underlying difference best accounts for this 'selective toxicity'?
options: Antibiotics act only on viruses, not human cells
Bacteria have a nucleus that antibiotics target
Bacteria are prokaryotes with a peptidoglycan wall and 70S ribosomes, which human (eukaryotic, 80S) cells lack
Human cells have a chitin wall that antibiotics spare
Bacteria and human cells share identical ribosomes
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Bacteria are prokaryotes with a peptidoglycan wall and 70S ribosomes, which human (eukaryotic, 80S) cells lack
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Selective toxicity exploits prokaryote-specific targets — the peptidoglycan wall and the 70S ribosome — that human eukaryotic cells do not possess.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 72-year-old man with a long-term urinary catheter has no fever, no suprapubic pain and normal inflammatory markers, but a routine urine culture grows E. coli. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: This most likely represents colonisation rather than infection, and antibiotics are not indicated in the absence of symptoms/host response
He has urosepsis and needs the Sepsis Six
He requires immediate catheter removal and blood cultures
He has a confirmed urinary tract infection and needs IV antibiotics
The culture proves contamination and should be ignored entirely
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: This most likely represents colonisation rather than infection, and antibiotics are not indicated in the absence of symptoms/host response
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: A positive culture without symptoms or a host response usually reflects colonisation (asymptomatic bacteriuria is common with catheters); treatment risks harm and resistance without benefit.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with Gram-negative bacteraemia develops fever, hypotension, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Which bacterial component is chiefly responsible for this systemic picture?
options: Endotoxin (lipopolysaccharide) from the Gram-negative outer membrane
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Endotoxin (lipopolysaccharide) from the Gram-negative outer membrane
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Endotoxin (LPS), released from the Gram-negative outer membrane, non-specifically triggers the inflammatory cascade causing fever, sepsis, DIC and shock.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which statement best distinguishes an exotoxin from an endotoxin?
options: Exotoxins are found only in Gram-negative organisms
Exotoxin is LPS released on lysis; endotoxin is a secreted protein
Endotoxin can be converted to a toxoid, but exotoxin cannot
Exotoxin is a secreted protein that can be made into a toxoid vaccine; endotoxin is the LPS of the Gram-negative wall
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Exotoxin is a secreted protein that can be made into a toxoid vaccine; endotoxin is the LPS of the Gram-negative wall
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Exotoxins are secreted proteins (often Gram-positive), specific and convertible to toxoids; endotoxin is the LPS of the Gram-negative outer membrane and drives non-specific sepsis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with an infected prosthetic hip joint has an organism that persists despite prolonged antibiotics, and cure ultimately requires removal of the prosthesis. Which virulence mechanism most likely explains this?
options: Biofilm formation on the prosthetic surface
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Biofilm formation on the prosthetic surface
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Biofilms on prostheses and catheters protect organisms from antibiotics and immunity, causing chronic, resistant infection that often needs device removal.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which set correctly matches all five microbial groups to their defining feature?
options: Bacteria = eukaryote with a nucleus; viruses = prokaryotes; fungi = acellular; parasites = protein only; prions = RNA-based organisms
Parasites = prokaryotes; bacteria = acellular; fungi = have no cell wall; viruses = eukaryotes; prions = a class of DNA virus
Fungi = acellular; prions = eukaryotes with a nucleus; viruses = chitin wall; bacteria = protozoa; parasites = DNA only
Bacteria = prokaryote; viruses = acellular (DNA or RNA); fungi = eukaryote with chitin wall; parasites = eukaryote (protozoa/helminths); prions = protein with no nucleic acid
All five groups are prokaryotes with peptidoglycan cell walls and 70S ribosomes, which is why antibiotics work on them
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Bacteria = prokaryote; viruses = acellular (DNA or RNA); fungi = eukaryote with chitin wall; parasites = eukaryote (protozoa/helminths); prions = protein with no nucleic acid
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The five-group framework: bacteria (prokaryote), viruses (acellular, DNA or RNA), fungi (eukaryote, chitin wall), parasites (eukaryote — protozoa and helminths), prions (protein, no nucleic acid).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A capsule is described as a key virulence factor in Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis. What is its principal role?
options: It resists phagocytosis by host immune cells
It enables attachment to host epithelium
It is the target of all beta-lactam antibiotics
It forms a biofilm on catheters
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: It resists phagocytosis by host immune cells
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: A polysaccharide capsule resists phagocytosis, a major reason encapsulated organisms such as pneumococcus and meningococcus are virulent (and why capsular vaccines are effective).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: According to the 'chain of infection', which intervention breaks the link of transmission for a droplet-spread respiratory pathogen?
options: Giving the patient a proton pump inhibitor
Isolating the patient and using appropriate respiratory precautions
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Isolating the patient and using appropriate respiratory precautions
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Infection control works by breaking a link in the chain; isolation and respiratory precautions interrupt droplet/airborne transmission, just as hand hygiene interrupts contact spread.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A researcher wants to prove that a newly discovered bacterium causes a specific disease. Which framework classically sets out the criteria for establishing microbial causation?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Koch's postulates set the classic criteria for proving causation: found in all cases, isolated in pure culture, reproduces disease in a healthy host, and re-isolated from that host.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which of the following is a recognised limitation of Koch's postulates?
options: They apply perfectly to every known pathogen
They have been shown to be entirely incorrect
They only apply to Gram-positive bacteria
They fail for organisms that cannot be cultured, asymptomatic carriers, and many viruses
They require an electron microscope to apply
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: They fail for organisms that cannot be cultured, asymptomatic carriers, and many viruses
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Koch's postulates do not hold for uncultureable organisms, asymptomatic carriers or viruses, though they remain the conceptual foundation of causation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A previously healthy commensal organism from a patient's own skin causes a bloodstream infection only after a central venous catheter is inserted and the patient becomes neutropenic. This organism is best described as which type of pathogen?
options: A strict commensal that never causes disease
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: An opportunistic pathogen is a commensal or low-virulence organism that causes disease only when host defences are breached or suppressed (e.g. a line in situ plus neutropenia).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A blood culture from a septic patient shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters. The laboratory reports the organism is catalase-positive and coagulase-positive. Which is the most likely organism?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Cocci in clusters that are catalase-positive (Staph, not Strep) and coagulase-positive identify Staphylococcus aureus; coagulase-negative staphylococci are epidermidis/saprophyticus.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: During the Gram stain, what is the role of the alcohol step, and why do Gram-negative bacteria end up pink?
options: It selectively lyses Gram-positive organisms, leaving only the Gram-negatives visible on the slide
It fixes the crystal violet permanently into the walls of all bacterial cells, whatever their structure
It stains the outer membrane of Gram-negative organisms purple while leaving Gram-positives unstained
It acts as a mordant, binding iodine into the peptidoglycan layer to fix the primary stain
It decolourises the thin-walled Gram-negatives (which then take the pink safranin counterstain), while the thick peptidoglycan of Gram-positives retains the crystal violet
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: It decolourises the thin-walled Gram-negatives (which then take the pink safranin counterstain), while the thick peptidoglycan of Gram-positives retains the crystal violet
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Alcohol decolourises Gram-negatives (thin peptidoglycan + outer membrane), so they take the pink safranin; Gram-positives retain the crystal violet–iodine complex and stay purple.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A young adult with an atypical pneumonia fails to improve on amoxicillin. Serology later confirms Mycoplasma pneumoniae. What best explains the treatment failure, and what is appropriate?
options: Mycoplasma is acid-fast and needs anti-tuberculous therapy
It is a viral pneumonia needing no antibiotic
Mycoplasma lacks a cell wall, so wall-targeting β-lactams are ineffective — use a macrolide (or tetracycline/quinolone)
Amoxicillin was underdosed; increase the dose
The organism produces a capsule that blocks amoxicillin; add a steroid
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Mycoplasma lacks a cell wall, so wall-targeting β-lactams are ineffective — use a macrolide (or tetracycline/quinolone)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Mycoplasma has no peptidoglycan wall, so β-lactams (which target the wall) don't work; atypicals are treated with macrolides, tetracyclines or quinolones.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Sputum from a patient with chronic cough, weight loss and haemoptysis is stained with Ziehl-Neelsen and shows red (acid-fast) bacilli. Which organism does this indicate?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Acid-fast bacilli on Ziehl-Neelsen staining, resulting from the waxy mycolic-acid wall, indicate mycobacteria such as M. tuberculosis, which do not stain reliably by Gram.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient has a deep, foul-smelling intra-abdominal abscess. Which class of organism predominates in such collections, and which antibiotic classically targets it?
options: Microaerophilic organisms; treated with a macrolide
Obligate aerobes; treated with an aminoglycoside
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Anaerobes dominate in abscesses, deep/necrotic tissue and the gut; metronidazole is the classic anti-anaerobe.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 40-year-old is due a splenectomy after trauma. Against which category of organism is vaccination especially important, and why?
options: Acid-fast bacilli, because asplenia reactivates TB
Encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus, meningococcus, Hib), because the spleen is key to clearing capsulated organisms
Spirochaetes, because they evade the spleen
Anaerobes, because the spleen filters them
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus, meningococcus, Hib), because the spleen is key to clearing capsulated organisms
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Asplenic/hyposplenic patients are at high risk from encapsulated organisms (pneumococcus, meningococcus, Hib) and should be vaccinated, as the capsule resists phagocytosis and the spleen is central to their clearance.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A lumbar puncture in a teenager with meningism shows Gram-negative diplococci in the CSF. Which organism is most likely?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Gram-negative diplococci point to Neisseria meningitidis; S. pneumoniae is a Gram-positive diplococcus, and Listeria and Haemophilus have different morphologies.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A ward outbreak of Clostridioides difficile diarrhoea prompts an infection-control review. Why is alcohol hand gel inadequate, and what is required?
options: C. difficile is Gram-negative and resists all measures
The organism is airborne, so respirators are the priority
Alcohol gel is adequate and no change is needed
C. difficile forms spores that resist alcohol, so soap-and-water handwashing plus sporicidal cleaning (e.g. chlorine) is needed
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: C. difficile forms spores that resist alcohol, so soap-and-water handwashing plus sporicidal cleaning (e.g. chlorine) is needed
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Spore-forming organisms such as C. difficile resist alcohol; mechanical removal by soap-and-water handwashing and sporicidal (chlorine-based) cleaning are required.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A throat swab from a child with tonsillitis grows a beta-haemolytic, Lancefield Group A streptococcus. Which organism is this?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Beta-haemolytic (complete haemolysis) Lancefield Group A streptococcus is S. pyogenes; Group B is S. agalactiae, and pneumococcus is alpha-haemolytic.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A urine culture on MacConkey agar grows pink (lactose-fermenting) Gram-negative rods that are oxidase-negative. Which organism is most consistent with this?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Lactose-fermenting (pink on MacConkey), oxidase-negative Gram-negative rods fit E. coli; Pseudomonas is oxidase-positive and a non-fermenter, and Salmonella/Shigella are non-fermenters.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which single laboratory result most reliably separates staphylococci from streptococci?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Catalase separates the Gram-positive cocci: staphylococci are catalase-positive, streptococci and enterococci are catalase-negative. Coagulase then separates S. aureus from other staphylococci.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A norovirus outbreak spreads through a ward despite staff using alcohol hand gel. What best explains this, and what should be done?
options: Norovirus is bacterial and needs antibiotics
Norovirus is airborne, so FFP3 masks are the key measure
Norovirus is enveloped and resistant to alcohol; use more gel
The gel was expired; no other change is needed
Norovirus is non-enveloped and resistant to alcohol, so soap-and-water handwashing and chlorine-based cleaning are required
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Norovirus is non-enveloped and resistant to alcohol, so soap-and-water handwashing and chlorine-based cleaning are required
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Non-enveloped viruses such as norovirus resist alcohol; soap-and-water handwashing and chlorine (hypochlorite) cleaning are needed to control spread.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A renal transplant patient on immunosuppression develops fever, cytopenias and deranged LFTs, and CMV is detected. What is the underlying reason CMV has caused disease now?
options: CMV was newly acquired from the graft only
Herpesviruses (including CMV) establish lifelong latency and reactivate when immunity falls, as with transplant immunosuppression
CMV integrates into the host genome like a retrovirus
CMV only causes disease in the immunocompetent
CMV is a non-enveloped virus resistant to the immune system
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Herpesviruses (including CMV) establish lifelong latency and reactivate when immunity falls, as with transplant immunosuppression
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Herpesviruses persist latently and reactivate under immunosuppression; CMV disease is characteristic in transplant recipients and HIV.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient newly diagnosed with HIV is started on antiretroviral therapy. Which virus-specific enzyme, characteristic of retroviruses, is a principal drug target?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Retroviruses use reverse transcriptase to convert RNA into DNA that integrates into the host genome; reverse transcriptase (with integrase and protease) inhibitors are core antiretroviral targets. Note reverse transcriptase is not exclusive to retroviruses — hepatitis B is a DNA virus that replicates via an RNA intermediate and is also treated with reverse transcriptase inhibitors.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: An older adult develops a painful vesicular rash in a single dermatome. Which process explains this presentation?
options: Primary varicella infection acquired that week
Bacterial superinfection of the skin only
Reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus from the dorsal root ganglia (shingles)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus from the dorsal root ganglia (shingles)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Shingles is reactivation of VZV latent in the dorsal root ganglia, producing a dermatomal vesicular rash, typically when immunity wanes.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Two patients have hepatitis. One acquired it from contaminated shellfish with an acute self-limiting illness; the other acquired it via blood and has developed chronic infection with cirrhosis. Which viruses are most likely, respectively?
options: Hepatitis A (faecal-oral, acute) and hepatitis B or C (blood-borne, chronic)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Hepatitis A (faecal-oral, acute) and hepatitis B or C (blood-borne, chronic)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Hepatitis A is faecal-oral and acute; hepatitis B and C are blood-borne and can become chronic with progression to cirrhosis/HCC. Vowels (A/E) faecal-oral/acute; consonants (B/C/D) blood-borne/chronic.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Why is aciclovir relatively non-toxic to human cells while effectively treating herpes simplex?
options: It is only activated by the viral thymidine kinase, concentrating the active drug in infected cells (selective toxicity)
It dissolves the viral lipid envelope directly
It is toxic to all dividing cells equally
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: It is only activated by the viral thymidine kinase, concentrating the active drug in infected cells (selective toxicity)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Aciclovir is phosphorylated to its active form chiefly by viral thymidine kinase, so it is activated selectively in herpesvirus-infected cells.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 3-year-old has a runny nose, mild fever and cough for two days and looks well. The parents request antibiotics. What is the best explanation for withholding them?
options: The child is too young to be given any antibiotic safely at this age
Antibiotics would cure the illness faster but are being rationed because of resistance concerns
Antibiotics are too expensive to justify prescribing for a self-limiting childhood illness
The illness is almost certainly viral; viruses lack the bacterial targets antibiotics act on, so antibiotics are ineffective and supportive care is appropriate
Antibiotics only work against non-enveloped viruses, and this illness is caused by an enveloped one
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: The illness is almost certainly viral; viruses lack the bacterial targets antibiotics act on, so antibiotics are ineffective and supportive care is appropriate
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Uncomplicated URTIs are viral; antibiotics don't work on viruses (no wall/ribosome/metabolism to target), so supportive care and safety-netting are appropriate.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Persistent infection with which virus is the principal cause of cervical cancer?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Persistent high-risk HPV infection causes cervical (and anogenital/oropharyngeal) cancer; HPV vaccination targets this.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Why must the influenza vaccine be reformulated each year?
options: Influenza is a DNA virus that is highly stable
People lose all immune memory within weeks
Influenza is an RNA virus with a high mutation rate (antigenic drift/shift), so circulating strains change
The vaccine degrades in storage annually
Antibiotics have made the old vaccine obsolete
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Influenza is an RNA virus with a high mutation rate (antigenic drift/shift), so circulating strains change
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Influenza's RNA genome mutates rapidly (drift/shift), changing surface antigens, so the vaccine is updated to match circulating strains.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which type of virus is most likely to survive on environmental surfaces and spread by the faecal-oral route?
options: Non-enveloped (naked) viruses such as norovirus and rotavirus
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Non-enveloped (naked) viruses such as norovirus and rotavirus
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Non-enveloped viruses have a tough protein capsid, survive on surfaces and in the GI tract, and typically spread faecal-orally; enveloped viruses are fragile.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Oseltamivir is used in influenza. Which step of the viral life cycle does it inhibit?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Oseltamivir inhibits neuraminidase, blocking release of new influenza virions from infected cells.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with untreated HIV and a CD4 count of 120 has three weeks of a dry cough, worsening exertional breathlessness and hypoxia, with bilateral perihilar infiltrates on chest X-ray. What is the most likely diagnosis and treatment?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: PCP is an AIDS-defining pneumonia at CD4 <200, with a dry cough, exertional hypoxia and bilateral perihilar infiltrates; treatment is co-trimoxazole.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with advanced HIV (CD4 40) has headache, fever and neck stiffness. CSF microscopy with India ink shows yeasts with a clear capsular halo. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: An encapsulated yeast on India ink in an HIV patient with low CD4 indicates cryptococcal meningitis (Cryptococcus neoformans); CrAg and culture confirm it.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A diabetic patient in ketoacidosis develops facial pain, a black necrotic eschar on the palate and rapid orbital involvement. Which infection must be recognised urgently?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Rhino-orbito-cerebral mucormycosis is an aggressive angioinvasive mould infection in diabetic ketoacidosis/immunocompromise, presenting with necrotic (black) tissue — a surgical emergency.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A neutropenic patient after chemotherapy develops persistent fever and pulmonary nodules; serum galactomannan is positive. Which infection is most likely?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Invasive aspergillosis is characteristic in the neutropenic and is supported by a positive galactomannan antigen; it carries a high mortality.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Amphotericin B is effective but nephrotoxic. What is its mechanism of action?
options: It binds ergosterol in the fungal membrane, forming pores
It inhibits β-glucan synthesis in the cell wall
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: It binds ergosterol in the fungal membrane, forming pores
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Amphotericin (a polyene) binds ergosterol and forms membrane pores; because human membranes use cholesterol it is comparatively selective, but nephrotoxicity is a key limitation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How do the azole antifungals (e.g. fluconazole) exert their effect?
options: By binding preformed ergosterol to make pores
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Azoles inhibit 14α-demethylase, blocking ergosterol synthesis; their similarity to human enzymes underlies hepatotoxicity and drug interactions.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with poorly controlled asthma has recurrent wheeze, fleeting pulmonary infiltrates, a high total IgE, eosinophilia and positive Aspergillus-specific IgE, with central bronchiectasis. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: ABPA is a hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus in asthma/CF, with high IgE, eosinophilia, fleeting infiltrates and central bronchiectasis — distinct from invasive disease or a fungus ball.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A dimorphic fungus is described as growing as a mould in the environment and as a yeast in the body. Which phrase captures this behaviour?
options: 'Mould in the cold, yeast in the heat'
'Yeast in the cold, mould in the heat'
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: 'Mould in the cold, yeast in the heat'
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Dimorphic fungi (Histoplasma, Blastomyces, Coccidioides) are moulds in the cold environment and yeasts at body temperature — 'mould in the cold, yeast in the heat'.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: An infant on a course of antibiotics develops white plaques on the tongue and buccal mucosa that leave a raw surface when scraped. What is the most likely cause?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Oral thrush is caused by Candida, an opportunist favoured by antibiotics, inhaled steroids, extremes of age and immunosuppression.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Why are antifungal drugs generally more toxic to patients than most antibacterial antibiotics?
options: Fungi have no cell membrane to target
Fungi are eukaryotes that share much cell machinery with human cells, leaving few selective targets
Antifungals target the human 80S ribosome deliberately
Fungi are prokaryotes with many unique targets
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Fungi are eukaryotes that share much cell machinery with human cells, leaving few selective targets
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Because fungi are eukaryotes like human cells, there are fewer fungus-specific targets, so antifungals (e.g. amphotericin, azoles) tend to be more toxic with a narrower therapeutic window.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient has thickened, discoloured toenails and scaling between the toes; skin scrapings with KOH show hyphae. What is the first-line treatment for this dermatophyte infection?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Dermatophyte (tinea) infections are treated with terbinafine (topical or oral) or azoles; terbinafine inhibits squalene epoxidase in ergosterol synthesis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 28-year-old returns from Nigeria with cyclical fevers, rigors, headache and mild jaundice; the spleen is palpable. What is the single most important initial investigation?
options: Thick and thin blood films (repeated up to three times)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Thick and thin blood films (repeated up to three times)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Fever in a returning traveller is malaria until proven otherwise; thick and thin blood films (×3 before exclusion) are the key investigation, with thick films to detect and thin films to speciate.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A traveller treated for Plasmodium vivax malaria is at risk of relapse weeks later. What is the reason, and what additional treatment addresses it?
options: Incomplete blood-stage cure only; extend artesunate
Dormant liver hypnozoites; add primaquine (after checking G6PD status)
Re-infection from the ward; repeat artemisinin
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Dormant liver hypnozoites; add primaquine (after checking G6PD status)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: P. vivax and ovale form dormant liver hypnozoites that cause relapse; primaquine eradicates them, given after checking G6PD status to avoid haemolysis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A backpacker returns with several weeks of bloating, foul-smelling, fatty, non-bloody diarrhoea and weight loss. Stool studies suggest a protozoan. What is the most likely organism and treatment?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Giardia causes chronic, fatty, non-bloody diarrhoea with malabsorption ('backpacker's'); treatment is metronidazole.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient returning from the tropics has bloody diarrhoea and, weeks later, right-upper-quadrant pain with a solitary liver lesion containing 'anchovy sauce' material. Which organism is responsible?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Entamoeba histolytica causes bloody dysentery and amoebic liver abscess ('anchovy sauce' pus); treatment is metronidazole plus a luminal agent.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with advanced HIV has headache and focal neurology; MRI shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions. Which parasitic infection is the most likely cause?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Cerebral toxoplasmosis (Toxoplasma gondii) is a classic opportunistic infection in advanced HIV, causing ring-enhancing brain lesions.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 6-year-old has intense perianal itching at night; a parent has seen tiny white worms. What is the diagnosis and first-line treatment?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Threadworm (Enterobius) causes nocturnal perianal itch in children, is confirmed with the sellotape test, and is treated with mebendazole (treat the household).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A traveller who swam in a freshwater lake in sub-Saharan Africa develops painless visible haematuria weeks later. Which infection is most likely, and what is the treatment?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Freshwater exposure with later haematuria suggests Schistosoma haematobium (which also predisposes to bladder cancer); treatment is praziquantel.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A returning traveller has a chronic illness and a markedly raised eosinophil count. Which category of organism should this particularly prompt you to consider?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Eosinophilia with a travel history points to tissue-invading helminths; protozoa more typically cause acute fever/diarrhoea without eosinophilia.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient from a rural area has iron-deficiency anaemia and a history of walking barefoot on contaminated soil. Which helminth is the most likely cause?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Hookworm larvae penetrate the skin of bare feet and cause chronic intestinal blood loss leading to iron-deficiency anaemia.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient has intense generalised itch, worse at night, with burrows visible in the finger webs and wrists; household members are also itchy. What is the diagnosis and treatment?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Scabies causes intense nocturnal itch with burrows in the finger webs/wrists and affects close contacts; treatment is topical permethrin, treating the whole household.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Before starting high-dose corticosteroids in a patient who lived for years in the tropics, which parasite is important to exclude/treat because of the risk of overwhelming hyperinfection?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Strongyloides persists by autoinfection and can cause life-threatening hyperinfection with immunosuppression (e.g. steroids); at-risk patients are screened and treated (ivermectin).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 65-year-old develops a dementia that progresses over weeks with prominent myoclonic jerks. He is afebrile, inflammatory markers and routine CSF are normal, and MRI shows cortical ribboning. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: A rapidly progressive dementia with myoclonus, no inflammation (normal CSF/markers) and cortical ribboning on MRI is characteristic of sporadic CJD.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Why are prions extraordinarily resistant to standard sterilisation methods such as autoclaving and alcohol?
options: They are enveloped, and the envelope reseals itself after heat or chemical damage
The misfolded protein is extremely stable and resists heat, chemicals and proteases, and it has no nucleic acid for irradiation to damage
They survive by hiding inside host cells, where sterilising agents cannot reach them
They form heat-resistant endospores in the same way as Clostridium and Bacillus species
They are protected by a thick polysaccharide capsule that heat and chemicals cannot penetrate
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: The misfolded protein is extremely stable and resists heat, chemicals and proteases, and it has no nucleic acid for irradiation to damage
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Routine sterilisation works mainly by denaturing protein; the aggregated prion protein resists heat, formalin, alcohol and proteases, and has no nucleic acid for irradiation to target — so standard autoclaving is not reliable and special decontamination or single-use instruments are required.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A man in his late 20s develops psychiatric and behavioural changes with painful sensory symptoms, followed by neurological decline over more than a year; MRI shows the pulvinar sign. Which diagnosis fits best?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Variant CJD affects younger patients, presents with psychiatric/sensory features first, runs a longer course and shows the pulvinar sign on MRI; it is linked to BSE-contaminated beef.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Why is there typically no fever, normal inflammatory markers and normal routine CSF in prion disease?
options: Because CSF is not affected by any brain disease
Because the prion is a misfolded 'self' protein and provokes no immune/inflammatory response
Because prions replicate too slowly to be detected
Because the patient is always immunosuppressed
Because antibiotics have already been given
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Because the prion is a misfolded 'self' protein and provokes no immune/inflammatory response
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Prions are misfolded host protein, seen by the body as 'self', so there is no immune response — hence no fever, normal inflammatory markers and normal routine CSF.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How does a prion cause more prion protein to form?
options: By templating the conversion of normal PrP into the misfolded β-sheet form (conformational change)
By integrating into the host genome
By hijacking host ribosomes to translate viral RNA
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: By templating the conversion of normal PrP into the misfolded β-sheet form (conformational change)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Prions propagate by conformational conversion — the misfolded PrP^Sc forces normal PrP^C to misfold — not by copying any genetic code.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which EEG finding is classically associated with sporadic Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease?
options: A completely normal EEG in all cases
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Periodic sharp-wave complexes are the classic EEG finding in sporadic CJD.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with suspected CJD requires neurosurgery. What is the key infection-control principle regarding the instruments?
options: No special precautions are needed, because prions are not transmissible between patients
Prions resist standard sterilisation, so instruments used on high-risk tissue are single-use, destroyed, or quarantined for re-use on that patient alone
Standard autoclaving at routine temperature and duration is sufficient to inactivate them
Only gloves are required, because transmission risk comes from the surgeon rather than the instruments
Alcohol wipes fully decontaminate the instruments and allow immediate reuse on other patients
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Prions resist standard sterilisation, so instruments used on high-risk tissue are single-use, destroyed, or quarantined for re-use on that patient alone
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Because prions resist standard sterilisation, instruments used on high-risk tissue (brain, spinal cord, cranial nerves and ganglia, posterior eye, pituitary) in a patient with or at risk of CJD are single-use, destroyed, or quarantined for that patient only, to prevent iatrogenic transmission.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which CSF investigation has become a key test supporting the diagnosis of prion disease?
options: Oligoclonal bands as the definitive test
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Routine CSF is normal, but RT-QuIC (prion-seeding assay) and 14-3-3 protein support the diagnosis; RT-QuIC is increasingly the key test.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which is the commonest form of prion disease in humans?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Sporadic CJD accounts for roughly 85% of cases and arises from spontaneous misfolding, typically in older adults.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Kuru and iatrogenic CJD (from contaminated instruments, dura mater grafts or human growth hormone) are examples of which category of prion disease?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Kuru (ritual cannibalism) and iatrogenic CJD are acquired/transmissible prion diseases; other categories are sporadic and inherited (PRNP mutations).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the unifying principle underlying the herpesvirus family?
options: They are cleared completely after primary infection
They are all treated with neuraminidase inhibitors
They are all RNA viruses with no latency
Primary infection → lifelong latency → reactivation when immunity drops
They only cause disease in the immunocompetent
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Primary infection → lifelong latency → reactivation when immunity drops
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The unifying herpesvirus principle is primary infection → lifelong latency → reactivation when immunity drops, which is why they dominate in immunosuppression.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: The '-ciclovir' antivirals (aciclovir, valaciclovir, ganciclovir) work by which mechanism?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The '-ciclovirs' inhibit viral DNA polymerase; resistance arises via mutation of viral thymidine kinase or DNA polymerase.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which herpesviruses form the neurotropic alpha group treated with aciclovir?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The alpha group of human herpesviruses — HSV-1, HSV-2, and VZV — is neurotropic and treated with aciclovir.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient presents with fever, confusion, and seizures, and imaging suggests temporal lobe involvement. What is the diagnosis and the urgent treatment?
options: Herpes simplex encephalitis (HSV-1, temporal lobe); urgent IV aciclovir
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Herpes simplex encephalitis (HSV-1, temporal lobe); urgent IV aciclovir
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Herpes simplex encephalitis (HSV-1) affects the temporal lobe and is the can't-miss diagnosis requiring urgent IV aciclovir.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: When is a patient with chickenpox (primary VZV) most infectious?
options: Only once the rash has crusted
Only during the fever phase after the rash
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Primary VZV (chickenpox) presents with fever + a vesicular rash (lesions at different stages) and is most infectious 1–2 days before the rash appears.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient has a painful vesicular rash confined to one dermatome that does not cross the midline. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Shingles (VZV reactivation) presents as a painful rash in a dermatomal distribution that doesn't cross the midline.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which complication of VZV involves the facial nerve, causing facial palsy plus ear vesicles?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Ramsay Hunt syndrome is a VZV complication affecting the facial nerve → facial palsy + ear vesicles. Ophthalmic zoster (V1) carries Hutchinson's sign and is sight-threatening.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which best describes the routine UK shingles vaccination offer for an immunocompetent adult?
options: Two doses of the recombinant (non-live) vaccine at age 50
A single dose of the recombinant (non-live) vaccine at age 80
An annual dose of the recombinant (non-live) vaccine from 65
A single dose of a live-attenuated vaccine at age 65
Two doses of the recombinant (non-live) vaccine at age 65
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Two doses of the recombinant (non-live) vaccine at age 65
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The UK shingles vaccine is recombinant and non-live, given as two doses, offered routinely to immunocompetent adults turning 65, with a 70–79 catch-up cohort, and to severely immunosuppressed adults from age 18. It replaced the older single-dose live vaccine.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A teenager with sore throat, fever, and lymphadenopathy is given amoxicillin and develops a florid maculopapular rash. What is the underlying diagnosis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Giving amoxicillin/ampicillin to someone with EBV causes a florid maculopapular rash — a classic SBA clue for EBV infectious mononucleosis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which investigation supports a diagnosis of EBV mononucleosis, and when does it become positive?
options: heterophile antibody test (Monospot), positive in the 2nd week
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: heterophile antibody test (Monospot), positive in the 2nd week
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: EBV shows a lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes on the film, deranged LFTs are common, and the heterophile antibody test (Monospot) is typically positive from the second week. It is often falsely negative in the first week and in children under about 12 — repeat it, or send EBV-specific serology (VCA IgM = acute infection).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient recovering from EBV mononucleosis asks about activity. What advice is given, and why?
options: Avoid contact sport ~4–6 weeks due to splenic rupture risk
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Avoid contact sport ~4–6 weeks due to splenic rupture risk
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: EBV mononucleosis is managed conservatively (resolves in 2–4 weeks), and contact sport should be avoided ~4–6 weeks because of the risk of splenic rupture.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which malignancy is associated with EBV?
options: Squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: EBV is associated with Burkitt's lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Hodgkin's lymphoma, and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient has a mononucleosis-like illness but the heterophile antibody test (Monospot) is negative. Which virus is most likely responsible?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: CMV typically causes a mononucleosis-like illness but is Monospot-negative — the discriminator from EBV (which is Monospot-positive); CMV is dormant in monocytes.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which is the most important manifestation of CMV in an HIV/AIDS patient?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: In the immunocompromised, CMV causes retinitis (HIV/AIDS), colitis, oesophagitis, pneumonitis, and hepatitis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Congenital CMV is the commonest congenital infection. Which classic feature results from it?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Congenital CMV is the commonest congenital infection and causes sensorineural deafness, microcephaly, and growth restriction.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the treatment for clinically significant CMV disease?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: CMV is treated with ganciclovir / valganciclovir.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with influenza is at risk and presents within 48 hours. What is the appropriate treatment and its mechanism?
options: Aciclovir — it inhibits viral DNA polymerase in herpesviruses
