Amoxicillin — it acts directly against the influenza virus
Oseltamivir or zanamivir — neuraminidase inhibitors that prevent viral release
Dexamethasone — an anti-inflammatory used to dampen the response
Ganciclovir — it inhibits viral replication in cytomegalovirus
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Oseltamivir or zanamivir — neuraminidase inhibitors that prevent viral release
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Oseltamivir and zanamivir are neuraminidase inhibitors: they block cleavage of sialic acid and so prevent release of new virions. They are given to at-risk patients within 48 hours of symptom onset, with annual vaccination used for prevention. Note the exception: in hospitalised, immunosuppressed or severe/complicated influenza, antivirals are still started even beyond 48 hours.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which organisms cause secondary bacterial pneumonia complicating influenza?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Influenza can be complicated by pneumonia — primary viral or secondary bacterial (Staph aureus, pneumococcus). Diagnosis is by viral nasal/throat swab PCR.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What virus causes COVID-19, and what is its incubation period?
options: A DNA herpesvirus; up to 21 days
SARS-CoV-2, a single-strand positive-sense RNA virus; up to 14 days
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: SARS-CoV-2, a single-strand positive-sense RNA virus; up to 14 days
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: COVID-19 is caused by SARS-CoV-2, a single-strand positive-sense RNA virus, with an incubation up to 14 days.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which presenting symptom and CXR finding are characteristic of COVID-19?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: COVID-19 presents with anosmia, cough, fever, myalgia, headache, and fatigue (respiratory failure if severe); the CXR shows bilateral lower-zone ground-glass infiltrates, and diagnosis is RT-PCR of an upper respiratory swab.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient is admitted with COVID-19 and requires supplemental oxygen. Which management is most appropriate?
options: Supportive care only, with no specific drug treatment at all
Dexamethasone with oxygen and respiratory support, plus remdesivir in selected patients
Intravenous aciclovir, as for herpes simplex encephalitis
Oseltamivir plus zanamivir, as for severe influenza infection
Ganciclovir plus valganciclovir, as for cytomegalovirus disease
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Dexamethasone with oxygen and respiratory support, plus remdesivir in selected patients
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Dexamethasone is given to hospitalised patients who need supplemental oxygen, alongside oxygen and respiratory support; remdesivir and tocilizumab are added in selected patients, with VTE prophylaxis throughout. Non-hospitalised patients at highest risk of progression are instead assessed for an oral antiviral such as nirmatrelvir/ritonavir.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes EBV from CMV mononucleosis?
options: EBV is Monospot-positive; CMV is Monospot-negative
EBV is Monospot-negative; CMV is Monospot-positive
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: EBV is Monospot-positive; CMV is Monospot-negative
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Both cause mononucleosis, but EBV is Monospot-positive and CMV is Monospot-negative.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: At which age is the first MMR-containing dose given in the UK childhood schedule?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The first MMR-containing dose is given at 12 months, alongside the PCV booster and the MenB booster. The vaccine used is now MMRV, which adds varicella. The second dose is at 18 months, not 3 years 4 months, and Hib/MenC is no longer part of the schedule (UKHSA).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which vaccines are given at the 8-week (2-month) visit in the UK schedule?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: At 8 weeks the schedule gives the 6-in-1 (DTaP/IPV/Hib/HepB), MenB (1st dose) and oral rotavirus (1st dose). There is no PCV at this visit — PCV is a single primary dose at 16 weeks, plus a booster at 1 year (UKHSA).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: The HPV vaccine is given at 12–13 years as a single dose. Which cancers and conditions does it protect against?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The HPV vaccine is given to girls and boys at 12–13 years as a single dose. It protects against HPV 16/18, which cause the majority of cervical and anal cancers, and 6/11, which cause the majority of genital warts.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which vaccines are given at the 14-year visit?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: At 14 years the schedule gives the 3-in-1 teenage booster (Td/IPV — tetanus, low-dose diphtheria, polio; NOT pertussis) plus MenACWY.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A pregnant woman asks which vaccines she should receive. Which is recommended and at what timing?
options: Pertussis-containing vaccine from 16 weeks, optimally 20–32 weeks, to protect the newborn
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Pertussis-containing vaccine from 16 weeks, optimally 20–32 weeks, to protect the newborn
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: In pregnancy the routine offers are a pertussis-containing vaccine from 16 weeks (optimally 20–32, usually at the anomaly scan, in every pregnancy), inactivated influenza in any trimester, and RSV vaccine from 28 weeks; COVID-19 only if she is in a currently eligible group. Other inactivated vaccines may be given when indicated. Live vaccines — MMR/MMRV, varicella, yellow fever, BCG, oral typhoid, live nasal flu — are contraindicated (UKHSA).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which of the following vaccines is contraindicated in pregnancy?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Live vaccines are contraindicated in pregnancy — MMR, varicella, and yellow fever.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: At what age is the shingles vaccine routinely offered to immunocompetent adults in the UK, and how many doses?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The UK shingles vaccine is recombinant and NOT live — given as TWO doses, offered routinely on turning 65, with a 70–79 catch-up cohort. Because it is non-live it is also offered to severely immunosuppressed adults from 18 years, who previously had to wait until 50 (UKHSA).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which vaccines are recommended in a patient with asplenia/splenic dysfunction?
options: Pneumococcal, Hib, MenACWY, meningococcal B, and annual influenza
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Pneumococcal, Hib, MenACWY, meningococcal B, and annual influenza
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: In asplenia/splenic dysfunction, pneumococcal, Hib, MenACWY, meningococcal B, and annual influenza are recommended.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which of the following is a live attenuated vaccine?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Live attenuated vaccines include MMR/MMRV, varicella, BCG, oral rotavirus, live attenuated nasal influenza, yellow fever and oral typhoid. Hepatitis B, IPV, DTaP and injectable influenza are inactivated or subunit. Note that the UK shingles vaccine is recombinant, not live (UKHSA).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which statement about live attenuated vaccines is correct?
options: A single dose is often sufficient, and they produce IgG + IgA antibodies with no adjuvant needed
They require multiple doses and a booster
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: A single dose is often sufficient, and they produce IgG + IgA antibodies with no adjuvant needed
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Live attenuated vaccines often need only a single dose (strong cell-mediated immunity), produce IgG + IgA, and need no adjuvant, but must not be given to immunocompromised or pregnant patients.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which feature distinguishes killed/inactivated/subunit vaccines from live vaccines?
options: They produce mainly IgG rather than mucosal IgA, need boosters, and are usually adjuvanted
They may cause a mild form of the disease they protect against
They are contraindicated in pregnancy and in immunosuppression
A single dose is always sufficient, with no booster ever needed
They produce both IgG and mucosal IgA and never require an adjuvant
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: They produce mainly IgG rather than mucosal IgA, need boosters, and are usually adjuvanted
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Inactivated and subunit vaccines produce mainly systemic IgG rather than mucosal IgA, need a primary course plus boosters, and are usually — though not always (IPV and standard inactivated influenza are not) — adjuvanted. They are safe in pregnancy and in immunosuppression, although the response may be reduced in significant immunosuppression.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How do the diphtheria and tetanus vaccines generate immunity?
options: Toxoid adsorbed onto aluminium adjuvant → antibodies against the toxin, not the bacteria
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Toxoid adsorbed onto aluminium adjuvant → antibodies against the toxin, not the bacteria
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Diphtheria + tetanus vaccines use toxoid adsorbed onto aluminium adjuvant (inactivated toxin → antibodies against the toxin, not the bacteria).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: The meningococcus and Hib vaccines are conjugate vaccines. What does conjugation to a carrier protein achieve?
options: A T-independent response with no memory
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Meningococcus + Hib vaccines are capsular polysaccharide conjugated to a carrier protein, giving a T-cell-dependent response → memory.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How does the hepatitis B vaccine generate immunity?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The hepatitis B vaccine is a recombinant viral surface antigen (HBsAg).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Why is the MMR vaccine given at 12 months and not earlier?
options: It requires an adjuvant only available later
Infants cannot mount any immune response before 12 months
It causes fever in younger infants
The vaccine is too toxic before 12 months
Maternal IgG (transplacentally acquired) would neutralise the live vaccine if given earlier; it wanes by ~6 months
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Maternal IgG (transplacentally acquired) would neutralise the live vaccine if given earlier; it wanes by ~6 months
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: MMR is given from 12 months because maternal IgG (transplacentally acquired) would neutralise the live vaccine if given before this; maternal IgG wanes by ~6 months.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with HIV and a CD4 count <200 is being considered for vaccination. What is the rule regarding live vaccines?
options: Live vaccines are recommended to boost immunity
Live vaccines are an absolute contraindication due to risk of vaccine-strain disease
Only inactivated vaccines cause vaccine-strain disease
Live vaccines are safe if given with an adjuvant
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Live vaccines are an absolute contraindication due to risk of vaccine-strain disease
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Live vaccines + immunocompromise is an absolute contraindication; in immunocompromised patients (HIV CD4 <200, on biologics, post-stem cell transplant) live vaccines risk vaccine-strain disease.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Why are unconjugated polysaccharide vaccines ineffective in children under 2 years?
options: They are only T-independent → no memory → not effective in <2 years
They require maternal IgG to work
They elicit a T-cell-dependent response with strong memory
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: They are only T-independent → no memory → not effective in <2 years
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Conjugated polysaccharide vaccines (PCV, Hib, MenACWY) elicit a T-cell-dependent response → memory; unconjugated vaccines are only T-independent → no memory → not effective in children under 2.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Why is pertussis vaccination in pregnancy particularly important, and when is pertussis most dangerous?
options: It prevents cervical cancer in the mother as well as pertussis in the baby
It protects the mother only — pertussis is most dangerous in adults, not infants
It replaces the infant pertussis schedule entirely, so no infant doses are needed
Maternal antibody crosses the placenta to protect the newborn before their own vaccines
It is a live vaccine that colonises the neonate and induces mucosal immunity
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Maternal antibody crosses the placenta to protect the newborn before their own vaccines
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Maternal pertussis vaccination at 16–32 weeks → antibodies passively transferred to the neonate → protects the newborn for the first few weeks before their own vaccines; this matters because pertussis is most dangerous in infants under 3 months.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which statement about HPV epidemiology and vaccine coverage is correct?
options: the 9-valent HPV vaccine covers only 50% of strains
HPV 16 + 18 cause 70% of cervical cancers, and the 9-valent HPV vaccine covers 90%+ of cervical cancer-causing strains
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: HPV 16 + 18 cause 70% of cervical cancers, and the 9-valent HPV vaccine covers 90%+ of cervical cancer-causing strains
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: HPV 16 + 18 cause 70% of cervical cancers, HPV 6 + 11 cause 90% of genital warts, and the 9-valent HPV vaccine now covers 90%+ of cervical cancer-causing strains.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Why was the whole-cell pertussis vaccine replaced by the acellular version?
options: The acellular version is live attenuated
The whole-cell version produced no immunity
The acellular version needs no doses
The whole-cell version was a toxoid
The acellular version (purified pertussis proteins) replaced whole-cell because of side effects
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: The acellular version (purified pertussis proteins) replaced whole-cell because of side effects
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The acellular pertussis vaccine contains purified pertussis proteins and replaced the whole-cell vaccine because of its side-effect profile; the number of components varies by product. It is not live, and the whole-cell vaccine did produce immunity — it was tolerability, not efficacy, that drove the change.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: The rotavirus vaccine is given orally in the infant schedule. What type of vaccine is it, and why is it important?
options: A toxoid vaccine — it prevents tetanus by neutralising the toxin
A conjugate polysaccharide — it prevents pneumococcal pneumonia
Live attenuated and given orally — a leading cause of severe infant diarrhoea
Recombinant surface antigen — it prevents hepatitis B infection
Inactivated whole organism — it prevents meningococcal meningitis
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Live attenuated and given orally — a leading cause of severe infant diarrhoea
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The rotavirus vaccine is live attenuated and oral; rotavirus is a leading cause of severe diarrhoea/hospitalisation in infants.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the central immunological problem in organ transplantation?
options: Donor organs become immunologically inert once they are perfused
The donor immune system always attacks the recipient
The recipient's immune system recognises donor tissue as non-self (via HLA mismatch) and mounts a rejection response
The graft receives an inadequate blood supply for its metabolic needs
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: The recipient's immune system recognises donor tissue as non-self (via HLA mismatch) and mounts a rejection response
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The central problem is that the recipient's immune system recognises donor tissue as non-self (via HLA mismatch) → mounts a rejection response → graft damage.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which HLA class is found on all nucleated cells and recognised by CD8+ T-cells?
options: HLA-DR only, expressed on antigen-presenting cells
Non-classical HLA-E, expressed only on NK cells
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: MHC Class I (HLA-A, -B, -C) is on all nucleated cells and recognised by CD8+ T-cells; MHC Class II (HLA-DR, -DQ, -DP) is on APCs/B-cells and recognised by CD4+ T-cells.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: In the '6-antigen match', which HLA locus is the most significant to match?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The most important loci to match are HLA-A, -B, and -DR (the '6-antigen match'), and DR is the most significant.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: ABO incompatibility in transplantation leads to which type of rejection?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: ABO incompatibility → hyperacute rejection, so ABO blood group must be compatible.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A pre-transplant crossmatch tests recipient serum against donor lymphocytes. A positive crossmatch indicates what?
options: Chronic rejection is inevitable but treatable
The donor and recipient are ABO incompatible only
The transplant is safe to proceed
Pre-formed anti-HLA antibodies → risk of hyperacute rejection → contraindication
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Pre-formed anti-HLA antibodies → risk of hyperacute rejection → contraindication
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The crossmatch detects pre-formed anti-HLA antibodies; a positive crossmatch means a risk of hyperacute rejection and is a contraindication.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: In allorecognition, which pathway involves recipient T-cells recognising intact donor HLA on donor APCs, and what does it drive?
options: The direct pathway; acute rejection (early, vigorous)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: The direct pathway; acute rejection (early, vigorous)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The direct pathway is where recipient T-cells recognise intact donor HLA on donor APCs → drives acute rejection (early, vigorous). The indirect pathway (recipient APCs process donor HLA) drives chronic rejection.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A transplanted kidney becomes mottled and thrombosed within hours of reperfusion. Which rejection type is this, and what is the mechanism?
options: Hyperacute; pre-formed recipient antibodies vs donor ABO/HLA → complement → thrombosis + necrosis
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Hyperacute; pre-formed recipient antibodies vs donor ABO/HLA → complement → thrombosis + necrosis
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Hyperacute rejection occurs in minutes–hours from pre-formed recipient antibodies vs donor ABO/HLA → complement → thrombosis + necrosis (Type II); it is irreversible, so the graft is removed, and it is prevented by crossmatch.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient develops rejection 3 months post-transplant that is T-cell-mediated with HLA mismatch. What is the type, hypersensitivity class, and typical outcome?
options: Acute; Type IV; often reversible with increased immunosuppression
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Acute; Type IV; often reversible with increased immunosuppression
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Acute rejection occurs days–6 months, is T-cell-mediated (cellular) ± antibody with HLA mismatch, is Type IV, and is often reversible with increased immunosuppression.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Chronic rejection is characterised by which mechanism and outcome?
options: Donor cells attacking the host; treatable
Antibody + cell-mediated → fibrosis, vascular damage (graft vasculopathy); largely irreversible → graft failure
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Antibody + cell-mediated → fibrosis, vascular damage (graft vasculopathy); largely irreversible → graft failure
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Chronic rejection occurs over months–years, is antibody + cell-mediated → fibrosis, vascular damage (graft vasculopathy), is mixed hypersensitivity, and is largely irreversible → graft failure.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A kidney transplant recipient has had a slowly rising creatinine and increasing proteinuria over 4 years, and graft biopsy shows interstitial fibrosis and vascular narrowing. What is this, and what can be done?
options: Chronic rejection — largely irreversible; slow progression with blood pressure and proteinuria control, and by maintaining immunosuppression and adherence
Calcineurin inhibitor toxicity alone — stopping tacrolimus will restore function
Graft-versus-host disease — reduce immunosuppression and start corticosteroids
Hyperacute rejection — remove the graft immediately, as it is irreversible
Acute T-cell-mediated rejection — high-dose corticosteroids will reverse it
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Chronic rejection — largely irreversible; slow progression with blood pressure and proteinuria control, and by maintaining immunosuppression and adherence
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Chronic rejection develops over months to years, is antibody plus cell-mediated, and produces interstitial fibrosis and graft vasculopathy. It is largely irreversible, so management is to slow progression — blood pressure and proteinuria control, maintaining immunosuppression and adherence, and planning for a return to dialysis or re-transplantation. Contrast hyperacute (minutes to hours, pre-formed antibodies, Type II, explant) and acute (days to 6 months, T-cell-mediated, Type IV, steroid-responsive).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: In graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), what happens, and in which transplant setting?
options: The host rejects the graft; solid-organ transplant
Pre-formed antibodies destroy the graft; kidney transplant
The donor's immune cells attack the recipient's tissues; bone marrow/stem cell transplant
The graft becomes fibrotic; heart transplant
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: The donor's immune cells attack the recipient's tissues; bone marrow/stem cell transplant
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: GVHD is the opposite of rejection: in bone marrow/stem cell transplants, the donor's immune cells attack the recipient's tissues (graft attacks host).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the classic triad of organs targeted in GVHD?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The classic GVHD triad targets skin (rash), gut (diarrhoea), and liver (deranged LFTs/jaundice).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How is GVHD prevented?
options: HLA matching, T-cell depletion of the graft, and drug prophylaxis (ciclosporin ± methotrexate)
Irradiating the donor stem cells before infusion
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: HLA matching, T-cell depletion of the graft, and drug prophylaxis (ciclosporin ± methotrexate)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: GVHD is prevented by best-possible HLA matching, T-cell depletion of the graft and drug prophylaxis (a calcineurin inhibitor, usually ciclosporin, with or without methotrexate). It is classified as acute (classically within 100 days) versus chronic, and treated with corticosteroids first-line. Crossmatch testing prevents hyperacute rejection, not GVHD. The transfusion form, transfusion-associated GVHD, is prevented by irradiating cellular blood components.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient is being worked up for a kidney transplant and is not immune to varicella. When can the live varicella vaccine be given?
options: Before transplantation, while the patient is still on the waiting list
At any time — live vaccines are safe in transplant recipients
At 3 months post-transplant, once the graft is stable
Never, in any transplant candidate or recipient
In the first week after transplantation, before immunosuppression takes effect
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Before transplantation, while the patient is still on the waiting list
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Live vaccines (MMR/MMRV, varicella, BCG, yellow fever, oral typhoid, live attenuated nasal influenza) are contraindicated once a patient is immunosuppressed, because of the risk of disseminated vaccine-strain disease (UKHSA). Give them before transplantation — ideally at least 4 weeks pre-operatively. Non-live vaccines (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19, hepatitis B, recombinant shingles) are safe and recommended lifelong after transplant, though responses are blunted; vaccinate household contacts as well.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Tacrolimus and ciclosporin form the immunosuppression backbone. What is their mechanism and a key caution?
options: Broad anti-inflammatory suppression; osteoporosis and diabetes are the key effects
Inhibit purine synthesis to reduce lymphocyte proliferation; marrow suppression
Deplete circulating T-cells directly; cytokine release syndrome is the risk
Block the mTOR pathway; gum hypertrophy and hirsutism are the key effects
Block calcineurin → ↓IL-2 → ↓T-cell activation; nephrotoxic with a narrow therapeutic index requiring TDM
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Block calcineurin → ↓IL-2 → ↓T-cell activation; nephrotoxic with a narrow therapeutic index requiring TDM
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, ciclosporin) block calcineurin → ↓IL-2 → ↓T-cell activation (the backbone); they are nephrotoxic with a narrow therapeutic index and need TDM.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Mycophenolate and azathioprine act by which mechanism?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Antiproliferatives (mycophenolate, azathioprine) inhibit purine synthesis → ↓lymphocyte proliferation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Basiliximab is given as induction at the time of transplant. What does it do?
options: Blocks the IL-2 receptor on activated T-cells
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Blocks the IL-2 receptor on activated T-cells
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Basiliximab is a monoclonal antibody against the IL-2 receptor on activated T-cells, given as induction around the time of transplant when the rejection risk is highest (NICE). It is not maintenance therapy — maintenance is a calcineurin inhibitor plus an antimetabolite plus a corticosteroid.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the standard maintenance immunosuppression regimen?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Standard maintenance is tacrolimus + mycophenolate + prednisolone.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the first-line treatment for an episode of acute rejection?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Acute T-cell-mediated rejection is treated with pulsed high-dose corticosteroids (IV methylprednisolone) first-line, with antibody therapy for steroid-resistant rejection. Antibody-mediated rejection is treated differently, with plasma exchange and IVIg. Reducing immunosuppression is what you do for PTLD, not for rejection, and explant is reserved for hyperacute rejection.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A transplant patient on long-term immunosuppression is at risk of opportunistic infection. Which prophylaxis is given for PCP?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Co-trimoxazole is PCP prophylaxis, and it also covers toxoplasma and nocardia. Valganciclovir is the wrong answer here because it is the CMV agent — used either as CMV prophylaxis (highest risk is a CMV-positive donor into a CMV-negative recipient) or as pre-emptive therapy guided by CMV viral load (PCR). Aciclovir covers HSV and VZV, not PCP. The opportunistic window is 1–6 months post-transplant.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which malignancy is EBV-driven and increased in transplant patients on immunosuppression?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: PTLD is the EBV-driven lymphoproliferative disorder of transplant recipients — the first step in management is to reduce immunosuppression, with rituximab and/or chemotherapy if that is insufficient. Skin cancer (chiefly SCC) is the commonest post-transplant malignancy but is not EBV-driven; HPV-related anogenital cancer and HHV-8-related Kaposi's sarcoma are also increased.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which drug-specific complication is correctly matched?
options: Ciclosporin → marrow suppression requiring TPMT testing before starting
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Tacrolimus: nephrotoxicity, new-onset diabetes after transplantation, tremor and hypertension. Ciclosporin: nephrotoxicity, hypertension, gum (gingival) hypertrophy and hirsutism — it is less diabetogenic than tacrolimus. Marrow suppression with TPMT testing beforehand is azathioprine; mycophenolate causes GI upset and marrow suppression and is a major teratogen.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Before starting azathioprine in a transplant patient, which test should be checked, and why?
options: HLA typing, to match the donor
ABO type, to prevent hyperacute rejection
TPMT, because of marrow suppression risk
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: TPMT, because of marrow suppression risk
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Azathioprine can cause marrow suppression, so TPMT is checked before starting it.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Acute inflammation is best described as consisting of which two responses?
options: An innate response and an adaptive response only
A vascular response (↑blood flow + ↑permeability) and a cellular response (recruiting neutrophils)
A humoral response and a cell-mediated response
A fibrotic response and a granulomatous response
A systemic response and a wound-healing response
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: A vascular response (↑blood flow + ↑permeability) and a cellular response (recruiting neutrophils)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Acute inflammation has a vascular response (↑blood flow + ↑permeability) and a cellular response (recruiting neutrophils to the site), driven by chemical mediators, producing the cardinal signs.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which cardinal sign of inflammation is caused by increased vascular permeability?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Swelling (tumor) is caused by increased vascular permeability → fluid leaks into tissue (exudate). Redness and heat are from increased blood flow, and pain is from mediators.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which mediators sensitise nerves to produce the pain (dolor) of inflammation?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Pain (dolor) results from mediators — bradykinin and prostaglandins — sensitising nerves.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Vasodilation in the vascular response is mediated by which of the following?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Vasodilation → ↑blood flow to the area → redness + heat, mediated by histamine, prostaglandins, and NO.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What distinguishes an inflammatory exudate from a simple transudate?
options: The transudate forms fibrin to wall off the area
The exudate is protein-rich, carrying antibodies, complement, and fibrinogen
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: The exudate is protein-rich, carrying antibodies, complement, and fibrinogen
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Inflammatory exudate is protein-rich, carrying antibodies, complement, and fibrinogen (which forms fibrin to wall off the area) — this distinguishes it from a simple transudate.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which is the correct order of the cellular response (neutrophil recruitment)?
options: Margination → rolling + adhesion → diapedesis → chemotaxis → phagocytosis
Margination → diapedesis → rolling + adhesion → phagocytosis → chemotaxis
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Margination → rolling + adhesion → diapedesis → chemotaxis → phagocytosis
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The sequence is margination → rolling + adhesion (selectins → integrins) → diapedesis/transmigration → chemotaxis (following gradients — chemokines, C5a) → phagocytosis (aided by opsonisation).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: During rolling and adhesion, neutrophils bind the endothelium via which molecules?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: In rolling + adhesion, neutrophils bind the endothelium via selectins → integrins.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Why does the FBC classically show neutrophilia in acute bacterial infection?
options: Neutrophils arrive first in acute inflammation, with macrophages later
Neutrophils only appear in chronic inflammation
Macrophages arrive first in acute inflammation
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Neutrophils arrive first in acute inflammation, with macrophages later
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Neutrophils arrive first (acute inflammation), then macrophages later (clean-up + chronic) — which is why the FBC shows neutrophilia in acute bacterial infection.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is opsonisation, and why does it matter?
options: Endothelial cells contracting to form gaps
Neutrophils squeezing through the vessel wall
Slowed blood flow letting leucocytes marginate
Coating the pathogen with antibody/complement to make phagocytosis far more efficient
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Coating the pathogen with antibody/complement to make phagocytosis far more efficient
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Opsonisation is coating the pathogen with antibody/complement, which makes phagocytosis far more efficient ('opsonins' = 'to prepare for eating').

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which mediator is released by mast cells and blocked by antihistamines?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Histamine is released by mast cells and causes early vasodilation + ↑permeability; antihistamines block it.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: NSAIDs exert their anti-inflammatory effect by inhibiting the production of which mediator, via which enzyme?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Prostaglandins are made from arachidonic acid via COX and cause vasodilation, pain, and fever; NSAIDs block COX → ↓prostaglandins → anti-inflammatory + analgesic + antipyretic.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Leukotrienes are derived from arachidonic acid via which enzyme, and what is a key action?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Leukotrienes are made from arachidonic acid via lipoxygenase and cause bronchoconstriction and ↑permeability; leukotriene antagonists are used in asthma.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which mediators are produced by macrophages and act as biologic drug targets in the systemic response?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6) are produced by macrophages and drive the systemic response (fever, acute-phase proteins); TNF/IL-6 are biologic drug targets.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How do steroids act as the most powerful anti-inflammatories?
options: By broadly suppressing inflammation (↓ mediators, ↓ phospholipase → ↓ arachidonic acid pathway)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: By broadly suppressing inflammation (↓ mediators, ↓ phospholipase → ↓ arachidonic acid pathway)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Steroids broadly suppress inflammation (↓ mediators, ↓ phospholipase → ↓ arachidonic acid pathway) — making them the most powerful anti-inflammatories.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 70-year-old is reviewed 24 hours after an emergency laparotomy. He is comfortable, apyrexial and haemodynamically normal, but his CRP is 180 mg/L. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: CRP is unaffected by surgery, so this indicates an anastomotic leak
A raised CRP reflects inflammation from any cause, including recent surgery, and must be read alongside the clinical picture
A CRP this high confirms bacterial infection and mandates broad-spectrum antibiotics
A normal CRP would have reliably excluded infection in this patient
A raised CRP excludes a viral cause and confirms a bacterial one
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: A raised CRP reflects inflammation from any cause, including recent surgery, and must be read alongside the clinical picture
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: CRP is a marker of inflammation, not a test for bacteria: surgery, trauma, burns, myocardial infarction, VTE, pancreatitis, autoimmune flares and malignancy all raise it, and it cannot distinguish bacterial from viral infection. It peaks 24–48 hours after any insult, so a high CRP the day after laparotomy is expected. Equally, a normal CRP does not exclude infection — it takes about 6 hours to rise and is blunted by corticosteroids and liver failure. The useful signal is the trend: a CRP that fails to fall, or rises again after day 3, is the one that suggests a complication.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How does fever arise in the systemic inflammatory response?
options: Prostaglandins act directly on skeletal muscle to generate heat
Pyrogenic cytokines act on the hypothalamus, raising prostaglandin E2 and the temperature set point
The liver raises body temperature via CRP
Peripheral vasodilation alone raises the core temperature
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Pyrogenic cytokines act on the hypothalamus, raising prostaglandin E2 and the temperature set point
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: IL-1, IL-6 and TNF-α act on the hypothalamus, raising PGE2 and therefore the temperature set point — the patient shivers and vasoconstricts until the new set point is reached. Because the final common step is prostaglandin, antipyretics (paracetamol, NSAIDs) work by reducing prostaglandin synthesis. Vasodilation is the mechanism of heat loss, not heat gain.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which acute-phase protein is the clinical inflammatory marker, and what drives its production?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: CRP is the clinical inflammatory marker, produced by the liver and driven by IL-6. Fibrinogen and ferritin are also acute-phase proteins. Albumin is a negative acute-phase protein — it falls in inflammation, so a low albumin in an unwell patient is not automatically malnutrition.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How do CRP and ESR compare as inflammatory markers?
options: CRP rises fast (IL-6-driven); ESR is slower and fibrinogen-related
Both rise at exactly the same rate
CRP measures red cells; ESR measures protein
CRP is slower and fibrinogen-related; ESR rises fast and is IL-6-driven
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: CRP rises fast (IL-6-driven); ESR is slower and fibrinogen-related
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: CRP rises fast (IL-6-driven) and ESR is slower (fibrinogen-related); both are clinical markers used to detect and monitor inflammatory/infective disease.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection is defined as:
options: An abscess — a walled-off collection of pus
Bacteraemia — bacteria present in the bloodstream
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: An abscess — a walled-off collection of pus
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection — the extreme end of the systemic inflammatory response. Bacteraemia is simply bacteria in the blood and may be transient and harmless. Septic shock is sepsis with hypotension requiring vasopressors plus a lactate above 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation. SIRS (deranged temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate and white cell count) is non-specific — trauma, burns, pancreatitis and surgery all produce it without any infection — and is no longer used to define sepsis; the UK screening tool is NEWS2 (NICE).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A localised collection of pus composed of dead neutrophils and debris is which outcome of acute inflammation?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: An abscess is a localised collection of pus (dead neutrophils + debris) — one of the outcomes of acute inflammation, alongside resolution, chronic inflammation, and fibrosis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which cells predominantly drive chronic inflammation?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Chronic inflammation is macrophage + lymphocyte-driven (not neutrophils), with simultaneous tissue destruction + repair (fibrosis). The acute-vs-chronic cell distinction is: acute = neutrophils; chronic = macrophages + lymphocytes.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A lymph node biopsy shows granulomas with central caseous necrosis, epithelioid macrophages and Langhans giant cells. Which diagnosis does this most strongly suggest?
options: A foreign-body reaction to retained suture material
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Central caseous ("cheesy") necrosis points to tuberculosis — caseating granulomas are the hallmark of mycobacterial infection. Sarcoidosis, Crohn's disease and granulomatosis with polyangiitis produce non-caseating granulomas; a foreign-body granuloma contains foreign material and giant cells with randomly scattered nuclei. Granuloma formation is a Type IV (delayed, T-cell) hypersensitivity response to a stimulus the immune system cannot clear. Histology is suggestive, not confirmatory — send tissue for acid-fast bacilli and mycobacterial culture.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A perianal abscess is incised and drained, and the cavity is packed and left open. How will this wound heal, and what is the main consequence?
options: By regeneration, with the tissue returning entirely to normal
It will not heal at all unless it is sutured closed
By primary intention — a fine linear scar with minimal granulation tissue
By secondary intention — the cavity fills from the base with granulation tissue, healing slowly with contraction and a larger scar
By delayed primary closure, with epithelium bridging the gap within 48 hours
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: By secondary intention — the cavity fills from the base with granulation tissue, healing slowly with contraction and a larger scar
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: A wound with tissue loss or contamination that is left open heals by secondary intention: granulation tissue fills the defect from the base upwards and epithelium creeps in from the edges. It is slower than primary intention (weeks to months), produces a larger scar with wound contraction, and carries a higher infection risk. Primary intention applies to clean, apposed edges such as a sutured incision. An abscess cavity is deliberately not closed — closing infected dead space over pus is how you get recurrence.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: By definition, when is an infection classified as healthcare-associated (an HCAI)?
options: When it is acquired ≥48h after admission and was not incubating on arrival
When it is present on admission
When it is caused by a resistant organism
When it occurs within 24h of discharge
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: When it is acquired ≥48h after admission and was not incubating on arrival
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: HCAIs (healthcare-associated/nosocomial infections) are acquired ≥48h after admission and not incubating on arrival.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: According to the organising principle, what is the single most effective infection-control intervention?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Every infection follows the chain of infection, and breaking any single link prevents transmission; the single most effective intervention is hand hygiene.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: In the chain of infection, which measure breaks the 'mode of transmission' link?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The mode of transmission (contact/droplet/airborne/vehicle) is broken by hand hygiene, PPE, and isolation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Breaking which link of the chain of infection involves vaccination, treating comorbidity, and nutrition?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The susceptible host (the patient at risk) link is addressed by vaccination, treating comorbidity, and nutrition.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Measles, TB, and varicella spread by which transmission route?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Airborne transmission involves small particles that stay suspended — TB, measles, and varicella.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: MRSA and C. difficile are chiefly spread by which route?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Contact transmission (direct/indirect) includes MRSA and C. diff.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A nurse is about to perform a clean/aseptic procedure. Which of the WHO '5 Moments for Hand Hygiene' does this represent?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The WHO 5 Moments are: before touching a patient, before a clean/aseptic procedure, after body-fluid exposure risk, after touching a patient, and after touching patient surroundings.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient has C. difficile infection. Which hand-hygiene method must be used, and why?
options: No hand hygiene is needed with gloves
Soap and water, because alcohol gel does not kill spores
Alcohol gel, because it is faster
Alcohol gel followed by gloves only
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Soap and water, because alcohol gel does not kill spores
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The classic exam point: alcohol gel is used for most situations, but soap and water is required for C. difficile — alcohol does not kill spores — and also for norovirus, which is a non-enveloped virus with no lipid envelope for alcohol to disrupt. Soap and water is likewise required whenever hands are visibly soiled. Note that the two organisms fail alcohol for different reasons: spores versus no envelope.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with pulmonary TB requires isolation. Which precaution and room are needed?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Airborne precautions (TB, measles, varicella) require a fit-tested FFP3 respirator and a negative-pressure single room with the door closed. Pulmonary and laryngeal TB need airborne + standard precautions — TB is not spread by contact or fomites, so contact precautions are added only for a draining extrapulmonary lesion.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with influenza is admitted. Which transmission-based precautions apply?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Droplet precautions (influenza, COVID-19, pertussis, meningococcus) require a surgical mask, eye protection if there is splash risk, and a single room — but a fit-tested FFP3 respirator is needed for aerosol-generating procedures such as intubation, bronchoscopy, open suctioning, CPR, non-invasive ventilation and high-flow nasal oxygen. Meningococcal droplet precautions can be stepped down after 24 hours of effective antibiotics.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which combination of precautions is required for a patient with C. difficile?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: C. diff needs contact + standard precautions (single room with en-suite, gloves and apron, soap and water). By contrast pulmonary TB needs airborne + standard, and chickenpox needs airborne + contact.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which HCAI is antibiotic-associated and spore-forming, and how is it prevented?
options: MRSA; contact precautions, risk-based screening and decolonisation
SSI; antibiotic prophylaxis before incision and maintaining normothermia
C. difficile; stewardship, prompt isolation, soap & water, oral vancomycin first-line
CLABSI; insertion and maintenance care bundles with early line removal
CAUTI; catheterise only when indicated and remove the catheter early
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: C. difficile; stewardship, prompt isolation, soap & water, oral vancomycin first-line
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: C. difficile is antibiotic-associated (the 4 Cs — clindamycin, cephalosporins, co-amoxiclav, ciprofloxacin) and spore-forming. Prevention is stewardship, prompt isolation in a single room with en-suite, soap-and-water hand hygiene and chlorine-based cleaning; treatment is oral vancomycin first-line with fidaxomicin second-line, stopping the causative antibiotic, and avoiding antimotility agents because of the risk of toxic megacolon.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How is MRSA prevented as an HCAI?
options: Contact precautions, screening + decolonisation (chlorhexidine wash, nasal mupirocin)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Contact precautions, screening + decolonisation (chlorhexidine wash, nasal mupirocin)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: MRSA (colonisation → infection; lines/wounds) is prevented with contact precautions and screening + decolonisation using chlorhexidine wash and nasal mupirocin.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the key prevention strategy for catheter-associated UTI (CAUTI)?
options: Prophylactic antibiotics for all catheterised patients
Avoid/remove catheters early and use aseptic insertion
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Avoid/remove catheters early and use aseptic insertion
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: CAUTI is prevented by catheterising only for a valid documented indication, aseptic insertion with a sterile closed drainage system, keeping the bag below bladder level, daily meatal hygiene, and above all reviewing the need daily and removing the catheter early. Prophylactic antibiotics for catheterised patients are not recommended and asymptomatic bacteriuria is not treated.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which measures are key to preventing central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI)?
options: Insertion care bundles, aseptic technique, and early removal
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Insertion care bundles, aseptic technique, and early removal
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: CLABSI is prevented by an insertion bundle — maximal sterile barrier precautions, chlorhexidine-in-alcohol skin prep, ultrasound guidance and avoiding the femoral site — and a maintenance bundle: scrub the hub before every access, aseptic non-touch technique, an intact dressing, minimising lumens and accesses, with daily review and early removal.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which set of measures reduces surgical site infection (SSI)?
options: Nasal mupirocin and a chlorhexidine body wash for every surgical patient
Negative-pressure isolation of the patient for 48 hours after the operation
Soap-and-water hand hygiene, ward closure and terminal cleaning of theatres
Antibiotic prophylaxis within 60 minutes before incision, chlorhexidine-alcohol skin prep, normothermia
Head elevation to 30–45° and regular oral care throughout the operation
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Antibiotic prophylaxis within 60 minutes before incision, chlorhexidine-alcohol skin prep, normothermia
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: SSI is reduced by antibiotic prophylaxis given within 60 minutes before incision (a single dose for most operations), chlorhexidine-alcohol skin preparation, maintaining normothermia and glycaemic control, and hair removal only if necessary using clippers on the day of surgery rather than a razor.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Norovirus causes ward and cruise-ship outbreaks. Which prevention measures are appropriate?
options: Soap & water, ward closure, and isolation
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Soap & water, ward closure, and isolation
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Norovirus (faecal-oral, outbreaks on wards/cruises) is managed with soap & water, ward closure, and isolation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: MRSA is resistant to β-lactams by which mechanism, and how are patients screened?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: MRSA is Staph aureus resistant to β-lactams via altered PBP2a. Screening uses a nasal swab plus other sites (groin/perineum, wounds, catheter urine), and in the UK it is targeted at high-risk patients and units rather than every admission; positives are decolonised with nasal mupirocin plus an antiseptic body wash for 5 days and then re-screened.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What are the '4 Cs' high-risk antibiotics for C. difficile?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The '4 Cs' high-risk antibiotics for C. difficile are clindamycin, cephalosporins, co-amoxiclav, and ciprofloxacin.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the current first-line management of C. difficile infection?
options: IV vancomycin only, because it achieves the highest bowel-lumen concentrations
Isolate + soap-and-water + oral vancomycin/fidaxomicin, and stop the offending antibiotic (metronidazole no longer first-line)
Alcohol gel, continue the precipitating antibiotic, and add loperamide for symptom control
Oral metronidazole first-line with immediate ward closure and terminal cleaning
IV metronidazole first-line, with alcohol gel for hand hygiene between patients
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Isolate + soap-and-water + oral vancomycin/fidaxomicin, and stop the offending antibiotic (metronidazole no longer first-line)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: C. diff management is isolate + soap-and-water + oral vancomycin/fidaxomicin (metronidazole is no longer first-line), plus stopping the offending antibiotic. Antibiotic use → loss of gut flora → toxin-producing C. diff overgrowth → pseudomembranous colitis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Why is antimicrobial stewardship considered a core part of infection control?
options: It eliminates the need for isolation
It prevents C. diff and resistance
It replaces the need for hand hygiene
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: It prevents C. diff and resistance
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Antimicrobial stewardship is core infection control because it prevents C. diff and resistance.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which of the following best describes outbreak management at the organisational level?
options: Identify, isolate, cohort, deep clean, and involve the IPC team
Vaccinate staff, then close the hospital
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Identify, isolate, cohort, deep clean, and involve the IPC team
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Outbreak management means recognising the outbreak, isolating or cohorting affected patients, deep cleaning and involving the IPC team. In practice this also means an outbreak control team, an agreed case definition and line list, restricting admissions and transfers (closing bays or the ward if necessary), excluding affected patients and staff until 48 hours symptom-free, and notifying UKHSA where the organism is notifiable.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which of the following is part of the standard precautions applied to every patient, always?
options: Sharps safety with no re-sheathing and use of sharps bins
A fit-tested FFP3 respirator for all patients
Nasal mupirocin decolonisation for all patients
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Sharps safety with no re-sheathing and use of sharps bins
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Standard precautions (applied to every patient always) include hand hygiene, PPE, sharps safety, respiratory hygiene, safe waste and linen disposal, cleaning and decontamination, and aseptic technique. Sharps safety also means never re-sheathing, disposing at the point of use, and knowing the injury drill: encourage bleeding and wash, report to occupational health immediately, risk assess the source, and start HIV PEP within 72 hours if indicated.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 3-year-old has had two episodes of Staphylococcus aureus osteomyelitis and a deep-seated abscess. Which arm of the immune system should be investigated first?
options: None — two episodes is within the normal range for a child of this age
Complement, because deep-seated recurrent infection points to the terminal pathway
Humoral (B-cell/antibody), because any recurrent bacterial infection implies antibody failure
NK cell number and function, because NK cells control staphylococcal infection
Phagocyte function, because catalase-positive organisms and abscesses point there
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Phagocyte function, because catalase-positive organisms and abscesses point there
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The organising principle of immunodeficiency is that the deficient arm predicts the infection pattern. Abscesses, osteomyelitis and catalase-positive organisms such as Staph aureus (or Aspergillus) in a young child point to a phagocyte defect — investigate neutrophil function with an NBT or DHR test for chronic granulomatous disease. Encapsulated bacteria point to humoral deficiency, opportunists to T-cell deficiency, and recurrent Neisseria to complement deficiency.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 58-year-old on rituximab for lymphoma develops his third episode of pneumococcal pneumonia in a year. How is his immunodeficiency best classified?
options: Secondary humoral (antibody) deficiency, caused by B-cell depletion
Secondary T-cell deficiency, caused by the underlying lymphoma
Secondary complement deficiency, caused by the underlying lymphoma
Primary humoral deficiency, most likely common variable immunodeficiency
Primary phagocyte deficiency, most likely chronic granulomatous disease
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Secondary humoral (antibody) deficiency, caused by B-cell depletion
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Secondary (acquired) immunodeficiency is far commoner than primary. Rituximab is an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody that depletes B-cells, causing a secondary humoral deficiency — hence recurrent infection with encapsulated bacteria such as S. pneumoniae. Check immunoglobulins; some patients need immunoglobulin replacement. Primary deficiency can present at any age but is much rarer and would not be the first explanation here.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient has recurrent infections with encapsulated bacteria (H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis) and recurrent sinopulmonary infections after 6 months of age. Which arm is deficient?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Humoral (B-cell/antibody) deficiency causes infections with encapsulated bacteria ('SHiN'), with the clue of recurrent sinopulmonary infections after 6 months of age.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A child presents with recurrent abscesses and osteomyelitis from Staph aureus and Aspergillus. Which immune arm is most likely deficient?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Phagocyte deficiency causes infections with catalase-positive bacteria (Staph aureus) and fungi (Aspergillus), with the clue of abscesses and osteomyelitis in childhood.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient has recurrent meningococcal disease. Which immune arm should be tested?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Complement deficiency, specifically of the terminal pathway (C5–C9/MAC), causes recurrent Neisseria infection — Neisseria have a thin cell wall and are killed mainly by direct MAC-mediated lysis, so losing the terminal pathway removes the main defence against them. A second episode of meningococcal disease is the trigger to screen complement.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which is the commonest cause of secondary immunodeficiency in UK clinical practice?
options: Extremes of age, through immune senescence
Nephrotic syndrome, through urinary immunoglobulin loss
Diabetes mellitus, through impaired neutrophil function
Chronic kidney disease, through uraemic immune dysfunction
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: HIV is the commonest cause of secondary immunodeficiency in UK practice — it progressively destroys CD4+ T-cells, giving a cell-mediated defect. Worldwide, protein-energy malnutrition is the commonest cause overall. Other secondary causes include immunosuppressive drugs (corticosteroids, rituximab, cytotoxics), haematological malignancy, protein loss, asplenia, diabetes and extremes of age.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Using the MHC 'Rule of 8', which cells recognise MHC class II, and what is the relationship?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Rule of 8: Class II (HLA-DQ/DR/DP, on APCs + B-cells) is recognised by CD4 (CD4 × MHC II = 8); Class I is recognised by CD8 (CD8 × MHC I = 8).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which complement components function as anaphylatoxins causing mast cell degranulation?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: C3/4/5a are anaphylatoxins (mast cell degranulation); C3b is opsonisation, C5a is neutrophil chemotaxis, and C5–9 is the membrane attack complex (kills Neisseria).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A boy develops recurrent URTIs/LRTIs with encapsulated organisms starting after 6 months of age. Investigations show absent B-cells and absent antibodies. What is the diagnosis and its genetic defect?
options: Selective IgA deficiency; IgA gene deletion
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: X-Linked Agammaglobulinaemia (XLA/Bruton's) is a BTK mutation → absent B-cells + absent antibodies; it presents after 6 months as maternal IgG wanes, with recurrent URTI/LRTI from encapsulated organisms.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How does CVID differ from XLA, and what are its associated risks?
options: It affects IgA alone, is usually asymptomatic, and carries no risk of lymphoma
It is less severe (low rather than absent antibodies), affects adults, causes bronchiectasis, and increases the risk of autoimmune disease and lymphoma
It causes hypocalcaemia and conotruncal cardiac defects from the third pharyngeal pouch
It is a phagocyte disorder producing abscesses with catalase-positive organisms
It has completely absent antibodies and presents in infancy as maternal IgG wanes
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: It is less severe (low rather than absent antibodies), affects adults, causes bronchiectasis, and increases the risk of autoimmune disease and lymphoma
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: CVID is like XLA but less severe (low rather than absent antibodies) and affects adults. Recurrent sinopulmonary infection leads to bronchiectasis, and there is granulomatous and GI disease, with an increased risk of autoimmune disease and lymphoma. It is treated with immunoglobulin replacement.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which is the most common primary immunodeficiency, and what transfusion precaution does it require?
options: CVID; all blood transfusions must be avoided entirely
CGD; only leukoreduced blood components may ever be given
Selective IgA deficiency; severe reactions occur only in those with anti-IgA antibodies, so routine pre-transfusion screening is not required
XLA; live vaccines may be given safely without precaution
CVID; only irradiated blood components may ever be given
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Selective IgA deficiency; severe reactions occur only in those with anti-IgA antibodies, so routine pre-transfusion screening is not required
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Selective IgA deficiency is the most common primary immunodeficiency and is usually asymptomatic. There is a small risk of anaphylaxis to blood products, but it is confined to those who have anti-IgA antibodies, so routine IgA screening before transfusion is not required. After a previous severe transfusion reaction, use IgA-deficient or washed components and discuss with the transfusion laboratory.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A neonate presents with tetany/hypocalcaemia at birth and a conotruncal cardiac defect. Which syndrome should you think of, and what is its mechanism?
options: Ataxia telangiectasia; a mutation in the ATM gene, inherited recessively
Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome; a WASP gene mutation on the X chromosome
DiGeorge (22q11.2 deletion); failure of the 3rd/4th pharyngeal pouches → thymic aplasia + hypoparathyroidism
SCID; combined failure of B-cell and T-cell development
Chronic granulomatous disease; loss of the NADPH oxidase complex
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: DiGeorge (22q11.2 deletion); failure of the 3rd/4th pharyngeal pouches → thymic aplasia + hypoparathyroidism
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: DiGeorge (22q11.2 deletion) results from failure of the 3rd/4th pharyngeal pouches → thymic aplasia (↓T-cells) + hypoparathyroidism (↓PTH → hypocalcaemia); CATCH-22, with tetany or hypocalcaemia at birth plus a cardiac defect being the clue.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which is the commonest acquired cause of T-cell deficiency?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: HIV/AIDS destroys CD4+ cells and is the commonest acquired T-cell deficiency; natalizumab (blocks T-cell extravasation) and cytotoxics are other secondary causes.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A boy under 5 has osteomyelitis and abscesses from Staph aureus, and an NBT test fails to turn blue. What is the diagnosis and its defect?
options: Chronic Granulomatous Disease; loss of NADPH oxidase → no respiratory burst
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Chronic Granulomatous Disease; loss of NADPH oxidase → no respiratory burst
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: CGD is commonly X-linked, though autosomal recessive forms occur, and results from loss of NADPH oxidase → no respiratory burst → can't kill catalase-positive organisms (Staph aureus, Aspergillus). It presents before age 5, and the NBT test fails to turn blue (or DHR flow cytometry is used).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A neonate has delayed umbilical cord separation and recurrent bacterial infections notably without pus. Which diagnosis and defect fits?
options: Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency; CD18 mutation → impaired phagocyte migration
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency; CD18 mutation → impaired phagocyte migration
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency is a CD18 mutation → impaired phagocyte migration → delayed umbilical cord separation and recurrent bacterial infections without pus.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 17-year-old has had two separate episodes of invasive meningococcal disease. Complement screening confirms a terminal pathway deficiency. What should be arranged alongside specialist immunology follow-up?
options: No further action is needed — two episodes can occur by chance
MenACWY and MenB vaccination, antibiotic prophylaxis and a febrile-illness plan
Lifelong corticosteroids to dampen the inflammatory response
Regular immunoglobulin replacement, as for antibody deficiency
Elective splenectomy to reduce the bacterial clearance burden
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: MenACWY and MenB vaccination, antibiotic prophylaxis and a febrile-illness plan
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Terminal complement (C5–C9/MAC) deficiency causes recurrent Neisseria infection, because Neisseria are killed mainly by direct MAC-mediated lysis. A second episode of meningococcal disease is the trigger to screen complement. Management is meningococcal vaccination (MenACWY and MenB, plus pneumococcal and Hib), antibiotic prophylaxis, education with a clear plan for prompt assessment of any fever, and family screening. The same risk applies to patients on terminal complement inhibitors such as eculizumab, who must be vaccinated before starting treatment.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 24-year-old has recurrent attacks of non-itchy facial and laryngeal swelling with abdominal pain and no urticaria. Antihistamines, corticosteroids and intramuscular adrenaline have made no difference to previous attacks. C4 is low. Which defect is responsible, and how is an acute attack treated?
options: Terminal C5–C9 (MAC) deficiency — give a non-sedating antihistamine and observe
IgE-mediated food allergy — give intramuscular adrenaline and admit for observation
Early complement (C1/C2/C4) deficiency — give intramuscular adrenaline and a steroid
C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency — give C1 esterase inhibitor concentrate or icatibant
C3 deficiency — give an oral corticosteroid course with adrenaline as required
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency — give C1 esterase inhibitor concentrate or icatibant
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency causes hereditary angioedema: recurrent non-itchy angioedema without urticaria, often with abdominal pain, and a low C4 even between attacks. It is bradykinin-mediated, so it does not respond to adrenaline, antihistamines or corticosteroids — the failure of those drugs is the diagnostic clue. Treat an acute attack with C1 esterase inhibitor concentrate or icatibant, assessing the airway first. In an undifferentiated patient with airway swelling you would still give adrenaline, because you cannot be certain of the diagnosis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which complement defect is associated with SLE-like autoimmunity plus infections with encapsulated bacteria?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Early complement (C1/C2/C4) deficiency is associated with SLE-like autoimmunity plus encapsulated bacterial infections.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A 'bubble baby' presents in infancy with failure to thrive, chronic candidiasis, and disseminated infection following live vaccines. What is the diagnosis and its commonest cause?
options: SCID; X-linked common gamma chain mutation (commonest), or ADA deficiency
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: SCID; X-linked common gamma chain mutation (commonest), or ADA deficiency
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: SCID is failure of both B and T cells (the 'bubble baby'); the commonest cause is X-linked common gamma chain mutation, with ADA deficiency another. It is a paediatric emergency needing stem cell transplant, and live vaccines must be avoided.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A male child has eczema, thrombocytopenia, and recurrent pyogenic infections. Which syndrome does the mnemonic 'WATER' identify?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome is X-linked ('WATER' — Wiskott/thrombocytopenia + Atopy/eczema + T-cell dysfunction + Elevated IgE/A + Recurrent pyogenic infections); eczema + thrombocytopenia + infections in a male = WAS.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: In Hyper-IgM syndrome, which mutation underlies the defect, and what is the antibody picture?
options: CD40L mutation; no class switching → IgM only (absent IgG/A/E)
Common gamma chain; failure of B and T cells
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: CD40L mutation; no class switching → IgM only (absent IgG/A/E)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Hyper-IgM syndrome results from a CD40L mutation → no class switching → IgM only (absent IgG/A/E); patients are susceptible to PCP and Cryptosporidium.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient has raised IgE, eosinophilia, coarse facies, retained primary teeth, and cold Staph abscesses without inflammatory signs. Which syndrome and mnemonic apply?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Hyper-IgE syndrome (Job's) shows raised IgE + eosinophilia → atopy, weak bones (pathological fractures), and cold Staph abscesses; the mnemonic FATED is coarse Facies, cold Abscesses, retained primary Teeth, raised IgE, Dermatological/eczema.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Ataxia telangiectasia is characterised by which mnemonic and inheritance?
options: CATCH-22 — cardiac defects and hypocalcaemia; a 22q11.2 microdeletion
FATED — coarse facies and cold abscesses; autosomal dominant inheritance
SHiN — the encapsulated organisms; X-linked inheritance
WATER — eczema, thrombocytopenia and infections; X-linked inheritance
AAA — Ataxia + oculocutaneous telangiectasia + Antibodies low; autosomal recessive (ATM gene)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: AAA — Ataxia + oculocutaneous telangiectasia + Antibodies low; autosomal recessive (ATM gene)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Ataxia telangiectasia is autosomal recessive (ATM gene), mnemonic 'AAA' — Ataxia + oculocutaneous telangiectasia (dilated capillaries, not angiomas) + Antibodies low (IgA, IgG subclasses, IgE) — with lymphopenia, a raised alpha-fetoprotein as the classic supporting test, increased leukaemia/lymphoma risk and high radiation sensitivity.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient who had a splenectomy is at risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI). Which organisms are the main threat?
options: Encapsulated bacteria — S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, N. meningitidis
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Encapsulated bacteria — S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, N. meningitidis
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The spleen clears encapsulated organisms, so asplenia risks OPSI with encapsulated bacteria — S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, and N. meningitidis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which blood film finding suggests hyposplenism/asplenia?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Howell-Jolly bodies on the blood film are the clue to asplenia/hyposplenism.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the management of a patient with asplenia?
options: Avoid all vaccines, because the response would be ineffective without a spleen
Regular immunoglobulin replacement alone, without vaccination or antibiotics
Vaccination at least 2 weeks before a planned splenectomy, phenoxymethylpenicillin prophylaxis, an alert card, and prompt treatment of febrile illness
Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation to restore splenic immune function
No specific measures are needed once the wound has healed after splenectomy
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Vaccination at least 2 weeks before a planned splenectomy, phenoxymethylpenicillin prophylaxis, an alert card, and prompt treatment of febrile illness
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Asplenia management is vaccination — pneumococcal, Hib, MenACWY, MenB and annual influenza, given at least 2 weeks before a planned splenectomy or from about 2 weeks after an emergency one; antibiotic prophylaxis with phenoxymethylpenicillin, or a macrolide if penicillin-allergic, offered lifelong after splenectomy; a patient alert card and education; and prompt medical assessment of any fever, because OPSI can kill within hours.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: The 'SPUR' mnemonic identifies when to suspect immunodeficiency. What does it stand for?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: SPUR = Severe, Persistent, Unusual (opportunistic organisms/sites), Recurrent — plus failure to thrive, family history, and infection from live vaccines.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which investigation specifically assesses phagocyte function in suspected CGD?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Neutrophil function tests (NBT/DHR) assess phagocyte function and are used in CGD; immunoglobulins assess humoral, lymphocyte subsets T-cell/combined, and CH50/C3/C4 complement.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which management principle is correct for immunodeficiency?
options: Prophylactic antibiotics are contraindicated because they drive resistance in these patients
Stem cell transplant is used for all antibody deficiencies, whatever the severity
Immunoglobulin replacement (IVIg or subcutaneous) for antibody deficiencies, and avoid live vaccines in T-cell/combined defects
Give live vaccines freely in T-cell and combined defects, since protection matters more
Specialist immunology referral should be avoided to prevent over-investigation
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Immunoglobulin replacement (IVIg or subcutaneous) for antibody deficiencies, and avoid live vaccines in T-cell/combined defects
