A single dose before travel, with no further monitoring needed
Daily dosing, and it is the cheapest of the available options
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Weekly, started 2–3 weeks before and continued 4 weeks after leaving
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Mefloquine is weekly, started 2–3 weeks before and continued 4 weeks after; the weekly dose aids adherence and starting early helps detect side effects, making it suitable for long trips.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A pregnant traveller needs malaria prophylaxis. Which statement is correct?
options: Atovaquone-proguanil is the first choice for pregnant travellers
Doxycycline is contraindicated; mefloquine can be used, and chloroquine + proguanil where appropriate
Primaquine is given routinely in pregnancy to prevent relapse
No chemoprophylaxis is needed in pregnancy, as immunity is enhanced
Doxycycline is the preferred option throughout pregnancy at any gestation
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Doxycycline is contraindicated; mefloquine can be used, and chloroquine + proguanil where appropriate
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Malaria is more severe in pregnancy, so advise against travel to a malarious area. If travel is unavoidable: mefloquine may be used, including in the first trimester where falciparum risk is high; chloroquine + proguanil (with folic acid 5 mg daily) where appropriate; doxycycline is contraindicated; atovaquone-proguanil is not recommended unless there is no suitable alternative. Where mefloquine resistance is documented there is no safe effective regimen — advise against travel (UKHSA).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: After significant exposure to P. vivax, primaquine is considered for relapse prevention. What must be checked first, and why?
options: G6PD status, because primaquine causes haemolysis in G6PD deficiency
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: G6PD status, because primaquine causes haemolysis in G6PD deficiency
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Primaquine is the only drug acting on liver hypnozoites and is used for presumptive anti-relapse therapy; G6PD must be checked first because primaquine causes haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient presents with a fever 8 months after returning from an endemic area. How should this be approached?
options: Malaria is excluded because it is more than 3 months
Any febrile illness during or up to a year after travel to an endemic area is malaria until excluded
Only investigate if there is a rash
Malaria only presents within 2 weeks of travel
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Any febrile illness during or up to a year after travel to an endemic area is malaria until excluded
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The 'D' (diagnose promptly) rule: any febrile illness during or up to a year after travel to an endemic area is malaria until excluded.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How is malaria diagnosed on blood films, and what is required to exclude it?
options: Blood cultures — two negative sets are enough to exclude malaria
A single thin film — one negative result is enough to exclude malaria
PCR only, with no need for blood films at any stage
Thick and thin films (thick detects, thin speciates); three negatives needed to exclude
Serology alone — a single negative test excludes malaria
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Thick and thin films (thick detects, thin speciates); three negatives needed to exclude
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Diagnosis uses thick and thin blood films (thick to detect parasites, thin to speciate and quantify); three films to exclude — repeat at 12–24 h and again 24 h later; one negative film never excludes malaria; rapid antigen tests are an adjunct.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which statement about falciparum malaria and the public-health status of malaria is correct?
options: Falciparum is a medical emergency requiring urgent treatment; malaria is a notifiable disease
Falciparum is self-limiting; malaria is confidentially surveilled
Falciparum is mild; malaria is not notifiable
Falciparum is the relapsing form; malaria is notifiable only in pregnancy
Falciparum requires no urgent treatment; malaria is non-notifiable
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Falciparum is a medical emergency requiring urgent treatment; malaria is a notifiable disease
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Falciparum malaria is a medical emergency requiring urgent treatment, and malaria is a notifiable disease.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is described as the single most-tested rule (highest-yield fork) in infective diarrhoea?
options: Never give antibiotics if E. coli O157 (Shiga-toxin) is possible, because they increase HUS risk
Antibiotics are mandatory for all travellers' diarrhoea
Always give loperamide to slow the diarrhoea
Stool culture must precede rehydration in every case
Always give antibiotics for bloody diarrhoea
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Never give antibiotics if E. coli O157 (Shiga-toxin) is possible, because they increase HUS risk
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Fork 2 (the highest-yield rule) is to never give antibiotics if E. coli O157 (Shiga-toxin) is possible, as antibiotics increase the risk of HUS.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient develops profuse vomiting 3 hours after eating reheated, handled food. Which organism is most likely?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: A very fast onset (1–6 h) of rapid vomiting after reheated/handled food points to Staph aureus, which acts via a preformed enterotoxin. The other very fast cause is Bacillus cereus (reheated rice).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient develops vomiting a few hours after eating reheated fried rice. Which organism is the classic cause?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Bacillus cereus from reheated rice has an emetic incubation of 1–5 h and is the classic 'fried rice' vomiting.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient has bloody diarrhoea and severe abdominal pain that mimics appendicitis after eating undercooked poultry. Which is the most likely organism, and which sequelae are recognised?
options: Campylobacter; Guillain-Barré syndrome and reactive arthritis
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Campylobacter; Guillain-Barré syndrome and reactive arthritis
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Campylobacter (commonest bacterial cause) comes from undercooked poultry, causes bloody diarrhoea with severe abdo pain mimicking appendicitis, and has Guillain-Barré and reactive arthritis as high-yield sequelae.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: If antibiotics are indicated for severe or high-risk Campylobacter, what is the first-line agent?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Clarithromycin is first-line if Campylobacter needs treating (azithromycin an alternative), reserved for severe illness or high-risk patients and most effective started within the first ~3 days. Ciprofloxacin is not relied on — UK Campylobacter fluoroquinolone resistance is high and systemic fluoroquinolones are restricted (MHRA). In bloody diarrhoea, hold antibiotics until E. coli O157 is excluded.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A child develops bloody diarrhoea after visiting a petting farm and eating an undercooked beefburger. Why must antibiotics be avoided?
options: Because antibiotics cause toxic megacolon directly
Because antibiotics are simply unnecessary in all diarrhoea
Because this suggests E. coli O157, and antibiotics increase the risk of HUS
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Because this suggests E. coli O157, and antibiotics increase the risk of HUS
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Undercooked beef and petting-farm exposure suggest E. coli O157 (STEC); its Shiga toxin can cause HUS, and antibiotics increase that risk — the single most-tested fact in this topic.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the triad of haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS)?
options: Fever + neck stiffness + altered mental status
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The HUS triad is AKI + microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia + thrombocytopenia; it is commonest in children and occurs in ~6% of O157 infections.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Besides E. coli O157, which other organism in this note also produces Shiga toxin and can cause HUS?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Shigella dysenteriae type 1 produces Shiga toxin and can cause HUS; the S. sonnei that dominates in the UK does not. Shigella spreads faecal-oral or via contaminated water and causes bloody diarrhoea. Note the absolute no-antibiotics rule belongs to E. coli O157 (STEC) — severe shigellosis is still treated.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient develops diarrhoea, cramps, fever and vomiting after eating undercooked eggs. Which complication is specifically associated with this organism?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Eggs/poultry point to Salmonella, which can cause bacteraemia and reactive arthritis; it is usually self-limiting, with antibiotics only if severe/invasive or high-risk.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How is Salmonella gastroenteritis distinct from typhoid / enteric fever?
options: They are caused by the same organism with identical presentation
Typhoid / enteric fever (Salmonella Typhi) is a systemic illness, distinct from non-typhoidal Salmonella gastroenteritis
Gastroenteritis is always systemic, typhoid is localised
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Typhoid / enteric fever (Salmonella Typhi) is a systemic illness, distinct from non-typhoidal Salmonella gastroenteritis
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Typhoid / enteric fever (Salmonella Typhi or Paratyphi) is a systemic illness — a returning traveller, typically from South Asia, with fever and headache, relative bradycardia, constipation before diarrhoea and rose spots. It is always treated with antibiotics and is notifiable, and a small minority become chronic carriers with the organism persisting in the gallbladder. This is distinct from the gastroenteritis caused by non-typhoidal Salmonella, which is usually self-limiting and not routinely treated.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A returning traveller has chronic, non-bloody, fatty diarrhoea after drinking contaminated water. Which organism is most likely, and what is the treatment?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Giardia (travel, contaminated water; incubation 1–3 weeks) causes chronic, non-bloody, fatty diarrhoea with malabsorption/steatorrhoea and is treated with metronidazole.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: An outbreak of vomiting and watery diarrhoea spreads rapidly through a hospital ward. Which organism is the most likely cause?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Norovirus is the commonest viral cause, spreads in outbreaks (cruise ships, wards), causes watery diarrhoea with vomiting, and is highly contagious.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient who recently finished a course of antibiotics develops diarrhoea with pseudomembranous colitis. Which organism is responsible?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: C. difficile is post-antibiotic, causes ± bloody diarrhoea and is characterised by pseudomembranous colitis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the priority assessment in a patient who is unwell with infective diarrhoea?
options: Identifying the exact causative organism before doing anything else
Starting empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics straight away
Giving loperamide to settle the diarrhoea quickly
Assessing dehydration — mucous membranes, skin turgor, pulse, BP and urine output
Performing an urgent colonoscopy to establish the diagnosis
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Assessing dehydration — mucous membranes, skin turgor, pulse, BP and urine output
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Assessing dehydration is the main thing that matters and the priority assessment in the unwell patient, looking for dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, tachycardia, hypotension, reduced urine output and prolonged CRT.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: When is stool MC&S (+ ova/cysts/parasites) indicated in infective diarrhoea?
options: Never — infective diarrhoea is always a purely clinical diagnosis
In every case of diarrhoea, regardless of severity or duration
Only once a course of empirical antibiotics has already failed
Only in patients under 5 years of age, and in nobody else
If bloody, systemically unwell, immunocompromised, recent travel, outbreak, or >7 days
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: If bloody, systemically unwell, immunocompromised, recent travel, outbreak, or >7 days
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Most cases need no investigation, but stool MC&S is indicated if there is bloody diarrhoea, the patient is systemically unwell or immunocompromised, recent travel, a suspected outbreak, or symptoms lasting >7 days.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient has bloody diarrhoea. Which targeted stool test is indicated, and why?
options: Stool Shiga-toxin / E. coli O157 testing, because it informs the no-antibiotics decision
C. diff toxin, to confirm recent antibiotics
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Stool Shiga-toxin / E. coli O157 testing, because it informs the no-antibiotics decision
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Bloody diarrhoea warrants stool Shiga-toxin / E. coli O157 testing, which informs the no-antibiotics decision.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: If HUS is suspected on bloods in infective diarrhoea, which findings are expected on the FBC and film?
options: Anaemia + thrombocytopenia, with a film showing schistocytes
Normal FBC with isolated raised CRP
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Anaemia + thrombocytopenia, with a film showing schistocytes
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: HUS gives anaemia and thrombocytopenia with schistocytes on the film, reflecting microangiopathic haemolysis as red cells are sheared through microthrombi. The clotting screen is NORMAL in HUS, which distinguishes it from DIC.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the mainstay of management for infective diarrhoea?
options: Loperamide for all patients, to reduce stool frequency quickly
Antiemetics alone, with no attention to fluid replacement
Routine hospital admission for every patient with diarrhoea
Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics started at first presentation
Rehydration — oral rehydration solution first-line, IV fluids if severely dehydrated
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Rehydration — oral rehydration solution first-line, IV fluids if severely dehydrated
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Rehydration is the cornerstone: oral rehydration solution first-line, with IV fluids if there is severe dehydration, shock or vomiting.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Why must antimotility agents such as loperamide be avoided in bloody / inflammatory diarrhoea and in suspected E. coli O157?
options: They risk toxic megacolon and prolonged toxin exposure, and in O157 they increase HUS risk
They worsen dehydration directly by increasing stool water loss
They cause immediate anaphylaxis in most patients with colitis
They induce haemolytic uraemic syndrome by themselves, without infection
They are simply ineffective and make no difference to stool frequency
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: They risk toxic megacolon and prolonged toxin exposure, and in O157 they increase HUS risk
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Antimotility agents are avoided in bloody or inflammatory diarrhoea, in suspected C. difficile and in possible E. coli O157: they risk toxic megacolon and prolong toxin exposure, and in STEC they increase the risk of HUS. In suspected STEC the rule is both-barrelled — no antibiotics and no loperamide.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which statement best summarises the selective antibiotic approach in infective diarrhoea?
options: Give antibiotics to everyone, to shorten the illness and reduce spread
Not routine; avoid entirely if E. coli O157 possible; consider if severe or systemically unwell
Antibiotics are mandatory for all bloody diarrhoea, whatever the organism
Give antibiotics only once symptoms have continued beyond 14 days
Give antibiotics only where a viral cause has been confirmed on stool testing
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Not routine; avoid entirely if E. coli O157 possible; consider if severe or systemically unwell
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Antibiotics are not routine — most infective diarrhoea is self-limiting, and antibiotics can prolong carriage or precipitate HUS. Avoid them entirely if E. coli O157 is possible. Consider them for severe Campylobacter or Shigella, systemic or immunocompromised illness, or specific organisms — Giardia with metronidazole, and C. difficile with oral vancomycin first-line and fidaxomicin second-line.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Why must soap and water (rather than alcohol gel) be used for hand hygiene in suspected C. difficile or norovirus?
options: Alcohol gel is ineffective against C. diff / norovirus
Alcohol gel causes skin irritation in these patients
Soap and water provides systemic protection
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Alcohol gel is ineffective against C. diff / norovirus
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: For infection control in C. diff / norovirus, alcohol gel is ineffective, so soap and water must be used; patients should also be isolated.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A food handler has had infective diarrhoea. What is the public-health exclusion rule?
options: Exclude from work until the stool culture is negative only
Exclude from work/school until 48 h symptom-free (especially food handlers)
Exclude only if antibiotics were given
Exclude for 14 days regardless of symptoms
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Exclude from work/school until 48 h symptom-free (especially food handlers)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The general rule is exclusion from work, school or nursery until 48 h symptom-free, and it applies to everyone — food handlers are simply the group in which it is most strictly enforced. Note the exception: for E. coli O157 and enteric fever, risk groups (food handlers, health and social care staff with patient contact, under-5s at nursery, and those unable to maintain hygiene) also need microbiological clearance with negative stool samples before returning.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which complication is the recognised 'can't-miss' in infective diarrhoea where antibiotics must not be given?
options: Post-infectious irritable bowel syndrome developing weeks later
HUS — after E. coli O157, where antibiotics and loperamide are both avoided
Toxic megacolon complicating an inflammatory colitis
Reactive arthritis following a campylobacter infection
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: HUS — after E. coli O157, where antibiotics and loperamide are both avoided
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: HUS is the can’t-miss complication. It follows Shiga-toxin-producing E. coli O157 (STEC) — where antibiotics and antimotility agents must both be avoided because each increases HUS risk. Shigella dysenteriae type 1 also produces Shiga toxin and can cause HUS, but severe shigellosis is still treated with antibiotics; the absolute no-antibiotic rule belongs to STEC. Other complications: Guillain-Barré and reactive arthritis after campylobacter, dehydration/AKI/shock, Salmonella bacteraemia, toxic megacolon, post-infectious IBS and C. difficile colitis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which organism causes meningococcal disease, and what is its Gram stain appearance?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Meningococcal disease is invasive infection with Neisseria meningitidis, a Gram-negative diplococcus, and is a medical emergency.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A GP suspects meningococcal disease in a child at home. What is the single most important action?
options: Give IV or IM benzylpenicillin (under 1y 300 mg, 1–9y 600 mg, 10y+ 1.2 g) and arrange immediate transfer
Prescribe oral antibiotics and review in 24 hours
Wait for the rash to confirm the diagnosis
Take blood cultures at home before doing anything else
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Give IV or IM benzylpenicillin (under 1y 300 mg, 1–9y 600 mg, 10y+ 1.2 g) and arrange immediate transfer
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: For strongly suspected meningococcal disease, give benzylpenicillin (or ceftriaxone) IV or IM at the earliest opportunity — under 1 year 300 mg, 1–9 years 600 mg, 10 years and over 1.2 g — but transfer to hospital must never be delayed to give it (NICE).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How do the dominant features of meningococcal meningitis differ from meningococcal septicaemia?
options: Meningitis = shock only; septicaemia = raised ICP only
Meningitis = headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, fever; septicaemia = non-blanching petechial/purpuric rash + shock
Both present identically with a rash
Meningitis = non-blanching rash + shock; septicaemia = headache + neck stiffness
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Meningitis = headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, fever; septicaemia = non-blanching petechial/purpuric rash + shock
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Meningococcal meningitis (meninges + CSF) presents with headache, neck stiffness, photophobia and fever; septicaemia (bloodstream) presents with a non-blanching petechial/purpuric rash and shock — the more lethal form.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which key danger is characteristic of meningococcal septicaemia rather than meningitis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The key dangers of septicaemia are septic shock, DIC and Waterhouse-Friderichsen, whereas the key dangers of meningitis are raised ICP and neuro damage.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A child with fever and lethargy has no rash. How should this influence the assessment for meningococcal disease?
options: The absence of a rash excludes meningococcal disease
The rash always appears before any other feature
The rash is caused by the meningitis, not the septicaemia
The non-blanching rash is caused by septicaemia and can be absent — its absence never excludes the diagnosis
A rash must be present for diagnosis
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: The non-blanching rash is caused by septicaemia and can be absent — its absence never excludes the diagnosis
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The non-blanching rash is caused by the septicaemia and can be absent in meningococcal disease; its absence never excludes the diagnosis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A neonate presents with bacterial meningitis. Which organisms are the typical causes in this age group?
options: Group B Strep, E. coli and Listeria
N. meningitidis and S. pneumoniae only
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Group B Strep, E. coli and Listeria
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: In neonates the typical organisms are Group B Streptococcus, E. coli and Listeria. Beyond the neonatal period N. meningitidis and S. pneumoniae predominate, with Listeria cover added for babies under 3 months, adults aged 60 and over, pregnancy and the immunocompromised.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which statement about viral meningitis is correct?
options: It is the commonest cause of meningitis overall and usually milder, caused by enteroviruses, HSV and VZV
It is rarer than bacterial meningitis and usually more severe
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: It is the commonest cause of meningitis overall and usually milder, caused by enteroviruses, HSV and VZV
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Viral meningitis (enteroviruses, HSV, VZV) is the commonest cause overall and usually milder than bacterial meningitis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the classic triad of the meningitic picture, and how sensitive is it?
options: Headache + vomiting + rash; always present at first presentation
Seizures + bulging fontanelle + fever; a picture specific to adults
Photophobia + limb pain + cold peripheries; present in about 90% of cases
Fever + neck stiffness + altered mental status; all three present in fewer than half of cases
Rash + shock + fever; present in essentially 100% of confirmed cases
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Fever + neck stiffness + altered mental status; all three present in fewer than half of cases
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The classic triad is fever, neck stiffness and altered mental status, but all three are present in fewer than half of adults — so its absence never excludes the diagnosis. Nearly all patients have at least two of headache, fever, neck stiffness and altered mental state.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: On examination, a patient has involuntary hip and knee flexion when the neck is flexed. Which sign is this?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Brudzinski's sign is involuntary hip/knee flexion on neck flexion; Kernig's sign is pain on knee extension with the hip flexed.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A non-blanching rash that does not fade under pressure is demonstrated using which bedside test, and what does it indicate?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The non-blanching petechial/purpuric rash is demonstrated with the glass/tumbler test (doesn't fade under pressure) and is part of the septicaemic picture, alongside cold peripheries, limb pain and signs of shock.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which presentation should raise suspicion of meningococcal disease in a baby, given how easily it is missed?
options: Non-specific fever, lethargy, poor feeding, a bulging fontanelle, high-pitched cry or hypotonia
Classic neck stiffness and photophobia, as in an older child or adult
An isolated headache with no other systemic features at all
Localised limb weakness with preserved feeding and normal tone
Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs, which are reliable at this age
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Non-specific fever, lethargy, poor feeding, a bulging fontanelle, high-pitched cry or hypotonia
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Babies/young children present atypically and are easily missed: fever, lethargy, poor feeding, bulging fontanelle, high-pitched cry, hypotonia and seizures.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with suspected meningitis has a reduced, fluctuating GCS and papilloedema. What does this mean for lumbar puncture?
options: LP is mandatory before any antibiotics
These are red flags for raised ICP that contraindicate LP
These findings have no bearing on LP
LP should be done only after the rash appears
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: These are red flags for raised ICP that contraindicate LP
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Red flags for raised ICP that contraindicate LP include reduced/fluctuating GCS, focal neurology, seizures, papilloedema and bradycardia + hypertension.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which blood investigation is the key confirmatory test in meningococcal disease, and why is it especially useful?
options: Blood culture, because it is quickest
CRP, because it is specific for meningococcus
Meningococcal PCR, because it remains positive after antibiotics
FBC, because it confirms the organism
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Meningococcal PCR, because it remains positive after antibiotics
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Meningococcal PCR is the key confirmatory blood test and remains positive even after antibiotics have been given.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: When should a lumbar puncture be performed relative to antibiotics in an acutely unwell patient with suspected meningitis?
options: Always before antibiotics, even if obtaining it delays treatment by several hours
Only after the patient has fully recovered and been discharged from hospital
Lumbar puncture is never indicated in suspected bacterial meningitis
Ideally before antibiotics, but never delay antibiotics; defer it in shock, coagulopathy or raised ICP
Only if the blood meningococcal PCR has already come back negative
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Ideally before antibiotics, but never delay antibiotics; defer it in shock, coagulopathy or raised ICP
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Ideally the LP is done before antibiotics, but antibiotics are never delayed for it in an acutely unwell patient. Ask two separate questions. Does the patient need a CT first? Only for signs of raised ICP, new focal neurology or seizures, or a reduced/falling GCS — and a normal CT does not make LP safe if those signs are present. Is LP safe at all right now? Shock, respiratory compromise, coagulopathy/DIC or infection over the site mean defer it until corrected — a CT does not help with any of those. In meningococcal septicaemia with a spreading purpuric rash, LP is not performed: diagnose on blood culture and blood PCR.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A CSF sample is cloudy with markedly raised neutrophils, high protein and a low glucose (CSF:plasma <½). What does this pattern indicate?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Bacterial meningitis shows cloudy/turbid CSF with markedly raised neutrophils, high protein and low glucose (CSF:plasma <½), because bacteria release proteins and consume glucose while the immune system sends neutrophils.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A CSF sample is clear with raised lymphocytes, normal/mildly raised protein and normal glucose. What does this indicate?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Viral meningitis shows clear CSF with raised lymphocytes, normal/mildly raised protein and normal glucose. (TB/fungal shows lymphocytes + high protein + low glucose.)

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A CSF sample shows lymphocytes with high protein and low glucose. Which category does this pattern fit?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: TB/fungal meningitis characteristically shows lymphocytes + high protein + low glucose — distinguishing it from the neutrophil-predominant bacterial pattern and the normal-glucose viral pattern.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the mainstay empirical hospital antibiotic for meningococcal disease, and when is amoxicillin added?
options: Benzylpenicillin alone; add amoxicillin only if there has been recent foreign travel
Amoxicillin alone in all cases, at any age and whatever the risk factors
Ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime); add amoxicillin if Listeria risk (under 3 months, 60 and over, pregnant)
Vancomycin as the mainstay; add amoxicillin routinely in all patients
Ciprofloxacin; add amoxicillin only if the organism is penicillin-resistant
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime); add amoxicillin if Listeria risk (under 3 months, 60 and over, pregnant)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Ceftriaxone or cefotaxime is the empirical mainstay at any age. IV amoxicillin is added for Listeria cover — automatically in babies under 3 months, and in adults aged 60 and over, pregnancy and the immunocompromised — because cephalosporins do not cover Listeria. Vancomycin is added only where penicillin- or cephalosporin-resistant pneumococcus is a risk.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the role of dexamethasone in bacterial meningitis, and when is it given?
options: It eradicates nasopharyngeal carriage, and is given to all close contacts
It is used only in viral meningitis, where antibiotics are not indicated
It replaces antibiotics altogether in patients with true penicillin allergy
It treats septic shock, and is given after the antibiotic course has finished
It reduces complications, especially hearing loss; given with or just before the first antibiotic dose
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: It reduces complications, especially hearing loss; given with or just before the first antibiotic dose
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Dexamethasone reduces neurological complications, especially hearing loss, in bacterial meningitis, with the greatest benefit in pneumococcal disease — given with or just before the first antibiotic dose in anyone over 3 months. It is not routinely given in meningococcal disease (NICE), and antibiotics are never delayed to give it.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Meningococcal disease is a notifiable disease. What does this require of the treating team?
options: Notify only after culture confirmation at 5 days
Report only if the patient dies
Notify the GP at the next routine letter
Notify the local health protection team (UKHSA) by telephone the same day, on clinical suspicion
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Notify the local health protection team (UKHSA) by telephone the same day, on clinical suspicion
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Meningococcal disease is notifiable on clinical suspicion, not on confirmation: telephone the proper officer of the local authority — in practice the local UKHSA health protection team — the same day, so contact tracing and prophylaxis can start within the critical window.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A household member of a confirmed meningococcal case needs prophylaxis. What is the first-line agent, and what is its purpose?
options: Dexamethasone for 4 days; to prevent sensorineural hearing loss in the contact
Amoxicillin for 5 days; to cover Listeria in older or pregnant contacts
Ceftriaxone as a single dose; to treat established invasive disease in the contact
Ciprofloxacin as a single dose, at any age including pregnancy; to eradicate nasopharyngeal carriage
Benzylpenicillin for 7 days; to prevent the non-blanching rash from developing
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Ciprofloxacin as a single dose, at any age including pregnancy; to eradicate nasopharyngeal carriage
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Ciprofloxacin as a single oral dose is first-line for close contacts, at any age including pregnancy, to eradicate nasopharyngeal carriage, with rifampicin as an alternative. The dose is 500 mg for 12 years and over, 250 mg for 5–11 years and 125 mg under 5, given ideally within 24 hours of the case being diagnosed.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with meningococcal septicaemia develops bilateral adrenal haemorrhage leading to adrenal failure. What is this complication called?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome is bilateral adrenal haemorrhage leading to adrenal failure, an acute complication of meningococcal disease alongside septic shock + DIC and raised ICP.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A child recovers from meningococcal disease. What is the commonest chronic sequela, and what follow-up does it require?
options: Epilepsy; a repeat lumbar puncture at 6 weeks to confirm clearance
Neurodevelopmental delay; repeat blood cultures at 6 weeks
Limb loss; no specific follow-up is needed after discharge
Sensorineural hearing loss; a formal hearing assessment within 4 weeks
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Sensorineural hearing loss; a formal hearing assessment within 4 weeks
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Sensorineural hearing loss is the commonest chronic sequela, so every patient needs a formal hearing assessment — ideally before discharge and within 4 weeks of being well enough to test. Early identification matters because cochlear implants work best when placed early. Children are also reviewed by a paediatrician 4–6 weeks after discharge. Note that dexamethasone is NOT routinely used in meningococcal disease; it belongs to bacterial meningitis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which vaccines are part of the prevention of meningococcal disease?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Prevention is MenB in infancy and MenACWY for teenagers and university entrants, plus chemoprophylaxis for close contacts. The separate Hib/MenC dose has been withdrawn from the UK schedule and MenC protection now comes from the adolescent MenACWY programme (UKHSA).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: According to Sepsis-3, what defines sepsis?
options: Two or more SIRS criteria with a documented source
Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Sepsis-3 defines sepsis as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection — it is the body's damaging reaction, not the infection itself.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which of the following correctly defines septic shock under Sepsis-3?
options: Bacteraemia with fever and tachycardia but no evidence of organ dysfunction
Sepsis with a single episode of hypotension that responds promptly to fluids
Any sepsis accompanied by a raised serum lactate, whatever the blood pressure
Sepsis needing vasopressors to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg plus lactate >2 mmol/L despite fluids
Sepsis accompanied by a non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Sepsis needing vasopressors to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg plus lactate >2 mmol/L despite fluids
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Septic shock is sepsis with persisting hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP ≥65 and a lactate >2, despite adequate fluid resuscitation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: How does bacteraemia differ from sepsis?
options: Bacteraemia is bacteria in the blood and may be transient or harmless, distinct from sepsis
Bacteraemia is defined by organ dysfunction
Bacteraemia is always more severe than sepsis
Bacteraemia is the same as septic shock
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Bacteraemia is bacteria in the blood and may be transient or harmless, distinct from sepsis
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Bacteraemia is simply bacteria in the blood, which may be transient or harmless, and is distinct from sepsis (which requires organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What type of shock does sepsis produce, and by what mechanism?
options: Distributive ('warm') shock from widespread vasodilation and capillary leak (NO-mediated)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Distributive ('warm') shock from widespread vasodilation and capillary leak (NO-mediated)
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The cytokine storm drives widespread NO-mediated vasodilation and capillary leak, producing a distributive ('warm') shock.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: In sepsis pathophysiology, what initiates the massive innate immune activation described as the 'cytokine storm'?
options: Direct bacterial toxin damage to myocardium
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Infection releases pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), which trigger massive innate immune activation — the cytokine storm that represents the dysregulation.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which of the following is listed as a risk factor for sepsis through immunocompromise?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Immunocompromise risk factors include chemotherapy, steroids, diabetes, HIV and asplenia; other groups include extremes of age, indwelling devices, recent surgery, pregnancy/peripartum, IVDU and chronic disease.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which tool is used to stratify sepsis risk in adults aged 16 or over in UK acute hospital settings, and why?
options: Lactate alone, because it rules sepsis in
SIRS, because it focuses on organ dysfunction
qSOFA, because it is the most specific
Blood cultures, because they confirm the diagnosis
NEWS2, a track-and-trigger score that is more sensitive than qSOFA and sets the urgency of treatment
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: NEWS2, a track-and-trigger score that is more sensitive than qSOFA and sets the urgency of treatment
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: NEWS2 is the UK standard for adults aged 16 or over in acute hospital, acute mental health and ambulance settings (NICE). Early warning scores are more sensitive for sepsis than qSOFA, which is no longer used as the screening tool, and the NEWS2 score determines how quickly antibiotics must be given — within 1 hour if NEWS2 is 7 or more, 3 hours if 5–6, and 6 hours if 1–4.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which set correctly states the qSOFA criteria, and what is its current role?
options: Temp, HR, WCC; preferred screening tool
GCS <15, RR ≥22, SBP ≤100; no longer recommended as a sole screening tool but useful as a predictor of poor outcome
SpO₂, RR, temperature; the definitive diagnostic test
MAP ≥65, lactate >2, urine output; diagnostic of septic shock
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: GCS <15, RR ≥22, SBP ≤100; no longer recommended as a sole screening tool but useful as a predictor of poor outcome
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: qSOFA comprises GCS <15, RR ≥22 and SBP ≤100 mmHg; ≥2 flags a higher risk of a poor outcome, which is not the same as the NICE "high risk" category. It is no longer recommended as a screening tool (less sensitive than early warning scores), and a low qSOFA does not exclude sepsis.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which of the following is a red flag prompting urgent action in suspected sepsis?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Red flags include altered mentation, SBP ≤90 (or a drop >40 from baseline), RR ≥25, SpO₂ needing O₂, lactate >2, reduced urine output, mottled/ashen skin and a non-blanching rash.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: The Sepsis Six is remembered as 'take 3, give 3'. Which option lists the three 'GIVE' components?
options: Oxygen, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, IV fluids
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Oxygen, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, IV fluids
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The three 'give' components are oxygen (target 94–98%, or 88–92% if at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure), IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, and IV fluids (250 mL of isotonic crystalloid over 10–15 minutes in an adult, reassessing after each bolus); the three 'take' are blood cultures, lactate and urine output. The revised bundle also requires a senior clinician to attend and ongoing monitoring.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the oxygen target in the Sepsis Six for a patient who is a known COPD retainer?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: The standard oxygen target is 94–98%, but 88–92% is used for a COPD retainer.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient is in septic shock. Blood cultures have not yet been obtained. What is the correct approach to antibiotics?
options: Never take blood cultures if shock is present
Withhold antibiotics until sensitivities are known
Give antibiotics only after the lactate result returns
Delay antibiotics until cultures are taken in all cases
Take blood cultures before antibiotics where possible, but do not delay antibiotics for them in shock
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Take blood cultures before antibiotics where possible, but do not delay antibiotics for them in shock
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: In septic shock and high-risk sepsis, delay to effective antibiotics costs lives — give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour. Take cultures before antibiotics where possible, but do not delay antibiotics for them in a shocked patient. In lower-risk patients (NEWS2 5–6, or 1–4) NICE allows 3 and 6 hours respectively, so the diagnosis can be clarified and therapy targeted.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What is the principle guiding fluid resuscitation in sepsis?
options: Give 250 mL of isotonic crystalloid over 10–15 minutes and reassess after each bolus
Restrict all intravenous fluids, as this is distributive shock
Give fluids only once the serum lactate has returned to normal
Withhold all fluids until vasopressors have already been started
Give a fixed large volume of fluid regardless of the response to it
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Give 250 mL of isotonic crystalloid over 10–15 minutes and reassess after each bolus
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Give the first bolus without delay in the high-risk patient — 250 mL of isotonic crystalloid over 10–15 minutes — then reassess. Repeat in 250 mL steps up to 1000 mL in total, then seek senior advice before giving more. Reassess after every bolus: heart rate, blood pressure, capillary refill, conscious level, urine output and repeat lactate. Both under- and over-resuscitation cause harm; if the blood pressure will not hold despite adequate fluid, the answer is vasopressors and critical care, not more litres. In pregnancy the bolus is 500 mL, and in under-16s 10 mL/kg to a maximum of 250 mL (NICE).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with sepsis from an abscess is on appropriate antibiotics but remains unwell. Why might antibiotics alone be insufficient, and what is needed?
options: No further action is needed; await the culture results before deciding
The patient needs vasopressors instead of antibiotics at this stage
Pus under pressure will not clear with antibiotics alone — source control is definitive
Antibiotics never work in sepsis; switch the patient to antiviral therapy
The antibiotic dose is too low; simply increase it and continue to observe
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: Pus under pressure will not clear with antibiotics alone — source control is definitive
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Antibiotics alone are not enough if there is a focus needing physical removal or drainage; a collection of pus under pressure will not clear without source control, which here is drainage (radiological or surgical).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A septic patient has an obstructed, infected kidney. What is the appropriate source control?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Source control for an obstructed + infected kidney is nephrostomy / stent (cross-referenced with renal calculi).

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A septic patient is diagnosed with ascending cholangitis. What is the appropriate source control?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Source control for ascending cholangitis is ERCP biliary decompression.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient with sepsis has an empyema. What is the appropriate source control?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Source control for an empyema is a chest drain; the overarching principle is to find the source and control it.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: After delivering the Sepsis Six, a patient's repeat lactate is not improving. What is the appropriate next step?
options: Repeat the same fluid bolus indefinitely
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Reassess after the Sepsis Six by repeating the lactate; if it is not improving, escalate to HDU/ICU.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: A patient in septic shock has hypotension that does not respond to adequate fluids. What is the first-line vasopressor and the target?
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Fluid-refractory hypotension in septic shock is treated with vasopressors — noradrenaline first-line — to maintain MAP ≥65.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Once culture sensitivities return in a septic patient on empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics, what is the appropriate antimicrobial step?
options: Switch to an antifungal regardless of results
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Antibiotics should be de-escalated from empirical broad-spectrum to the narrowest effective agent once cultures and sensitivities return, in line with stewardship. Review the antibiotic at 48–72 hours against the cultures and the clinical response, switch IV to oral when the patient is improving, and set a stop date.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: Which of the following is described as a long-term complication of sepsis?
options: Reversal of organ dysfunction within minutes
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: Long-term, sepsis can cause post-sepsis syndrome with physical and cognitive impairment; acute complications include septic shock, multi-organ dysfunction, DIC and death.

conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.question: What does a lactate >2 signify in sepsis, and where does this threshold also appear?
options: It confirms bacteraemia; it appears in the SIRS criteria
It marks tissue hypoperfusion; it is the threshold in the septic shock definition
It reflects over-resuscitation; it appears in the fluid protocol
It excludes sepsis; it appears in the qSOFA score
It indicates recovery; it appears in the discharge criteria
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.answer: It marks tissue hypoperfusion; it is the threshold in the septic shock definition
conditions__INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOL.explanation: A lactate over 2 mmol/L marks tissue hypoperfusion, upgrades a moderate-risk patient to high risk, and is the threshold used in the septic shock definition. A lactate over 4 mmol/L marks a markedly higher risk and demands urgent senior and critical care input. Repeat the lactate after resuscitation, as clearance tracks the response. A normal lactate does not exclude sepsis.
